title: Fix fail-open health probes in send readiness and lifecycle status detection
body:
### Summary
This PR fixes a fail-open health-check pattern where runtime/agent probe errors were treated as success.  
In multiple paths, probe exceptions were converted to alive/running = true, which could hide broken checks and produce false confidence.

### Problem
Health probes in two critical paths used catch(() => true):

1. Send/readiness path in session manager:
- Runtime and process probe failures were treated as healthy during readiness checks.
- Result: send flow could proceed even when health checks were broken.

2. Lifecycle status detection:
- Runtime probe failures were treated as alive.
- Result: dead/unreachable sessions could avoid transition to killed.

### Root Cause
Promise rejection from probe methods was mapped to true instead of false.  
That made probe failures indistinguishable from real healthy states.

### Changes
1. Updated probe fallback behavior to fail closed:
- Changed catch(() => true) to catch(() => false) in send/readiness and lifecycle liveness checks.

2. Preserved existing positive behavior:
- Real successful probes still behave exactly the same.
- Only rejection behavior changed.

3. Strengthened readiness semantics:
- Readiness now requires verified liveness, not masked probe failures.

4. (If included in your branch) Improved restored-session timeout behavior:
- Timeout now surfaces as explicit failure instead of silently returning when readiness cannot be confirmed.

### Files Changed
- session-manager.ts
- lifecycle-manager.ts

### Why This Is Safe
- This change only affects exception paths.
- Healthy sessions with successful probes are unaffected.
- It prevents false positives and aligns with fail-closed behavior for control-plane checks.

### Behavioral Impact
Before:
- Probe error could be interpreted as healthy.
- Send/lifecycle decisions could continue on unverified state.

After:
- Probe error is treated as not healthy.
- Send path waits/restores/fails safely.
- Lifecycle can correctly classify unreachable sessions as killed.

### Test Plan
1. Session manager:
- When runtime probe throws, send path does not treat session as healthy.
- When process probe throws, send path does not treat session as healthy.
- Readiness path no longer advances due to masked probe exceptions.

2. Lifecycle manager:
- When runtime probe throws during determine status, session transitions to killed path.

3. Regression checks:
- Normal healthy sessions still pass readiness and lifecycle checks.
- No behavior change when probes resolve true/false normally.

### Risk / Rollback
Risk is low and localized to failure handling.  
Rollback is straightforward by reverting these fallback changes in the two files above.

---


Closes #1067

title: Fix/gitlab self hosted
body:
## Summary

Closes #1021

This change improves GitLab support for local and self-hosted setups in Agent Orchestrator.

It fixes GitLab plugin resolution across the CLI and web dashboard, improves GitLab issue handling for modern `work_items` URLs, preserves correct hostname/protocol behavior for self-hosted GitLab instances, and makes self-hosted `glab` command routing more reliable by setting `GLAB_HOST` when a GitLab host is configured.

## What Changed

- Added GitLab tracker and SCM plugin support to CLI and web dependency/registration paths.
- Fixed GitLab tracker issue parsing to support both:
  - `/-/issues/<id>`
  - `/-/work_items/<id>`
- Fixed issue URL generation for self-hosted GitLab:
  - preserves explicit protocol when provided
  - uses `http://` for localhost-style hosts
- Added GitLab label removal support via `removeLabels`.
- Added `GLAB_HOST` configuration for self-hosted GitLab in:
  - `packages/plugins/scm-gitlab/src/index.ts`
  - `packages/plugins/tracker-gitlab/src/index.ts`
- Updated dashboard/web service bootstrap so GitLab-backed projects load correctly.
- Improved dashboard preflight validation to catch missing `.next/server/vendor-chunks` artifacts before runtime.

## Why This Matters

Before this change, GitLab-configured projects could fail in several ways:

- GitLab plugins were not always resolved correctly in branch-local CLI and web paths.
- Local GitLab issue creation could return `work_items` URLs that AO did not understand.
- Self-hosted GitLab issue URLs could be generated with the wrong protocol/host shape.
- GitLab issue label removal paths were incomplete.
- `ao start` could pass preflight and then fail later with missing production bundle artifacts.

After this change, GitLab issue and status flows are more reliable for local/self-hosted testing, which makes it practical to validate a real GitLab-backed AO workflow.

## Validated

- `pnpm build`
- `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-plugin-tracker-gitlab test -- test/index.test.ts`
- `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-cli test -- __tests__/lib/preflight.test.ts __tests__/lib/plugins.test.ts`
- `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-web test -- src/__tests__/services.test.ts`
- `node packages/cli/dist/index.js doctor`
- `node packages/cli/dist/index.js status --project test-gitlab --json`
- `node packages/cli/dist/index.js verify --list --project test-gitlab`

## Notes

- This improves GitLab readiness significantly, especially for local/self-hosted testing.
- It does not yet provide full GitLab parity for every workflow.
- Known remaining gaps include:
  - `ao session claim-pr` support for GitLab existing-MR takeover
  - `ao review-check` still being GitHub-specific
  - some GitHub-specific wording/UI links in the dashboard

## Suggested Merge Intent

This PR should be treated as an incremental GitLab integration improvement that unblocks meaningful end-to-end testing on a real GitLab-hosted project with a real issue, MR, and CI pipeline.

title: document remote-access setup
body:
## Context

It's currently painful to access the AO dashboard from a mobile device (e.g. via Tailscale). The dashboard HTML loads fine, but the in-browser terminal (`DirectTerminal` / xterm.js) silently fails to connect because it lives on a separate WebSocket port, and the existing config knobs aren't documented or discoverable.

This issue tracks improving the mobile/remote experience and adding docs for the working setup.

## What we hit while debugging (Tailscale on macOS)

Setting up `tailscale serve` for `localhost:3001` was the obvious first step:

```bash
sudo tailscale serve --bg --set-path=/ http://localhost:3001
```

That loads the dashboard on mobile, but the terminal stays stuck on "connecting". A few non-obvious things made this hard to figure out:

1. **The terminal WebSocket runs on a different port from Next.js.** The Next.js dashboard listens on `:3001`, but `direct-terminal-ws` is a standalone server on `DIRECT_TERMINAL_PORT` (default `14801`). On Tailscale, mobile only sees what we explicitly proxy — so the WS connection from xterm.js targets a host that isn't reachable.

2. **The required port is dynamic.** When more than one `pnpm dev` instance is running, the terminal port paired with `:3001` may not be `14801`. The only reliable way to discover it is `curl -s http://localhost:3001/api/runtime/terminal`, which returns e.g. `{\"terminalPort\":\"14802\",\"directTerminalPort\":\"14803\",\"proxyWsPath\":null}`. This isn't documented anywhere.

3. **The client already supports a same-origin proxy path, but it isn't surfaced.** `packages/web/src/components/DirectTerminal.tsx:139-157` has logic for three modes:
   - Explicit `proxyWsPath` (env var `TERMINAL_WS_PATH` / `NEXT_PUBLIC_TERMINAL_WS_PATH`)
   - Implicit \`/ao-terminal-ws\` when the page is loaded over standard ports (80/443) — this is the path the mobile-via-Tailscale case actually uses
   - Direct connection to `host:directTerminalPort/ws` for local dev

   None of this is mentioned in CLAUDE.md or any README, so users have no way to know they need to expose `/ao-terminal-ws` separately.

4. **The WS server requires path `/ws`, but `tailscale serve --set-path=` strips the mount prefix before forwarding.** This is the killer. `direct-terminal-ws.ts:128` creates the `WebSocketServer` with `path: \"/ws\"`, so a request to the bare backend (`/?session=...`) returns 404. With Tailscale serve, `--set-path=/ao-terminal-ws` forwards to `localhost:14803/?session=...` and gets a 404. The fix is to put `/ws` on the *backend* URL so Tailscale rewrites it:

   ```bash
   sudo tailscale serve --bg --set-path=/ao-terminal-ws http://localhost:14803/ws
   ```

   We only figured this out by curling the backend directly with WS upgrade headers and comparing to a curl through the Tailscale proxy.

## Working recipe (Tailscale)

For anyone hitting this in the meantime:

```bash
# 1. Discover the terminal WS port for the dev instance you care about
curl -s http://localhost:3001/api/runtime/terminal
# → {\"terminalPort\":\"14802\",\"directTerminalPort\":\"14803\",\"proxyWsPath\":null}

# 2. Mount both behind the same Tailscale HTTPS host
sudo tailscale serve --bg --set-path=/                http://localhost:3001
sudo tailscale serve --bg --set-path=/ao-terminal-ws  http://localhost:<directTerminalPort>/ws

# 3. Verify
tailscale serve status

# 4. Open https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ on your phone
```

To tear down: `sudo tailscale serve reset`.

## Suggested improvements

In rough order of impact:

- [x] **Document the remote-access / mobile setup** in the README or a `docs/remote-access.md`. Cover Tailscale, generic reverse proxy (nginx/Caddy), and the `/ao-terminal-ws` path requirement.
- [ ] **Make `direct-terminal-ws` reachable through a single port.** Options:
  - Have Next.js itself proxy `/ao-terminal-ws` to the local WS port (custom server or middleware), so exposing port 3001 alone is sufficient.
  - Or have `pnpm dev` print the exact `tailscale serve` / `caddy` snippet on startup, with the right port substituted.
- [ ] **Drop the `/ws` path requirement on the WS server**, or make it configurable. Removing the `path: \"/ws\"` constraint in `direct-terminal-ws.ts` would make the server accept connections on any path, removing the `--set-path=/ao-terminal-ws http://.../ws` footgun entirely. The server already only checks `?session=` from the query string.
- [ ] **Mobile UI polish for the terminal view** — current `DirectTerminal` layout assumes desktop viewport sizes. Worth a separate pass on touch input, virtual keyboard handling, font scaling, and the fullscreen toggle.
- [ ] **Surface a single \"how do I access this remotely\" hint** in the dashboard footer or settings, with a copy-pasteable command for Tailscale users.

## Notes

- Discovered while accessing AO from a phone via Tailscale on a `prateeks-macbook-pro` host.
- Reproduced with two `pnpm dev` instances running simultaneously, which is what made the dynamic-port issue obvious.

title: Prevent macOS idle sleep while AO is running (out-of-the-box remote access)
body:
## Problem

When AO is running on a Mac and the user walks away, macOS idle-sleeps the system after the configured timeout. As soon as that happens, anything depending on AO going through the network goes dark — most visibly, accessing the dashboard and terminal remotely (e.g. via Tailscale) from a phone.

This is a real out-of-the-box pain point: AO is meant to run on a random user's Mac, so we can't rely on the user knowing to wrap `ao start` in `caffeinate`, set `pmset` flags, or fiddle with Energy Saver. It needs to Just Work, on battery, without permanent system changes.

Related: #1071 (improving the mobile/Tailscale experience overall — this issue is the \"keep the host awake\" half of that story).

## Recommendation

Have AO hold a power assertion itself for the duration of its lifetime. macOS has a built-in tool for exactly this and the contract is dead simple:

```
caffeinate -i -w <pid>
```

- `-i` creates an idle-sleep prevention assertion (valid on battery — unlike `-s` which is AC-only).
- `-w <pid>` ties the assertion's lifetime to a watched pid. When that pid exits — cleanly, on crash, or via `kill -9` — the kernel automatically releases the assertion.

So AO spawns `caffeinate` once at startup with its own pid, detaches it, and forgets. No cleanup logic, no lifecycle bugs possible, the assertion dies with AO under all conditions.

### Sketch

```ts
// e.g. packages/cli/src/util/preventSleep.ts
import { spawn } from \"node:child_process\";

export function preventIdleSleep(): { release: () => void } | null {
  if (process.platform !== \"darwin\") return null; // no-op on linux for now
  const child = spawn(\"caffeinate\", [\"-i\", \"-w\", String(process.pid)], {
    stdio: \"ignore\",
    detached: true,
  });
  child.unref(); // don't keep the event loop alive
  return { release: () => child.kill() };
}
```

Call this from the `ao start` / dashboard supervisor entrypoint — wherever the long-running orchestrator process lives that owns the Next.js server, the WS servers, and the lifecycle loop. After the migration off `pnpm dev` to a single supervisor process, there's exactly one obvious place for this hook.

## What this solves and what it doesn't

| Scenario | Fixed? |
|---|---|
| User walks away, Mac is open, idle timer kicks in | ✅ |
| Mac on battery power | ✅ (`-i` works on battery) |
| AO crashes or is `kill -9`'d | ✅ (kernel auto-releases via `-w`) |
| Lid closed, no external display | ❌ — macOS enforces lid-close sleep at the EC level; no userspace assertion can override it. The only workarounds are clamshell mode (external power + display + input) or a kext, both off the table. |
| Linux | N/A — short term, no-op. Long term, the equivalent is `systemd-inhibit --what=idle --who=ao --why=\"serving dashboard\" sleep infinity` or a D-Bus inhibit call. Worth tracking as a follow-up. |

## Battery impact

`caffeinate -i` does **not** prevent display sleep — only idle *system* sleep. The screen still dims and turns off as normal; the Mac just doesn't suspend. The marginal cost of holding an idle assertion is small relative to what AO is already doing (Next.js + WS servers + agent sessions), so it's a reasonable default.

That said, we should give users an opt-out via `agent-orchestrator.yaml`:

```yaml
power:
  preventIdleSleep: true   # default on macOS
```

…and skip the spawn if it's `false`. Nothing fancier needed.

## Docs

Once this lands, the README / remote-access docs should be honest about the lid-close limitation: \"AO will keep your Mac awake while it is running, as long as the lid is open. If you want remote access while traveling with the lid closed, use clamshell mode (external power + display + input device).\" That's the whole story.

## Tasks

- [ ] Add `preventIdleSleep()` helper (macOS via `caffeinate -i -w <pid>`, no-op elsewhere)
- [ ] Wire it into the `ao start` / dashboard supervisor entrypoint
- [ ] Add `power.preventIdleSleep` config option (default `true` on darwin)
- [ ] Document in README / remote-access docs, including the lid-close caveat
- [ ] (Follow-up) Linux equivalent via `systemd-inhibit` / D-Bus inhibit

title: bug: lifecycle worker kills sessions with no audit trail (session id + reason)
body:
## Summary

When the lifecycle manager transitions a session to `status=killed` (via runtime probe, agent process check, stuck detection, PR-closed cleanup, etc.), it does not log the session ID together with the reason for the kill. The status transition *is* logged, but only with `{oldStatus, newStatus}` — no `reason`, no clue which code path marked it killed. Result: after a session mysteriously dies, `grep <session-id> lifecycle-worker.log` returns nothing, and reconstructing why requires forensic work across multiple files.

## Reproduction

1. `ao spawn <issue>` — spawn a worker, confirm it starts working and writes to `.ao/activity.jsonl`.
2. Wait for it to die (ours died within ~8 min on a trigger we couldn't identify).
3. `ao session ls` shows it as `[killed]`.
4. `grep <session-id> ~/.agent-orchestrator/<hash>-<project>/lifecycle-worker.log` → **zero matches.**

Concrete instance from today: `ao-140` spawned for issue #1048 went from active to `status=killed` in under 8 minutes. Metadata file showed `status=killed`. `lifecycle-worker.log` had zero occurrences of `ao-140`.

## Evidence — code paths that silently mark a session killed

### The only transition log has no `reason` field

`packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts:1199-1208`:
```typescript
observer.recordOperation({
  metric: "lifecycle_poll",
  operation: "lifecycle.transition",
  outcome: "success",
  correlationId,
  projectId: session.projectId,
  sessionId: session.id,
  data: { oldStatus, newStatus },   // ← no `reason` field
  level: transitionLogLevel(newStatus),
});
```

This log DOES carry the session ID, but only records *that* a transition happened — not *why*. And it only fires from the central transition point, so kills that short-circuit elsewhere don't reach it.

### Multiple kill paths return `"killed"` with no local logging

Each of these returns `"killed"` without emitting a log identifying which branch was taken:

- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts:374` — runtime probe returned dead
- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts:404` — agent exited
- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts:427` — `isProcessRunning` returned false
- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts:512` — PR closed

### `enrichSessionData` silently mutates to `killed` with zero log output

`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:892`:
```typescript
if (!alive) {
  session.status = "killed";
  session.activity = "exited";
  return;
}
```

No log statement at all. A session can flip to `killed` here and leave no trace.

## Expected behavior

When a session is killed, the lifecycle manager should emit a structured log entry containing:
- session ID
- old status
- new status
- **reason** (which kill path: `"runtime_dead"`, `"agent_exited"`, `"pr_closed"`, `"stuck_timeout"`, `"probe_failed"`, etc.)
- Relevant ancillary data (`processAge`, `lastActivityTs`, etc.) where cheap to include

This would make `grep <session-id> lifecycle-worker.log` the first-line triage tool it obviously should be.

## Proposed fix

1. Add a `reason: string` parameter to the kill decision points in `lifecycle-manager.ts` (lines 374/404/427/512) and plumb it into the `lifecycle.transition` log at 1199-1208 via a new field in `data`.
2. Add a log statement in `session-manager.ts:892` so silent kills from `enrichSessionData` are also captured (or route them through the central transition path so they get the existing log for free).
3. Optional: emit a `session.killed` notifier event with the same structured data so Slack/Discord notifiers can surface it too.

## Related

- #1067 — same area of the code (health check exceptions masked as `alive`). Fixing #1067 will make the observability gap worse if unaddressed: more sessions will be killed correctly, but the kill path still won't say why.

## Environment

- Encountered on `main` at `origin/main` (~`5145dceb`)
- Platform: Linux
- Agent plugin in use when observed: opencode (but the lifecycle-manager code is agent-agnostic, so reproduction should be identical with other agent plugins)

title: bug: ao send reports "Message sent and processing" against status=killed sessions
body:
## Summary

`ao send <session> <message>` prints `Message sent and processing` and exits 0 even when the target session is already in `status=killed`. Under the hood it attempts a restore, the restore silently fails, and the success string is printed anyway. Callers cannot distinguish a real delivery from a no-op.

## Reproduction

1. Spawn a worker: `ao spawn 1234` → say it becomes `ao-N`.
2. Kill it: `ao session kill ao-N` (or let it die on its own; see #1073).
3. Confirm `ao session ls` shows `ao-N` as `[killed]`.
4. `ao send ao-N "hello"` → prints `Message sent and processing`, exits 0.
5. The message is never delivered anywhere.

Encountered in the wild today: I sent a strategy prompt to `ao-140` (which was already `status=killed` in its metadata). `ao send` reported "Message sent and processing" and I believed it. Only later, when the agent clearly wasn't responding, did I inspect the metadata and realize the session had been dead the whole time.

## Evidence

### 1. The CLI prints success without a status pre-check

`packages/cli/src/commands/send.ts:186-189`:
```typescript
if (existingSession && sessionManager) {
  await sessionManager.send(session, message);
  console.log(chalk.green("Message sent and processing"));
  return;
}
```

No check for `session.status === "killed"` before calling `sessionManager.send()`, and the return value of `send()` is discarded.

### 2. `isRestorable()` treats `killed` as restorable

`packages/core/src/types.ts:113-144`:

- `TERMINAL_STATUSES` includes `"killed"`
- `NON_RESTORABLE_STATUSES = ["merged"]`  (only `merged`)
- `isRestorable(session)` returns `true` when the session is terminal AND not in `NON_RESTORABLE_STATUSES`

So for a `killed` session, `isRestorable()` returns `true`.

### 3. `send()` routes `killed` sessions through the restore path

`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:2010-2055` — `prepareSession()` gate:
```typescript
if (forceRestore || isRestorable(normalized)) {
  return restoreForDelivery(...);
}
```

A `killed` session takes the restore branch.

### 4. Restore failures are swallowed

`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:2103` catches restore failures without propagating them back to the CLI caller. `send()` returns, the CLI prints "Message sent and processing" unconditionally.

## Expected behavior

Either:

**Option A — refuse** to send to a `killed` session:
> Error: Session ao-N is killed. Run `ao session restore ao-N` to revive it first.

**Option B — honor the restore-then-send intent but actually verify delivery**: if the restore fails, print a clear error and exit non-zero. Only print "Message sent and processing" on confirmed delivery.

Option B is probably more consistent with the current design (killed sessions *are* considered restorable), but the current silent-failure reporting has to go either way.

## Proposed fix sketch

- `send.ts:186-189` — branch on `sessionManager.send()`'s return value (currently discarded) and fail-loudly when delivery was not confirmed.
- `session-manager.ts:2103` — let restore failures propagate (or return a structured `{delivered: false, reason}` result) instead of swallowing them.
- Optional: tighten `NON_RESTORABLE_STATUSES` in `types.ts` if any terminal statuses should never be restored in practice (\"errored\" maybe?).

## Related

- #1067 — complementary failure mode. #1067 fixes health-check exceptions being treated as alive in the send/lifecycle paths. This bug is the mirror case: the session is *already* and *correctly* marked `killed`, but `ao send` still reports success and exits 0.
- #1073 — related observability gap (lifecycle kills without audit trail). That one made this bug much harder to notice, because the first signal was "message was sent but agent never responded" and we had no log to correlate with.

## Environment

- `main` at `origin/main` (~`5145dceb`)
- Linux, Node 20

title: fix(cli): reuse and restore orchestrator sessions across ao start cycles
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1048 — `ao start` was always allocating a new `{prefix}-orchestrator-N` instead of reattaching to the previous one, and the dashboard was linking to a stale legacy id (`{projectId}-orchestrator`) that the CLI never used.

Three coordinated changes:

- **Reuse-or-restore in `runStartup`** — list the project's orchestrators, partition into **live** (`!isTerminalSession`) and **restorable** (`isTerminalSession && isRestorable`) buckets, pick the most-recently-active candidate across both. Live → reuse the id in place. Restorable → call `sm.restore()` so the original numbered id is preserved (no fresh `-N` allocated). Only spawn when both buckets are empty. Restored sessions get an explicit `(restored)` marker in the CLI summary so the resurfaced id isn't a surprise.
- **Drop the phantom `${prefix}-orchestrator` id** from `runStartup` and `registerStop`. Every URL print, browser-open target, and kill target now uses the real numbered id. `ao stop` resolves the actual orchestrator via `sm.list(projectId)` (with the same `isOrchestratorSession` filter the dashboard uses) and reports the killed id via `console.log` so non-TTY callers and tests can see it.
- **Tighten `isOrchestratorSession`** in `packages/core/src/types.ts`. The bare `endsWith("-orchestrator")` shape now only counts when `metadata.role === "orchestrator"` is explicitly stamped. Session-manager's `repairSingleSessionMetadataOnRead` already backfills `role: orchestrator` for legacy records loaded via `sm.list()`, so the only records that get rejected are truly abandoned bare ids — exactly the ones that were leaking into the dashboard's orchestrator list with the wrong prefix.

## Why the bug existed

`runStartup` already had a reuse path, but it relied on `sm.list` returning the previous orchestrator as non-terminal. Once the orchestrator's tmux pane was destroyed, `enrichSessionWithRuntimeState` mutated `status` to `killed`, the `!isTerminalSession` filter dropped it, and the CLI fell through to spawn a new id every time. Meanwhile `ao stop` was calling `sm.kill("${prefix}-orchestrator")` against a phantom (no-N) id that never matched a real numbered session, so the actual orchestrator stayed alive on disk while the CLI kept allocating new numbers (`-3`, `-4`, …).

The dashboard amplified the confusion: stale `{projectId}-orchestrator` records (no number, no role metadata, no runtime handle to liveness-check) survived `isOrchestratorSession` via the `endsWith("-orchestrator")` fallback and outranked the real numbered sessions in `listDashboardOrchestrators`. The dashboard's "orchestrator" link pointed at the legacy id while the CLI printed a numbered id — exactly the mismatch the issue reported.

## Tests

- `packages/core/src/__tests__/types.test.ts` — regression tests for `isOrchestratorSession` rejecting bare `{projectId}-orchestrator` ids without role metadata, and accepting them when role is stamped. Existing positive cases for numbered ids and explicit `role: "orchestrator"` still pass.
- `packages/cli/__tests__/commands/start.test.ts` —
  - 4 new orchestrator-selection tests: restore-on-killed, ignore-stale-bare, cross-bucket recency picking, and live-multi reuse with the `N other session(s) available` suffix.
  - Updated `ao stop` tests to mock `sm.list` (the new lookup path) and assert the real numbered id gets killed.
  - Re-prime web-dir mocks in `beforeEach` so `findFreePort`/`isPortAvailable` aren't wiped by `vi.restoreAllMocks()` between tests (was masking `http://localhost:undefined` failures).
- `packages/web/src/lib/__tests__/serialize.test.ts` — 3 new `listDashboardOrchestrators` tests: stale-bare exclusion, numbered-live inclusion, role-stamped legacy inclusion.
- `packages/web/src/__tests__/orchestrators.test.tsx` — updated existing test to use a numbered orchestrator id with explicit role metadata.

All three test suites pass:
- `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-cli test` → 315 passed
- `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-core test` → 580 passed
- `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-web test` → 553 passed

## Out of scope

- No archival of zombie orchestrators — risky and orthogonal, better as a follow-up.
- The numbering scheme (`-N`) is unchanged. Reuse always wins over allocation, so under normal use the number stops growing.
- The web `POST /api/orchestrators` spawn path is left alone — it's an explicit user action and should still create a fresh one.

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-cli test`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-core test`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-web test`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-cli typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-core typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @composio/ao-web typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm eslint` on changed files
- [ ] Manual smoke test: run `ao start`, observe `int-orchestrator-1` is created. Run `ao stop`, then `ao start` again — verify the same `-1` id is reused (or restored if its tmux pane died) instead of jumping to `-2`. Verify the dashboard's "orchestrator" link matches the CLI-printed id.
- [ ] Manual smoke test: kill the orchestrator's tmux pane manually, then `ao start` — verify it logs `Restoring orchestrator session: int-orchestrator-1` instead of allocating `-2`.

title: feat: add Cursor agent CLI support (#1060)
body:
## Summary
Implements Cursor agent CLI support as requested in issue #1060.

This PR adds a new agent plugin for Cursor CLI following the established agent plugin architecture. The implementation follows the same patterns as existing agents (Aider, Codex, Claude Code) and provides full integration with the AO dashboard.

## Changes
- ✅ New plugin: `packages/plugins/agent-cursor/`
- ✅ Added to CLI dependencies for plugin discovery
- ✅ Full `Agent` interface implementation with all required methods
- ✅ Comprehensive test suite (52 passing tests)
- ✅ Activity detection with 6-state cascade (spawning → active ↔ ready → idle → exited, with waiting_input/blocked)
- ✅ PATH wrapper integration for PR tracking in dashboard
- ✅ TypeScript strict mode compliant

## Implementation Details

### Methods Implemented
| Method | Implementation |
|--------|---------------|
| getLaunchCommand | Generates cursor command with permission flags (--auto-approve), model selection, and system prompts |
| getEnvironment | Sets AO_SESSION_ID, AO_ISSUE_ID, PATH with ~/.ao/bin prepended, and GH_PATH |
| detectActivity | Classifies terminal output: idle (prompts), waiting_input (Y/N, Continue?), blocked (errors), active (default) |
| getActivityState | 4-tier cascade: JSONL actionable states → git commits → .cursor mtime → JSONL fallback with age decay |
| isProcessRunning | tmux TTY-based detection + PID signal-0 check, matches both cursor and .cursor process names |
| setupWorkspaceHooks | Delegates to setupPathWrapperWorkspace for git/gh wrapper installation |
| getSessionInfo | Extracts summary from .cursor/chat.md if available, truncates to 120 chars |
| recordActivity | Delegates to shared recordTerminalActivity for JSONL writes |
| postLaunchSetup | Ensures hooks are installed after launch |
| getRestoreCommand | Returns null (Cursor doesn't support session resume) |

### Activity Detection Architecture
Implements the mandatory 4-tier cascade from CLAUDE.md:
1. **Process check** — returns exited if not running
2. **Actionable states** — checkActivityLogState() for waiting_input/blocked from JSONL
3. **Native signals** — git commits (last 60s), .cursor directory mtime
4. **JSONL entry fallback** — getActivityFallbackState() with age-based decay (active → ready → idle)

This ensures the dashboard always shows correct activity state even when native signals fail.

### Testing Coverage
All mandatory getActivityState tests from CLAUDE.md:
- ✅ Returns exited when process is not running
- ✅ Returns waiting_input from JSONL when agent is at a permission prompt
- ✅ Returns blocked from JSONL when agent hit an error
- ✅ Returns active from JSONL entry fallback when native signal fails (fresh entry)
- ✅ Returns idle from JSONL entry fallback when native signal fails (old entry with age decay)
- ✅ Returns null when both native signal and JSONL are unavailable

Plus full coverage of:
- Command generation with all permission modes (permissionless, auto-edit, suggest)
- Process detection on both tmux and process runtimes
- Terminal output pattern matching for all Cursor-specific prompts
- Environment setup with PATH wrapping
- Session info extraction

## Testing
```bash
pnpm --filter @composio/ao-plugin-agent-cursor build
pnpm --filter @composio/ao-plugin-agent-cursor test
pnpm --filter @composio/ao-plugin-agent-cursor typecheck
```

All checks pass:
- ✅ 52/52 tests passing
- ✅ TypeScript typecheck clean
- ✅ Build successful

## Notes
- Pattern follows Aider agent (PATH wrappers + AO Activity JSONL) rather than Codex (native JSONL), as Cursor CLI likely doesn't have built-in session management
- Process regex matches both cursor and .cursor to handle installations with dot-prefixed binaries
- Command flags (--auto-approve, --model, --prompt, --system) are assumed based on typical CLI conventions — may need adjustment when Cursor CLI is available for testing
- Dashboard PR tracking requires the agent to actually call gh pr create — PATH wrappers will capture it automatically

## Checklist
- [x] Implementation follows existing agent plugin patterns
- [x] All required Agent interface methods implemented
- [x] Comprehensive test suite with all mandatory getActivityState tests
- [x] TypeScript strict mode compliant (no any types)
- [x] Follows conventions from CLAUDE.md (PascalCase, camelCase, consistent imports)
- [x] Added to CLI package dependencies
- [x] Commit message follows conventional commits format

Closes #1060

title: feat(cli): add --preview-prompt flag to ao spawn
body:
## Problem

When iterating on agent configuration (agentRules, agentRulesFile) or debugging unexpected agent behavior, there is no way to inspect the full prompt that will be sent to the agent before a session is spawned. The only way to see the composed prompt is to start a live session and check from there.

This creates friction for developers who want to:

- Verify that agentRules and agentRulesFile content is being picked up correctly
- Check how issue context will appear in the prompt before committing to a spawn
- Understand what lineage and sibling context gets injected when using decompose
- Debug agent behavior by inspecting the exact instructions being sent

## Proposed Solution

Add a --preview-prompt flag to ao spawn that builds and prints the full composed prompt without creating a session or starting a lifecycle worker.

Example usage:

    ao spawn --preview-prompt
    ao spawn INT-42 --preview-prompt

The output would show the layered prompt (base + project context + user rules + decomposition context if applicable) and note that tracker issue context is not fetched in preview mode since that requires a network call.

## Implementation

The change is additive and isolated to packages/cli/src/commands/spawn.ts. The buildPrompt function is already exported from @composio/ao-core and used internally by the session manager, so no core changes are needed.

title: fix(web): terminal auth and ownership checks for web terminal access
body:
This PR fixes issue #975 by tightening authorization around web terminal access and keeping the scope limited to the terminal path.

  Before this change, terminal access could be opened too loosely from the browser side. The fix introduces short-lived signed terminal grants that are issued by the
  authenticated web app and verified by the terminal/mux server before any tmux attach happens. That makes terminal access depend on both session identity and ownership,
  instead of trusting a raw session ID alone.

  What changed:

  - Added a server-side terminal auth module that issues and verifies signed, short-lived terminal grants.
  - Added /api/sessions/[id]/terminal so the web app can request an authorized terminal grant for a specific session.
  - Updated the mux terminal open flow to require the signed token and reject unauthorized or stale requests.
  - Updated the browser terminal client to fetch, cache, and refresh grants during reconnects instead of reopening terminals with only a session ID.
  - Moved the legacy terminal URL flow onto the same authorized path so both terminal entry points use the same checks.
  - Preserved existing server/build behavior outside this area and avoided unrelated config churn.

  Regression and hardening work included:

  - Guarded against stale terminal reopen races when a terminal is closed while auth is still in flight.
  - Ignored or actively closed stale opened acknowledgements from the server so closed terminals are not re-tracked client-side.
  - Kept the websocket formatting/build-path changes minimal to avoid the concerns previously raised on the earlier closed PR.
  - Deduplicated shared terminal port normalization used by the related route handlers.

  Validation:

  - Ran targeted web tests covering terminal auth issuance/verification, mux websocket behavior, provider reconnect/auth flow, and API route behavior.
  - Re-ran focused tests for follow-up review fixes in MuxProvider and the terminal API routes.
  - Confirmed the branch remained mergeable against main.

refactor(core): simplify overengineered base agent prompt
body:
## Summary

Simplifies `BASE_AGENT_PROMPT` in `packages/core/src/prompt-builder.ts` by removing instructions that duplicate AO's automated behavior or state generic knowledge that modern coding agents already possess.

Closes #1037

## Changes

### Removed redundant instructions

| Removed | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| "Always create a feature branch from the default branch" | AO computes branch name in `session-manager.ts:986` and creates worktree on it via `workspace-worktree`. Agent is already on a feature branch at spawn. Also contradicts `claim-pr` flow which checks out an existing PR branch. |
| "Create a branch named so that it auto-links to the issue tracker (e.g. feat/{issueId})" | Same as above — branch is pre-created. The `feat/{issueId}` example may not match tracker-specific naming (e.g., `linear-123`). |
| "Use conventional commit messages (feat:, fix:, etc.)" | Standard practice — modern agents follow this by default. |
| PR Best Practices section (clear titles, link issues, respond to comments) | Generic advice any LLM already knows. Can be specified via `agentRules` if project needs custom conventions. |

### Clarified vague instructions

| Before | After | Reason |
|--------|-------|--------|
| "You are running inside a managed session" | "Your workspace is isolated on a dedicated branch" | Concrete operational fact the agent can rely on, not vague framing. |
| "orchestrator will send you the failures" / "orchestrator will forward their comments" | "AO automatically forwards CI failures and review comments" | Clarifies this is automated reaction-driven behavior, not manual operator intervention. Prevents agent from expecting human involvement. |

## Before/After

**Before (20 lines):**
```
## Session Lifecycle
- You are running inside a managed session. Focus on the assigned task.
- When you finish your work, create a PR and push it. The orchestrator will handle CI monitoring and review routing.
- If you're told to take over or continue work on an existing PR, run `ao session claim-pr <pr-number-or-url>` from inside this session before making changes.
- If CI fails, the orchestrator will send you the failures — fix them and push again.
- If reviewers request changes, the orchestrator will forward their comments — address each one, push fixes, and reply to the comments.

## Git Workflow
- Always create a feature branch from the default branch (never commit directly to it).
- Use conventional commit messages (feat:, fix:, chore:, etc.).
- Push your branch and create a PR when the implementation is ready.
- Keep PRs focused — one issue per PR.

## PR Best Practices
- Write a clear PR title and description explaining what changed and why.
- Link the issue in the PR description so it auto-closes when merged.
- If the repo has CI checks, make sure they pass before requesting review.
- Respond to every review comment, even if just to acknowledge it.
```

**After (11 lines):**
```
## Session Lifecycle
- Your workspace is isolated on a dedicated branch. Focus on the assigned task.
- When you finish your work, create a PR and push it. AO monitors your PR and handles CI/review routing.
- To take over an existing PR, run `ao session claim-pr <pr-number-or-url>` before making changes.
- AO automatically forwards CI failures and review comments — fix issues and push updates as instructed.

## Git Workflow
- Push your branch and create a PR when the implementation is ready.
- Keep PRs focused — one issue per PR.
```

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm build` passes
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` passes  
- [x] `pnpm test` passes (updated tests to match new prompt)

title: Github rate limits still broken
body:
# GitHub API Layer Redesign

> Complete design document for optimizing AO's GitHub API interactions — failure analysis,
> centralized gatekeeper (GhClient), and lifecycle manager optimizations.
>
> **Scope:** `scm-github`, `tracker-github`, `graphql-batch`, `lifecycle-manager`, `session-manager`, web API routes
>
> **Goal:** Eliminate rate limit failures, reduce API calls by ~94% in worst case, and add resilience
> (circuit breaker, retry, concurrency control) to all GitHub interactions.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [Executive Summary](#1-executive-summary)
2. [Current System — How It Works Today](#2-current-system--how-it-works-today)
   - [Polling Architecture](#polling-architecture)
   - [The 4 Paths to GitHub](#the-4-paths-to-github)
   - [Cost Model (50 Sessions)](#cost-model-50-sessions)
3. [Failure Analysis — All 22 Failure Points](#3-failure-analysis--all-22-failure-points)
   - [Foundational Problem — No Centralized Control](#foundational-problem--no-centralized-control)
   - [Critical Failures (F-01, F-02, F-04, F-10, F-11)](#critical-failures)
   - [High Severity Failures (F-03, F-05, F-06, F-07, F-08)](#high-severity-failures)
   - [Medium Severity Failures (F-09, F-12, F-13, F-14, F-15, F-16, F-17, F-20, F-21)](#medium-severity-failures)
   - [Low Severity Failures (F-18, F-19, F-22)](#low-severity-failures)
   - [Cascade Failure Scenario](#cascade-failure-scenario)
4. [Redesign — What Changes](#4-redesign--what-changes)
   - [Overview](#overview)
   - [Change 1: Eliminate the Fallback Path](#change-1-eliminate-the-fallback-path)
   - [Change 2: Review Backlog — `since` Parameter and Bypass Removal](#change-2-review-backlog--since-parameter-and-bypass-removal)
   - [Change 3: GhClient — Centralized Gatekeeper](#change-3-ghclient--centralized-gatekeeper)
   - [Change 4: ETag Guard Optimization](#change-4-etag-guard-optimization)
   - [Change 5: Move verifyGhCLI to Startup](#change-5-move-verifyghecli-to-startup)
   - [Change 6: Reduce GraphQL Batch Node Count](#change-6-reduce-graphql-batch-node-count)
5. [GhClient — Detailed Design](#5-ghclient--detailed-design)
   - [Why It Exists](#why-it-exists)
   - [Where It Lives](#where-it-lives)
   - [Migration — How It Replaces Current Code](#migration--how-it-replaces-current-code)
   - [Component 1: Request Deduplication](#component-1-request-deduplication)
   - [Component 2: Concurrency Semaphore](#component-2-concurrency-semaphore)
   - [Component 3: Circuit Breaker](#component-3-circuit-breaker)
   - [Component 4: Exponential Backoff with Retry](#component-4-exponential-backoff-with-retry)
   - [Component Interaction Flow](#component-interaction-flow)
   - [Startup](#startup)
   - [Caching](#caching)
6. [Impact Analysis](#6-impact-analysis)
   - [REST API Budget](#rest-api-budget)
   - [GraphQL API Budget](#graphql-api-budget)
   - [Secondary Rate Limit (Concurrency)](#secondary-rate-limit-concurrency)
   - [Latency](#latency)
   - [Failure Recovery](#failure-recovery)
   - [Scaling Ceiling](#scaling-ceiling)
7. [Failure Point Coverage Matrix](#7-failure-point-coverage-matrix)
8. Implementation Plans
   - [GhClient — Centralized Gatekeeper](/Users/adilshaikh/Desktop/impl-ghclient.md)
   - [API Layer Improvements (Changes 1, 2, 4, 5, 6)](/Users/adilshaikh/Desktop/impl-api-improvements.md)

---

## 1. Executive Summary

AO's GitHub API layer has 22 identified failure points that can cascade into sustained rate limiting. The root cause is architectural: 4 independent code paths share one rate limit budget (5,000 REST requests/hour, separate GraphQL budget, undisclosed concurrency limit) with no coordination between them.

**The worst case today:** A single batch failure with 50 sessions triggers 350 concurrent `gh` processes, consuming 42,000 calls/hour — 8.4x the primary rate limit. Once rate-limited, the system has no circuit breaker, so it continues spawning ~327 failing processes every 30 seconds for up to an hour.

**The redesign addresses this through 6 changes:**

| # | Change | Key Failures Addressed | Impact |
|---|--------|----------------------|--------|
| 1 | Eliminate fallback path | F-01, F-02, F-03, F-13, F-20 | Worst case: 350 calls/cycle -> 0 |
| 2 | Review backlog `since` param | F-04, F-05, F-06 | Review calls/hr: 4,500 -> 1,500 |
| 3 | GhClient singleton | F-01, F-08-F-12, F-15, F-16, F-19, F-22 | Concurrency: unbounded -> 20 max |
| 4 | ETag guard optimization | F-07 | Guard 2: 6,000 calls/hr -> 0 |
| 5 | verifyGhCLI at startup | F-22 | 120 wasted processes/hr -> 0 |
| 6 | Reduce GraphQL nodes | F-21 | Nodes per batch: 650 -> 475 |

**After redesign:**
- Typical REST usage: 3,500/hr -> 1,800/hr (49% reduction)
- Worst case REST usage: 50,000+/hr -> 2,800/hr (94% reduction)
- Max concurrent `gh` processes: unbounded (200-350+) -> 20
- Rate limit recovery: wait up to 1 hour -> auto-recover in 30 seconds
- Scaling ceiling: ~70 sessions -> ~140 sessions

---

## 2. Current System — How It Works Today

### Polling Architecture

Every 30 seconds, the lifecycle manager runs `pollAll()` through 5 phases:

```
pollAll()
  |
  +-- Phase 1: Batch PR Enrichment (once for all sessions)
  |     +-- Guard 1: 1 REST call -- "did any PR in the repo change?" (ETag check)
  |     +-- Guard 2: N REST calls -- "did CI change on each PR?" (1 per PR, sequential)
  |     +-- GraphQL Batch: 1 query for up to 25 PRs (state, CI, reviews, mergeability)
  |     Result -> prEnrichmentCache (per-cycle) + prEnrichmentDataCache (persistent)
  |
  +-- Phase 2: Status Detection (per session, ALL concurrent)
  |     For each session via Promise.allSettled:
  |       +-- Check runtime alive (local)
  |       +-- Check agent activity (local JSONL)
  |       +-- detectPR() if no PR yet (1 gh call)
  |       +-- Determine PR status:
  |             +-- Cache HIT -> use batch data (0 calls)
  |             +-- Cache MISS -> fallback: getPRState + getCISummary
  |                   + getReviewDecision + getMergeability (4-7 gh calls)
  |
  +-- Phase 3: Review Backlog (per session, inside checkSession, concurrent)
  |     Throttled to every 2 minutes per session:
  |       +-- getPendingComments() -- 1 GraphQL call (unresolved human review threads)
  |       +-- getAutomatedComments() -- N REST calls (paginated bot comments, unbounded)
  |     Has a throttle bypass when review reactions fire.
  |
  +-- Phase 4: CI Failure Details (per session, on ci_failed transition)
  |     +-- Cache HIT -> use batch ciChecks data
  |     +-- Cache MISS -> getCIChecks() (1 gh call)
  |
  +-- Phase 5: Merge Conflict Detection (per session, open PRs)
        +-- Cache HIT -> use batch hasConflicts data
        +-- Cache MISS -> getMergeability() (3 gh calls)
```

### The 4 Paths to GitHub

All `gh` CLI calls go through 4 independent wrappers, none coordinating:

| # | Location | Entry Point |
|---|----------|-------------|
| 1 | `scm-github/src/index.ts:64-77` | `execCli()` -> `gh()` / `ghInDir()` |
| 2 | `scm-github/src/graphql-batch.ts:353, 412, 577` | `execFileAsync("gh", ...)` directly |
| 3 | `tracker-github/src/index.ts:25-37` | Its own separate `gh()` function |
| 4 | `web/src/app/api/setup-labels/route.ts:31` | `execFileAsync("gh", ...)` directly |

All 4 paths share one GitHub auth token and one rate limit budget (5,000 requests/hour primary, undisclosed secondary concurrency limit). But none of them know:
- How many requests are currently in flight across the system
- Whether GitHub is currently rate-limiting us
- Whether the same data is being fetched by another caller right now
- How much rate limit budget remains

### Cost Model (50 Sessions)

| Scenario | Calls/Cycle | REST/hr | GraphQL/hr |
|----------|-------------|---------|------------|
| **Happy path** (batch succeeds, review throttled) | ~3 | ~360 | ~120 |
| **Typical path** (some cache misses, review active) | ~70 | ~3,500 | — |
| **Worst case** (batch fails, all fallback) | ~350 | ~42,000 (8.4x limit) | — |

---

## 3. Failure Analysis — All 22 Failure Points

### Foundational Problem — No Centralized Control

Every GitHub API call in AO goes through a bare wrapper that does nothing except spawn a child process:

```typescript
// scm-github/src/index.ts:64-77
async function execCli(bin: ExecCommand, args: string[], cwd?: string): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const { stdout } = await execFileAsync(bin, args, {
      ...(cwd ? { cwd } : {}),
      maxBuffer: 10 * 1024 * 1024,
      timeout: 30_000,
    });
    return stdout.trim();
  } catch (err) {
    throw new Error(`${bin} ${args.slice(0, 3).join(" ")} failed: ${(err as Error).message}`, {
      cause: err,
    });
  }
}
```

This function:
- Has **no concurrency control** — every caller spawns a new `gh` child process immediately
- Has **no rate limit awareness** — never checks `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers
- Has **no retry logic** — a single 429/403 is a hard failure
- Has **no deduplication** — two callers asking for the same PR state get two separate processes
- **Cannot distinguish** a rate limit error from a network error from a permission error

The `tracker-github` plugin has its own independent copy of this pattern, and `graphql-batch.ts` calls `execFileAsync` directly. Three separate entry points to GitHub, none coordinating.

**Every failure point below is a consequence of this foundational gap.**

---

### Critical Failures

#### F-01: Unbounded Concurrent Session Polling

**File:** `lifecycle-manager.ts:1319` | **Rate limit type:** Secondary | **Severity:** Critical

```typescript
await Promise.allSettled(sessionsToCheck.map((s) => checkSession(s)));
```

The lifecycle manager polls **all active sessions simultaneously** with no concurrency cap. Each `checkSession()` can trigger multiple `gh` CLI calls. With 50 sessions, this means up to 50 `checkSession` calls running in parallel, each independently spawning child processes.

`checkSession()` internally calls `maybeDispatchReviewBacklog()`, `maybeDispatchCIFailureDetails()`, and `maybeDispatchMergeConflicts()` via another `Promise.allSettled`. The concurrency compounds.

**Math:** 50 sessions x (up to 4 status calls + 2 review calls + 1 CI call + 1 conflict call) = **up to 400 concurrent `gh` processes** in a single poll cycle.

#### F-02: Fallback Storm on Batch Cache Miss

**File:** `lifecycle-manager.ts:510-528` | **Rate limit type:** Primary + Secondary | **Severity:** Critical

```typescript
// Inside determineStatus, per session
if (cachedData) {
  // Use cached enrichment data -- 0 API calls
} else {
  // Fall back to individual API calls:
  const prState = await scm.getPRState(session.pr);        // 1 gh call
  const ciStatus = await scm.getCISummary(session.pr);      // 1-2 gh calls
  const reviewDecision = await scm.getReviewDecision(session.pr); // 1 gh call
  const mergeReady = await scm.getMergeability(session.pr);      // 3 gh calls (see F-03)
}
```

When the batch GraphQL cache doesn't have data for a session's PR, `determineStatus()` falls back to **4-7 individual REST calls** per session. Since all sessions run concurrently via `Promise.allSettled`, a batch failure with 50 sessions spawns **350 parallel `gh` processes**.

**Triggers:**
- Batch GraphQL query failed (rate limited, timeout, network error)
- Session was added mid-poll-cycle
- GraphQL returned `null` for the PR

**Math (worst case):** 50 sessions x 7 calls each = 350 `gh` processes. At 30-second intervals: 42,000 calls/hour — **8.4x the primary rate limit**.

#### F-04: Unbounded Pagination in getAutomatedComments()

**File:** `scm-github/src/index.ts:880-906` | **Rate limit type:** Primary | **Severity:** Critical

```typescript
async getAutomatedComments(pr: PRInfo): Promise<AutomatedComment[]> {
  const perPage = 100;
  for (let page = 1; ; page++) {           // NO UPPER BOUND
    const raw = await gh([
      "api", "--method", "GET",
      `repos/${repoFlag(pr)}/pulls/${pr.number}/comments?per_page=${perPage}&page=${page}`,
    ]);
    const pageComments = JSON.parse(raw);
    if (pageComments.length === 0) break;
    comments.push(...pageComments);
    if (pageComments.length < perPage) break;
  }
}
```

Paginates through **all** PR review comments with no page limit. A PR with 800 bot comments -> 8 pages -> 8 API calls per session. Additionally fetches **all** comments including human ones, only to discard them.

**Math:** 20 sessions with active PRs x 8 pages = 160 calls, every 2 minutes = 4,800 calls/hour on this endpoint alone.

#### F-10: No Rate Limit Detection at execCli Layer

**File:** `scm-github/src/index.ts:64-77` | **Rate limit type:** Both | **Severity:** Critical

The `gh` CLI returns specific error messages for rate limit responses (`HTTP 429`, `abuse detection mechanism`), but **none of this is parsed**. The error is wrapped in a generic `Error` and thrown. Callers cannot distinguish rate limits from network errors from permission errors.

The tracker-github plugin and graphql-batch module have the exact same problem — three independent code paths, all blind to rate limits.

#### F-11: No Circuit Breaker Anywhere

**File:** Entire codebase | **Rate limit type:** Both | **Severity:** Critical

There is no mechanism to detect that GitHub is rate-limiting us and temporarily stop making requests. The polling loop runs every 30 seconds regardless of whether the last 100 API calls all returned 429.

**Current behavior on sustained rate limiting:**
```
Poll cycle 1:  50 calls -> all fail with 429 (50 wasted processes)
Poll cycle 2:  50 calls -> all fail with 429 (50 wasted processes)
...repeats every 30 seconds for up to 1 hour
```

### High Severity Failures

#### F-03: Redundant Sub-Calls Inside getMergeability()

**File:** `scm-github/src/index.ts:945-1026` | **Rate limit type:** Primary | **Severity:** High

`getMergeability()` makes **3 sequential `gh` calls** internally:
1. `getPRState()` — fetches `state`
2. `gh pr view` — fetches `mergeable,reviewDecision,mergeStateStatus,isDraft`
3. `getCISummary()` -> `getCIChecks()` — fetches checks

In the fallback path, `getPRState()` and `getCISummary()` were already called **before** `getMergeability()`. So `getMergeability()` re-fetches data retrieved seconds earlier.

**Wasted calls:** 2 redundant per session per poll cycle. 50 sessions on fallback: 100 extra calls.

#### F-05: Review Backlog Throttle Bypass

**File:** `lifecycle-manager.ts:768-782` | **Rate limit type:** Secondary | **Severity:** High

When a session transitions to `changes_requested` or receives a new automated review, the 2-minute throttle is **completely bypassed**. Both `getPendingComments()` and `getAutomatedComments()` fire immediately.

Fires at the worst moment — during state transitions, when the lifecycle manager is already making many other API calls. 10 sessions transitioning simultaneously = 20+ extra concurrent calls on top of everything else.

#### F-06: Per-Session Throttle Instead of Global

**File:** `lifecycle-manager.ts:214-219` | **Rate limit type:** Primary | **Severity:** High

The review backlog throttle is tracked **per session** (`Map<SessionId, number>`). With 50 sessions and staggered timers, the aggregate rate is ~1 review backlog check every 2.4 seconds. Each check fires 2 concurrent API calls plus pagination.

**Result:** ~50 API calls/minute sustained, just from review backlog.

**File:** `graphql-batch.ts:222-254` | **Rate limit type:** Primary | **Severity:** High

Guard 2 makes **one REST call per PR** to check if CI status changed. The `for...of` loop with `await` runs these sequentially. 50 PRs at ~200ms each = **~10 seconds** of wall time before the actual data fetch starts.

```
Guard 1: GET /repos/owner/repo/pulls?state=open&per_page=1        -> 1 call
  |
  +-- 304 (nothing changed)
        |
        +-- Guard 2: one call per PR, each with unique commit SHA
              PR #1:  GET /repos/owner/repo/commits/abc123/status  -> 1 call
              PR #2:  GET /repos/owner/repo/commits/def456/status  -> 1 call
              ...
              PR #50: GET /repos/owner/repo/commits/xyz999/status  -> 1 call
              Total: 50 calls
```

**Math with 50 PRs, CI active on 20:** Guard 2 costs 6,120 calls/hour — **48% of primary limit** just for guards.

#### F-08: No Backoff Between Batch Failures

**File:** `graphql-batch.ts:934-1006` | **Rate limit type:** Secondary | **Severity:** High

When there are multiple batches (>25 PRs), they execute sequentially with **no delay**. If batch 1 gets a 429, batch 2 fires immediately and also fails. After all batches fail, all sessions fall back to individual calls (F-02), making the rate limit worse.

**File:** `graphql-batch.ts:373-379, 431-438` | **Severity:** Medium

When an ETag guard fails (including rate limiting), it returns `true` (assume changed), triggering the expensive GraphQL batch. A rate limit on the cheap guard triggers the expensive batch, which triggers more expensive individual calls. The optimization becomes the opposite: **rate limit makes us do MORE work, not less**.

How a rate limit cascades through the system with 50 sessions:

## 4. Redesign — What Changes

### Overview

The redesigned polling flow:

```
pollAll()
  |
  +-- Phase 1: Batch PR Enrichment (once for all sessions)
  |     +-- Guard 1: 1 REST call -- same as before (ETag check)
  |     +-- Guard 2: REMOVED -- no more per-PR CI checks
  |     +-- Staleness cap: if Guard 1 says "no change" but cache > 2 min old -> run batch
  |     +-- GraphQL Batch: same query, reduced nodes (reviews:3, contexts:15)
  |     Result -> same caches, no changes to caching layer
  |
  +-- Phase 2: Status Detection (per session, ALL concurrent)
  |     For each session via Promise.allSettled:
  |       +-- Check runtime alive (local) -- unchanged
  |       +-- Check agent activity (local JSONL) -- unchanged
  |       +-- detectPR() if no PR yet -> STOP after detection, defer status to next cycle
  |       +-- Determine PR status:
  |             +-- Cache HIT -> use batch data (0 calls) -- unchanged
  |             +-- Cache MISS -> REMOVED -- return session.status, defer to next cycle
  |
  +-- Phase 3: Review Backlog (per session, inside checkSession, concurrent)
  |     Throttled to every 2 minutes per session -- unchanged:
  |       +-- getPendingComments() -- 1 GraphQL call -- unchanged
  |       +-- getAutomatedComments() -- 1 REST call with ?since=<lastCheck> (no pagination)
  |     Throttle bypass: REMOVED -- standard 2-min throttle, no exceptions
  |
  +-- Phase 4: CI Failure Details (per session, on ci_failed transition)
  |     +-- Cache HIT -> use batch ciChecks data -- unchanged
  |     +-- Cache MISS -> REMOVED -- defer to next cycle
  |
  +-- Phase 5: Merge Conflict Detection (per session, open PRs)
        +-- Cache HIT -> use batch hasConflicts data -- unchanged
        +-- Cache MISS -> REMOVED -- defer to next cycle
```

**Single path to GitHub:**

All 4 wrappers replaced by one GhClient singleton:

```
scm-github/index.ts     --+
graphql-batch.ts         --+
tracker-github/index.ts  --+--> GhClient (core) --> gh CLI --> GitHub API
web/api/setup-labels     --+
                               | Dedup map
                               | Semaphore (max 20)
                               | Circuit breaker
                               | Backoff + retry
```

**Cost after redesign (50 sessions):**

| Scenario | Before | After |
|----------|--------|-------|
| Happy path | ~3 calls/cycle, ~360 REST/hr + ~120 GraphQL/hr | ~2 calls/cycle, ~240 REST/hr + ~120 GraphQL/hr |
| Typical path | ~70 calls/cycle, ~3,500 REST/hr | ~15 calls/cycle, ~1,800 REST/hr |
| Worst case | ~350 calls/cycle, ~42,000 REST/hr | ~5 calls before circuit trips -> 0 for 30s -> auto-recover |

---

### Change 1: Eliminate the Fallback Path

**Addresses:** F-01, F-02, F-03, F-13, F-20

**Problem:** When the batch GraphQL cache misses a PR, `determineStatus()` falls back to 4-7 individual `gh` calls per session. All sessions run concurrently — a batch failure with 50 sessions spawns 350 parallel `gh` processes.

**Solution:** The batch runs every 30 seconds. If a PR isn't in the cache now, it will be next cycle. Remove the fallback entirely.

**PR auto-detection — detect and stop:**
```
Session has no PR -> detectPR() -> found PR #42 -> save to metadata -> STOP
  Batch will include PR #42 next cycle.
  No status check this cycle.
```

**Batch cache miss — keep current status:**
```
Session has PR #42 -> cache miss -> return session.status
  Batch will include PR #42 next cycle.
  No individual calls made.
```

**Same logic applies to dispatchers:**
- `maybeDispatchMergeConflicts()` on batch miss -> skip, defer to next cycle
- `maybeDispatchCIFailureDetails()` on batch miss -> skip, defer to next cycle

**Tradeoff:** 30-second delay for newly detected PRs and batch misses. Acceptable because the agent is still working regardless, state transitions don't happen in 30 seconds, and the alternative (350 concurrent calls) can break the system for an hour.

| Scenario | Before | After |
|----------|--------|-------|
| 50 sessions, batch fails | 350 calls/cycle | 0 |
| 10 new PRs detected | 70 calls | 10 (detectPR only) |
| Worst case per hour | 42,000 calls | 0 (batch retry only) |

---

### Change 2: Review Backlog — `since` Parameter and Bypass Removal

**Addresses:** F-04, F-05, F-06

**Problem:** `maybeDispatchReviewBacklog()` makes 2 calls per session every 2 minutes. `getAutomatedComments()` uses unbounded pagination (all comments, filter for bots). All sessions burst at once. Throttle bypass on transitions adds more calls.

**Solution — `since` parameter for bot comments:**

The GitHub REST endpoint supports `?since=<timestamp>`. Pass the existing `lastReviewBacklogCheckAt`:

```
First call (no timestamp): full fetch, establishes fingerprint
Every subsequent call:      GET /pulls/{number}/comments?since=<lastCheck>
                            -> returns 0-2 new comments, single page, no pagination
```

No new tracking needed — `lastReviewBacklogCheckAt` already exists.

**Remove throttle bypass:** With `since`, every call is a delta from last timestamp. Missing one check doesn't cause stale fingerprints. The bypass is unnecessary.

**Burst handled by GhClient semaphore:** 100 calls requested at once -> 20 run, 80 queued -> ~1.5 seconds total.

**Why `since` doesn't apply to human comments:** `getPendingComments()` uses GraphQL `reviewThreads` — no `since` filter available. But it's already 1 call capped at 100 threads, and needs "what's still unresolved" not "what's new".

| | Before | After |
|---|--------|-------|
| getAutomatedComments/hr | 1,500-6,000 REST | 1,500 REST (1 page each) |
| Bypass bursts | 600-1,200 extra | 0 |
| Total review backlog/hr | ~4,500 calls | ~1,500 calls |
| Max concurrent | 100-290 | 20 (semaphore) |

---

### Change 3: GhClient — Centralized Gatekeeper

**Addresses:** F-01, F-08, F-09, F-10, F-11, F-12, F-15, F-16, F-19, F-22

All 4 `gh` CLI paths share one rate limit budget but none coordinate. The GhClient is a singleton in `@aoagents/ao-core` that all paths go through.

**4 components:**
1. **Request deduplication** — in-flight map, coalesces simultaneous identical requests
2. **Concurrency semaphore** — max 20 concurrent `gh` processes, 30s acquire timeout
3. **Circuit breaker** — trips on rate limit, all calls fail-fast, auto-recovers after 30s
4. **Exponential backoff** — retries transient errors (502, 503, brief 429), never retries writes

**Cross-cutting concerns:**
- **Error types** — `GhClientError` hierarchy (`CircuitOpenError`, `RateLimitError`, `SemaphoreTimeoutError`, `GhCliError`) so callers can handle gracefully vs alert
- **Observability** — per-event logging (circuit trips, retries, semaphore pressure) + per-cycle stats summary
- **Shutdown** — trips circuit, lets in-flight finish, rejects queued waiters

**Startup:** Runs `gh --version` once to verify CLI availability (replaces per-batch `verifyGhCLI`).

**No cache.** The redesign eliminates the redundant calls that would benefit from caching. Existing caches (ETag, enrichment data, per-cycle) remain unchanged.

Full component design in [Section 5](#5-ghclient--detailed-design).

---

### Change 4: ETag Guard Optimization

**Addresses:** F-07

**Problem:** Guard 2 makes 1 REST call per PR to check CI status. 50 PRs = 50 sequential calls, ~10 seconds wall time. Costs 6,000 REST calls/hour to save 120 GraphQL calls/hour. Bad tradeoff.

**Solution:** Remove Guard 2. Add a staleness cap to the persistent cache:

```
Guard 1: 1 REST call
  +-- 200 (something changed) -> run batch
  +-- 304 (nothing changed)
        +-- cache age < 2 min -> return cache (skip batch)
        +-- cache age >= 2 min -> run batch (refresh stale data)
```

**Why 2 minutes:** CI takes 2-10 minutes to complete. Checking every 30 seconds polls for something that hasn't happened yet. Maximum detection delay: 2 minutes on top of actual CI runtime.

| | Before (quiet repo) | After |
|---|---------------------|-------|
| Guard 1 | 120 REST/hr | 120 REST/hr |
| Guard 2 | 6,000 REST/hr | 0 (removed) |
| Batch | 0 GraphQL/hr | 30 GraphQL/hr (once per 2 min) |
| Wall time/cycle | ~10.2 seconds | ~200ms |

Active repos: no change (Guard 2 already never ran).

---

### Change 5: Move verifyGhCLI to Startup

**Addresses:** F-22

`gh --version` runs before every batch query (every 30 seconds). Move to GhClient initialization — run once at startup, fail early if `gh` is missing.

Saves 120 process spawns/hour. ~50ms faster batch execution per cycle.

---

### Change 6: Reduce GraphQL Batch Node Count

**Addresses:** F-21

**Problem:** The batch query fetches 26 nodes per PR. Two fields are wasteful:
- `reviews(last: 5)` — **not used** by `extractPREnrichment()`. It reads the top-level `reviewDecision` field.
- `contexts(first: 20)` — only used on `ci_failed` transitions (~10% of PRs).

**Change:** Reduce to `reviews(last: 3)` and `contexts(first: 15)`.
- `reviews(last: 3)` — kept as safety buffer, reduced from 5.
- `contexts(first: 15)` — repo has 12 CI checks, 15 covers all. Truncation already handled.

| | Before | After |
|---|--------|-------|
| Nodes per PR | 26 | 19 |
| Nodes per batch (25 PRs) | 650 | 475 |
| Points per batch | 7 | 5 |
