title: ci(web): detect unused CSS custom properties in globals.css (warn-only)
body:
## Summary
- Adds `packages/web/scripts/check-css-tokens.mjs`, a dependency-free Node audit that parses `--color-*` token definitions out of `packages/web/src/app/globals.css` and reports dead tokens (zero references across `packages/web/src/**` and `DESIGN.md`) plus multi-token groups that resolve to the same literal value (likely duplicates).
- Exposes it as `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-web lint:css-tokens`.
- Wires a new `css-tokens` CI job with `continue-on-error: true` so the audit is warn-only until the baseline is cleaned up.

## Flags
- `--all` — audit every `--*` token, not just `--color-*` (the issue explicitly calls this out as optional).
- `--strict` — exit non-zero on findings, for flipping to failing once the baseline is clean.

## Notable behaviour
- Groups duplicate-value detection by scope (`:root` vs `.dark`) so light/dark redefinitions of the same token don't appear as false positives.
- Skips `var(--…)` aliases and no-ops (`transparent`, `inherit`, `none`) when hunting for duplicate values.
- Self-definition lines in `globals.css` don't count as references, but cross-token references inside `globals.css` (e.g. `--color-bg-primary: var(--color-bg-base)`) do — so backward-compat aliases that reference another token stay "used" on the alias target side but the alias itself is flagged dead if nobody else reads it.

## Initial findings (reproducible via `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-web lint:css-tokens`)
- 7 dead `--color-*` tokens: `--color-accent-purple`, `--color-accent-violet`, `--color-alert-ci-unknown`, `--color-border-emphasis`, `--color-border-muted`, `--color-column-header`, `--color-tint-violet`.
- 23 duplicate-value groups pointing at likely consolidation candidates (e.g. `--color-accent-green` / `--color-ci-pass` / `--color-status-merge` / `--color-status-working` all resolve to the same green).

These are intentionally surfaced but not enforced yet, per the issue.

title: fix(web): prevent kanban card blink on attention-level column changes
body:
Fixes #1446

## Summary

The `kanban-card-enter` entrance animation (`opacity: 0 → 1`, `translateY: 8px → 0`) was unconditionally applied to every `SessionCard`. When a card's attention level oscillated between kanban zones on consecutive SSE updates, React unmounted the card from one column and remounted it in another, re-triggering the animation and causing a visible blink.

## Fix

Added a module-level `Set<string>` (`enteredSessionIds`) that tracks which session IDs have already played their entrance animation. The `kanban-card-enter` class is now conditionally applied — only on the very first mount of a session. Subsequent remounts (e.g., column changes) skip the animation.

**Changed file:** `packages/web/src/components/SessionCard.tsx`
- Added `enteredSessionIds` Set at module scope
- Added `hasEntered` state derived from the Set
- Conditionally apply `kanban-card-enter` only when `!hasEntered`

## Test

1. Have a session in the dashboard whose attention level is borderline between zones
2. Verify the card does NOT blink when it moves between columns on SSE updates
3. Verify that genuinely NEW sessions still play the entrance animation

body:
Closes #1424.

## Summary
- Add `recordActivityViaTerminal(classifier)` to `@aoagents/ao-core` — factory that returns the standard `recordActivity` implementation (null-check `workspacePath`, delegate to `recordTerminalActivity`).
- Replace the identical 5-line `recordActivity` wrapper in `agent-aider`, `agent-codex`, `agent-cursor`, and `agent-opencode` with a 1-line factory call.

- Update `CLAUDE.md` plugin-authoring guide to point at the new factory.

## Why option (a), not option (b)
Issue #1424 proposed two options, with (b) (lifecycle-manager default) preferred. I went with (a) (factory) after discovering (b) changes behavior for agents that don't use AO activity JSONL:

- Claude Code uses its own native JSONL (`~/.claude/projects/`) and doesn't override `recordActivity`. Under (b), the lifecycle manager would start calling `recordTerminalActivity` for Claude Code every poll cycle, producing orphan `.ao/activity.jsonl` writes nothing reads.
- It also broke lifecycle-manager tests whose mock agent defines `detectActivity` but intentionally omits `recordActivity`.

Option (a) keeps opt-in semantics, leaves the lifecycle manager untouched, and is truly no behavior change for any existing agent. See https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/issues/1424#issuecomment-4291773453.

title: lifecycle: terminated sessions never revive when probes later disagree — causes dashboard state flicker (idle → killed → ready)
body:
## Summary

Once the lifecycle state machine latches a session to `session.state = "terminated"` with `reason = "runtime_lost"`, there is **no inverse transition** back to a live state. If subsequent probes observe the runtime alive, the process alive, and recent activity, the session stays `terminated` forever. Different dashboard code paths read different fields on the Session object, producing a visible `idle → killed → ready` flicker.

This is a distinct defect from #989 (race at session *creation*) and #1187 (dead sessions staying `working`). This bug is about a **live** session that was momentarily flagged and cannot recover from the terminal decision, even with strong live evidence.

---

## Evidence

### 1. State machine has no revive transition

`packages/core/src/lifecycle-status-decisions.ts:305-347`:

- **Lines 305-318**: `runtime=dead && process=alive` OR `runtime=alive && process=dead` OR `runtime=dead && recentActivity` → `detecting` with reason `runtime_lost` (transient).
- **Lines 335-347**: `runtime=dead && process=dead && !recentActivity` → `KILLED`, `session.state = terminated`, `sessionReason = runtime_lost`.

There is no inverse transition. Once `session.state = terminated`, subsequent probes showing `runtime = alive && process = alive && activity = active` do NOT flip the session back to a live state.

### 2. Concrete metadata artifact

Captured from `~/.agent-orchestrator/15c372b67170/sessions/ao-17`:

```
session.state        = "terminated"
session.reason       = "runtime_lost"
session.terminatedAt = 2026-04-21T20:50:16.964Z

runtime.state          = "alive"
runtime.reason         = "process_running"
runtime.lastObservedAt = 2026-04-21T20:54:04.694Z

lifecycleEvidence = activity_signal=valid via_native activity=active at=2026-04-21T20:54:03.284Z
```

Runtime was observed alive **4 seconds after** the session was marked terminated, with active recent activity — but the session stayed `terminated`.

### 3. Probe sensitivity

`isProcessRunning` in agent plugins (tmux path) is a single TTY + `ps` regex check. One missed poll window flips the session to `detecting`, and from there it can latch to `terminated` within a few poll cycles if activity evidence is momentarily stale.

### 4. User-visible symptom

Dashboard and session detail pages flicker `idle → killed → ready` as different code paths read different fields on the Session object. The session is live and working, but the UI is unusable.

---

## Proposed Fixes (maintainers to decide)

### Option 1 — Add a revive transition

In `lifecycle-state.ts` / `lifecycle-status-decisions.ts`: if `session.state = terminated` with `reason = runtime_lost`, `runtime.state = alive`, `processProbe = alive`, and recent activity, transition the session back to the prior live state (e.g. `idle` or `ready`).

### Option 2 — Harden the probe

Require two consecutive dead reads OR >30s of silence from `isProcessRunning` before the state machine can reach the `KILLED` terminal decision. This prevents a single transient probe miss from latching the session.

**Preferably both** — harden the probe AND allow revive. Per the project's anti-over-engineering philosophy, if one has to be picked, pick the simpler one that fixes the bug (probably Option 2: hardening the probe, since it prevents the latch from happening in the first place and keeps the terminal-decision semantics intact).

---

## Related issues / PRs

- #989 — Orchestrator session immediately marked as 'killed' despite running fine. Related but distinct: #989 is a race during session *creation* where `isProcessRunning` returns false before the agent has launched. This bug is about a mature, running session that gets latched to `terminated` after a transient probe miss, with no way back.
- #1187 — Zombie sessions: `isProcessRunning()` gated behind conditional checks, dead sessions stay "working". This is the inverse symptom (dead stays live). Both issues point at the fragility of `isProcessRunning` as a single-sample truth source.
- #1068 — Fix fail-open health probes (`.catch(() => true)` → `.catch(() => false)`). Complementary: tightening probe correctness interacts with how quickly a session can latch to terminated.
- #1379 — Add ground truth verification before CI/review lifecycle transitions. Same theme: avoid trusting a single transient signal for a terminal decision.
- #1414 — Unify CanonicalSessionState and SessionStatus. The dual state representation is the root cause of the *visible* flicker (different surfaces read different fields).
- #456 — Dashboard startup race showing 'Exited'. Different code path, but same user-visible outcome for a live session.
- #1300 (merged) — Redo session lifecycle reporting and UI flow. Introduced the current `lifecycle-status-decisions.ts` architecture this bug lives in.

title: bug(spawn): batch-spawn and `ao spawn` succeed when no daemon is polling the project — silent observability blackout
body:
## Summary

`ao spawn` and `ao batch-spawn` currently succeed even when the running `ao` daemon is not polling the target project. They print a stderr warning and then proceed to create full worktrees, tmux panes, and session metadata — but none of the lifecycle-driven behavior that a session needs to be useful (CI-failure routing, review-comment routing, revive transitions, event log, state advance) is actually wired up for that project.

The result is a silent observability blackout: the dashboard looks normal, sessions appear to run, and there is no visible indication that lifecycle reactions are dead. This is a footgun.

## Evidence

Warning emitted during a real batch-spawn of 23 sessions (from `packages/cli/src/commands/spawn.ts:78`):

```
⚠ The running AO instance (pid 66487) is not polling project \"agent-orchestrator\".
  Run `ao start agent-orchestrator` so the new session is tracked.
```

The spawn proceeded anyway and 23 sessions were created with full worktrees and tmux panes.

### Downstream effects observed

- No `~/.agent-orchestrator/15c372b67170-events.jsonl` is being written for this project (the project-scoped event log never gets created because nothing is polling).
- Lifecycle polling doesn't run — session metadata isn't being advanced by the daemon.
- The only reason PR URLs appear in metadata at all is that `next-server` (pid 66865) is separately polling `gh` via the dashboard web routes. That's partial, not a substitute for the lifecycle manager.
- Stale `terminated` states in metadata never get recovered because there is no revive poll.
- CI-failure routing, review-comment routing, and other lifecycle reactions are silently dead for every session in this batch.

A stderr warning is not sufficient. The user-visible dashboard looks normal; sessions appear to run; nothing in the UI hints that these sessions are un-orchestrated.

## Source

The warning is printed unconditionally without any enforcement, here:

`packages/cli/src/commands/spawn.ts:73-81`

```ts
if (!running.projects.includes(projectId)) {
  console.log(
    chalk.yellow(
      `⚠ The running AO instance (pid ${running.pid}) is not polling project \"${projectId}\". Run \`ao start ${projectId}\` so the new session is tracked.`,
    ),
  );
}
```

The check exists, it just doesn't gate anything.

## Proposed options (for maintainers to decide)

From most to least aggressive:

1. **Refuse to spawn** when the daemon isn't polling this project, with a clear actionable error (`Run \`ao start <project>\` first`). Simplest and probably correct — if the session can't be operated, it shouldn't be created. Matches the anti-over-engineering philosophy of this codebase.
2. **Auto-start project polling** inside the existing `ao` daemon when a spawn happens. Slight complexity (the daemon needs to pick up a new project at runtime), but removes the footgun entirely.
3. **Keep the warning** but also flag every session spawned in this state as \"unpolled\" in the dashboard so the blackout is visible. Least invasive but adds UI surface and still lets bad state exist.

My recommendation: **option 1**. If you can't operate the session, don't create it.

## Related work

- **PR #1308** (merged, commit `e45f34e1`) — \"fix: restore dead orchestrators on ao start\". Fixes a sibling daemon-reuse problem: `ao start` would spawn a duplicate orchestrator instead of reusing a dead-but-restorable one. Related theme (daemon/orchestrator lifecycle footguns around `ao start`) but does not cover the spawn-vs-polling mismatch.
- **Issue #1306** — original `ao start` intermittent-replacement report that led to #1308. Related class of problem.
- **Issue #1102** — `ao start` opens stale orchestrator session instead of picker page. Same area.
- **Issue #1279** — `ao start` in folder A shows dashboard of AO running on project B. Also daemon/project-association adjacent.
- **Issue #1188** — upgraded CLI silently attaches to stale daemon, no version-mismatch detection. Same failure mode class: spawn/start proceeds silently when daemon state is wrong.
- **Issue #1073** — lifecycle worker kills sessions with no audit trail. Tangentially related lifecycle-observability gap.

None of the above cover this exact bug: spawn succeeding while the daemon is not polling the project.

## Acceptance criteria

- Running `ao spawn <project> <issue>` or `ao batch-spawn <project> ...` when the daemon exists but does not include `<project>` in its polling set either:
  - fails fast with a clear error telling the user to run `ao start <project>` (option 1), OR
  - causes the daemon to start polling the project before any session is created (option 2), OR
  - creates the sessions but surfaces an unmistakable \"unpolled\" indicator in the dashboard for each affected session (option 3).
- No session is ever created in a state where the lifecycle manager will silently not run for it.

title: ao send: synthesizes a bogus runtimeHandle from sessionId when metadata is missing the handle, spawning duplicate unprefixed tmux sessions
body:
## Summary

`ao send` can spawn a **duplicate, zombie tmux session** and run a second agent instance on the same worktree/branch when a session's metadata is missing its `runtimeHandle`. The fallback code in `prepareSession` silently synthesizes a handle using the bare `sessionId` (no project-hash prefix), and `restore()` then creates a brand-new tmux session under that wrong name — alongside the real, still-running session.

This causes real corruption: two Claude instances editing the same worktree simultaneously.

## Evidence

### Offending code

`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:2295-2317` (`prepareSession`):

```typescript
const handle =
  current.runtimeHandle ??
  ({
    id: sessionId,                  // ← bare sessionId, no project hash prefix
    runtimeName,
    data: {},
  } satisfies RuntimeHandle);
const normalized = current.runtimeHandle ? current : { ...current, runtimeHandle: handle };

if (forceRestore || isRestorable(normalized)) {
  return restoreForDelivery(...);   // → restore(sessionId) → spawns new tmux with the synthesized handle
}
```

### Why it's wrong

Real tmux sessions are named `{projectHash}-{sessionId}` (e.g. `15c372b67170-ao-17`). When `runtimeHandle` is missing (see sibling issue about handle loss), the synthesized handle uses just `ao-17`, so `restore()` creates a new tmux session literally called `ao-17` — **not** the real one.

### Concrete artifact observed

```
$ tmux list-sessions | grep ao-17
15c372b67170-ao-17: 1 windows (created Wed Apr 22 02:19:45 2026)   ← real Claude working on PR #1439
ao-17:              1 windows (created Wed Apr 22 02:23:49 2026)   ← zombie spawned by ao send
```

Both tmux panes show PR #1439 — **two Claude instances running on the same worktree/branch simultaneously.**

### Secondary failure mode

This also triggers the error `restored session did not become ready for delivery` (`session-manager.ts:2284`), because `waitForRestoredSession` polls with the wrong handle id and times out. In batch briefings, that timeout cancels parallel `ao send` calls.

## Requested fix

1. **Do NOT synthesize a handle from `sessionId` alone.** If `current.runtimeHandle` is null, refuse to send and surface a clear error like:

   > `session ao-17 is missing its runtime handle — use 'ao session ls' to inspect or 'ao session restore' explicitly`

2. (Connected to sibling issue) **Fix the root cause** by not blanking the handle on terminated state transitions.

This should be **deleting ~6 lines of synthesis code**, not adding a recovery layer. The fallback is actively harmful: it corrupts data by pretending a handle exists when none does.

## Related

- #1074 (closed) — `ao send` reports success for `killed` sessions; same `prepareSession` → `restoreForDelivery` path. That fix addressed the CLI-reporting side; this issue is the underlying data-corruption hazard in the restore path itself.
- #1067 — health-check exceptions masked as "alive" in send/lifecycle; complementary failure mode where the send path trusts stale/bogus state.
- #853 — file-based messaging protocol; longer-term, removing tmux-messaging would sidestep this class of bug.

## Environment

- `main` at `origin/main` (~`59f66f4d`)
- macOS (Darwin 24.2.0), Node 20

title: observability: unify lifecycle/runtime/agent logs into a correlated, persistent, structured event stream so the orchestrator can self-debug
body:
## Summary

I just spent an hour end-to-end troubleshooting two bugs (state-flicker #1454 and a zombie-tmux case). To do it I had to cross-reference six different log/state surfaces, several of which are optional, silently absent, or structurally unqueryable. This is a meta-issue: the reason I cannot self-debug the bugs I am filing is that the log streams are scattered and structurally inadequate.

The orchestrator does not have the observability it needs to self-debug. A single persistent, correlated, structured event stream would collapse this forensic work from "multiple files and grep gymnastics" to `ao logs <session> --follow`.

## Gap table — what I had to cross-reference

| Stream | Path | Problems |
|---|---|---|
| Session metadata | `~/.agent-orchestrator/{hash}/sessions/{id}` | Flat key=value, only latest state. `lifecycleEvidence` is a single string that overwrites on every probe — no history |
| Lifecycle events | `~/.agent-orchestrator/{hash}-events.jsonl` | **Only exists when a daemon is polling the project.** For the current project (hash `15c372b67170`), this file is absent — no events captured at all |
| API log | `~/.agent-orchestrator/{hash}-{project}/logs/api.jsonl` | Exists inconsistently (present for `c058bd58e962-agent-orchestrator`, absent for `15c372b67170`) |
| Per-session activity | `{worktree}/.ao/activity.jsonl` | Only written by agents using the AO activity pattern (Aider, OpenCode). **Not written for Claude Code** — it uses native JSONL in `~/.claude/`, which is outside AO's reach |
| `ao start` stdout/stderr | nowhere | `lsof` shows PIPE fds only. Daemon logs are not persisted |
| tmux | `tmux list-sessions` / `capture-pane` | Ground truth for runtime — had to use this because AO's own state said terminated when tmux said alive |

## Specific gaps that make self-debug impossible

1. **No probe history.** `lifecycle-status-decisions.ts` makes state decisions from `runtimeProbe`, `processProbe`, and `activityEvidence`. The inputs are thrown away. You cannot answer "when did runtime_alive flip to runtime_dead and why."
2. **No correlation id.** A session transition that involves an API call, a probe, and a reaction has no shared id — you cannot trace the chain end to end.
3. **No daemon logs.** Stdout/stderr of `ao start` is piped, not logged. When the reaction engine makes a bad call, nothing is captured.
4. **Events file is optional by accident.** Project-not-polled → no events file → silent blackout. Should be append-always, even for projects not actively polled.
5. **`lifecycleEvidence` is prose, not data.** A string like `activity_signal=valid via_native activity=active at=...` cannot be queried (e.g. "how many times has this session flipped state today"). Should be a structured append-only log.

## Proposed (for maintainer discussion — not prescribing implementation)

1. **Single persistent append-only log per project** at a well-known path, always written, even when no daemon is polling. One JSONL line per probe, per transition, per reaction, per API call.
2. **Structured record** with a consistent envelope: `{ts, sessionId, kind: "probe"|"transition"|"reaction"|"api"|"agent", runtimeProbe, processProbe, activityProbe, fromState, toState, reason, correlationId, ...}`.
3. **Correlation id** threaded from lifecycle tick → reaction → API call → session metadata write, so a single user-visible transition is traceable across subsystems.
4. **Daemon stdout/stderr** piped to a rotated file at a predictable path.
5. **CLI `ao logs [session|project] [--follow]`** to inspect without filesystem spelunking.
6. **`ao doctor`** command that checks for common observability gaps (no daemon polling, missing events.jsonl, stale metadata, per-session activity file absent when expected).

**Anti-over-engineering note:** this does not need to be a new logging framework. A single JSONL append plus a CLI command is enough to unblock self-debug. The existing utilities (`readLastJsonlEntry`, `appendActivityEntry`, the per-session `.ao/activity.jsonl` pattern) already cover 80% of the write path. What is missing is a project-level, always-on, correlated stream and a way to read it without `find`/`grep`/`jq`.

## Related issues (prior art — please cross-link on triage)

There are adjacent pieces of this already filed. This meta-issue rolls them up:

- **#855** — Proposal: replace split-brain architecture with durable JSONL append-only event log. Covers the state-persistence angle (lifecycle state hydration from a replayable log). Strong structural overlap with (1)/(2) above. If #855 lands, the write path is solved — this issue would still need (3) correlation ids, (4) daemon logs, (5) CLI, (6) doctor on top.
- **#336** — feat: session event log and terminal history persistence. Covers the per-session detail view ("dead sessions should still be inspectable") and a `GET /api/sessions/:id/events` endpoint. Complementary — this issue is the project-level stream, #336 is the per-session view onto it.
- **#1073** — bug: lifecycle worker kills sessions with no audit trail (session id + reason). A concrete symptom of gap (1) and (5): when a session is killed via one of the short-circuit paths in `lifecycle-manager.ts`, no structured log captures *which* kill path fired. Fixing #1073 in isolation patches one class of events; fixing it inside the framework proposed here gives it the right home.
- **#1454** — lifecycle: terminated sessions never revive when probes later disagree. The state-flicker bug I was debugging when I hit this observability wall. Not caused by the observability gap, but the gap is why it took an hour instead of five minutes.
- **#1414** — refactor(core): unify CanonicalSessionState and SessionStatus. Dual state representation feeds the "lifecycleEvidence is a single overwriting string" problem; a unified state plus a structured history log together clean this up.
- **#92** — `ao stop logs 'Dashboard stopped' even when no dashboard was running`. Tiny but same theme: the few log lines we do emit are not trustworthy because they are not sourced from a single state-of-truth stream.
- **#614** — send-to-agent reaction silently no-ops when message field is missing. Directly in the "reaction made a bad call, nothing was captured" class — exactly what (3) is for.

## Out of scope

- Metrics, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing. Not needed for self-debug. A local JSONL stream and a CLI is enough.
- Log rotation strategy beyond "do not let it grow unbounded" — maintainers to choose (compaction like #855, size cap, daily rotation — all fine).
- Replacing the per-session `.ao/activity.jsonl` pattern. That pattern is working; the gap is at the project/lifecycle layer, not per-session activity.

## Success criteria

- I can run `ao logs <session-id>` and see every probe, transition, reaction, and API call that touched that session, in order, with a correlation id joining related entries.
- I can run `ao logs <project>` and see the same at project scope.
- The log exists even when no daemon is actively polling the project (append-always).
- `ao doctor` flags a project that is missing expected streams.
- Re-debugging the #1454 flicker from logs alone takes under five minutes.

title: session-manager: runtimeHandle and tmuxName are dropped to null when lifecycle transitions to terminated, losing routing information permanently
body:
## Summary

On transition to `terminated` (session state machine reason `runtime_lost`), AO drops the top-level `runtimeHandle` and `tmuxName` metadata keys **and** nulls `statePayload.runtime.handle` / `statePayload.runtime.tmuxName`. This is permanent data loss: the runtime name is the only routing key that ties `ao send <id>`, dashboard terminal attach, and `isAlive()` probes to the actual tmux session. Once blanked, any subsequent poll that sees the runtime alive again (the runtime wasn't actually gone, it was a transient probe disagreement) has nothing to re-attach to.

The fix is surgical: **stop blanking the handle on `terminated`**. Keep it until the session is truly cleaned up (worktree removed, metadata archived). Terminating the *session* does not invalidate the runtime's address.

## Evidence

Two sibling sessions from the same project, same orchestrator, same machine. Both have a live tmux pane and a live Claude process. One has its routing info intact, the other lost it.

**ao-1 — healthy (runtime metadata intact):**

```
worktree=/Users/equinox/.worktrees/agent-orchestrator/ao-1
branch=feat/1412
status=review_pending
tmuxName=15c372b67170-ao-1
issue=1412
project=agent-orchestrator
agent=claude-code
createdAt=2026-04-21T20:45:00.286Z
runtimeHandle={"id":"15c372b67170-ao-1","runtimeName":"tmux","data":{"createdAt":1776804300286,"workspacePath":"/Users/equinox/.worktrees/agent-orchestrator/ao-1"}}
stateVersion=2
statePayload={"version":2,"session":{"kind":"worker","state":"idle","reason":"awaiting_external_review",...},"pr":{"state":"open",...},"runtime":{"state":"alive","reason":"process_running","lastObservedAt":"2026-04-21T21:32:18.522Z","handle":{"id":"15c372b67170-ao-1","runtimeName":"tmux","data":{...}},"tmuxName":"15c372b67170-ao-1"}}
...
```

**ao-17 — broken (top-level `runtimeHandle=` and `tmuxName=` absent, statePayload runtime handle/tmuxName null, yet runtime.state=alive):**

```
worktree=/Users/equinox/.worktrees/agent-orchestrator/ao-17
branch=feat/1428
status=pr_open
issue=1428
project=agent-orchestrator
agent=claude-code
createdAt=2026-04-21T20:49:45.107Z
stateVersion=2
statePayload={"version":2,"session":{"kind":"worker","state":"terminated","reason":"runtime_lost","startedAt":"2026-04-21T20:49:47.235Z","completedAt":null,"terminatedAt":"2026-04-21T20:50:16.964Z","lastTransitionAt":"2026-04-21T20:50:16.964Z"},"pr":{"state":"none","reason":"not_created","number":null,"url":null,"lastObservedAt":null},"runtime":{"state":"alive","reason":"process_running","lastObservedAt":"2026-04-21T20:54:04.694Z","handle":null,"tmuxName":null}}
lifecycleEvidence=activity_signal=valid via_native activity=active at=2026-04-21T20:54:03.284Z
promptDelivered=true
agentReportedState=started
agentReportedAt=2026-04-21T20:49:53.579Z
restoredAt=2026-04-21T20:53:49.292Z
pr=https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/pull/1439
```

Note the paradox in ao-17's `statePayload.runtime`: `state: "alive"`, `reason: "process_running"`, `lastObservedAt: 2026-04-21T20:54:04.694Z`, but `handle: null, tmuxName: null`. A later poll correctly re-detected liveness, but by then the address was already gone.

**The tmux session is actually alive:**

```
$ tmux capture-pane -p -t 15c372b67170-ao-17 | tail -6
⏺ PR opened: https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/pull/1439

  What changed
  - Added max-lines: ["error", ...] to the root eslint.config.js.
  ...

  ⏵⏵ bypass permissions on (shift+tab to cycle) · PR #1439
```

So Claude is alive, doing work, on a tmux session named `15c372b67170-ao-17` — but AO has forgotten that name.

## Timeline (reconstructed from `statePayload` timestamps)

1. `2026-04-21T20:49:45.107Z` — `createdAt`. Session spawned with real `runtimeHandle` / `tmuxName` written.
2. `2026-04-21T20:49:47.235Z` — `startedAt`. Agent launched.
3. `2026-04-21T20:49:53.579Z` — `agentReportedAt`, state `started`.
4. `2026-04-21T20:50:16.964Z` — `terminatedAt` with `reason: runtime_lost`. **This is the write that blanked the handle.** A probe disagreement (tmux probe said dead, activity said alive, or similar — same failure mode described in #1063 and #989) pushed the state machine to `terminated`.
5. `2026-04-21T20:53:49.292Z` — `restoredAt`. Something tried to restore the session.
6. `2026-04-21T20:54:03.284Z` — `lifecycleEvidence` shows a fresh active activity signal. Runtime is genuinely alive.
7. `2026-04-21T20:54:04.694Z` — `runtime.lastObservedAt`. State flipped back to `alive`, but `handle` and `tmuxName` remain null because the top-level keys were already deleted by step 4 and `parseCanonicalLifecycle → synthesizeRuntimeState` has nothing to rehydrate from.

## Root cause (code trace)

The write path that blanks the fields is `buildLifecycleMetadataPatch` in `packages/core/src/lifecycle-state.ts`:

```ts
// packages/core/src/lifecycle-state.ts:465
export function buildLifecycleMetadataPatch(
  lifecycle: CanonicalSessionLifecycle,
  previousStatus?: SessionStatus,
): Partial<Record<string, string>> {
  return {
    stateVersion: "2",
    statePayload: JSON.stringify(lifecycle),
    status: deriveLegacyStatus(lifecycle, previousStatus),
    pr: lifecycle.pr.url ?? "",
    runtimeHandle: lifecycle.runtime.handle ? JSON.stringify(lifecycle.runtime.handle) : "",
    tmuxName: lifecycle.runtime.tmuxName ?? "",
    role: lifecycle.session.kind === "orchestrator" ? "orchestrator" : "",
  };
}
```

An empty string **deletes** the key — see `applyMetadataUpdates` in `packages/core/src/metadata.ts:173`:

```ts
if (value === "") {
  const { [key]: _removed, ...rest } = next;
  ...
}
```

So whenever `lifecycle.runtime.handle` / `lifecycle.runtime.tmuxName` are null at write time, the top-level keys get wiped from disk.

The `terminated` transition itself comes from `resolveProbeDecision` in `packages/core/src/lifecycle-status-decisions.ts:340`:

```ts
if (
  input.runtimeProbe.state === "dead" &&
  input.processProbe.state === "dead" &&
  !recentActivitySupportsLiveness
) {
  return createLifecycleDecision({
    status: SESSION_STATUS.KILLED,
    evidence: `runtime_dead process_dead ${input.activityEvidence}`,
    detectingAttempts: 0,
    sessionState: "terminated",
    sessionReason: "runtime_lost",
  });
}
```

Neither this decision nor `applyDecisionToLifecycle` (in `lifecycle-transition.ts`) explicitly nulls the handle — they only set `session.state = "terminated"`. So where does the null come from?

Answer: after the first `terminated` write with blanked top-level keys, the *next* poll cycle re-reads metadata with `parseCanonicalLifecycle → synthesizeRuntimeState` (`lifecycle-state.ts:230`), which falls through to `handle: null, tmuxName: null` (lines 248–249) because the top-level `runtimeHandle` and `tmuxName` keys are already gone. The state payload's null handle is then written back and persists.

So the flow is:
1. Probe disagreement trips a `terminated + runtime_lost` decision.
2. `applyDecisionToLifecycle` sets `session.state = "terminated"` but does NOT touch the handle — however, at this point the in-memory `lifecycle.runtime.handle` may already be null (from an earlier error/probe-fail path that set `runtime.state = "missing"` and let the handle drift), or the current decision path does not preserve it on write.
3. `buildTransitionMetadataPatch` / `buildLifecycleMetadataPatch` writes `runtimeHandle: ""` and `tmuxName: ""` — **deleting** them from the flat key-value file.
4. Next poll reads the file back, sees no top-level `runtimeHandle` / `tmuxName`, and `synthesizeRuntimeState` cannot recover them because they were the only source.
5. Even if the runtime comes back alive on the next probe, AO has no name to attach to.

## Why this bug matters

- `ao send ao-17` cannot route — no handle.
- Dashboard terminal attach cannot open — no tmux name.
- See the sibling issue about `prepareSession` synthesizing a fake handle to paper over this, which papers over the symptom and creates a *different* routing bug.
- This stacks on the intermittent probe races already reported in #1063 (orchestrator falsely marked killed during startup) and #989 (orchestrator immediately marked killed due to agent process not yet on TTY). Those bugs produce the transient `terminated` transition; this bug makes the damage permanent.

## Requested fix

Keep it small. Do **not** build a "handle recovery" system.

1. **Stop writing empty string for `runtimeHandle` / `tmuxName`** in `buildLifecycleMetadataPatch` (`packages/core/src/lifecycle-state.ts:474-475`) and `buildTransitionMetadataPatch` (`packages/core/src/lifecycle-transition.ts:152-153`). If the in-memory lifecycle's runtime handle is null, *leave the existing key on disk alone* — do not emit the key in the patch at all. Only explicit cleanup (worktree removed, session archived) should ever delete it.
2. **Don't let `synthesizeRuntimeState` produce `handle: null, tmuxName: null` if the raw metadata has neither AND `statePayload` previously had them.** Better: when `normalizePayloadLifecycle` merges payload over synthesized, prefer the last-known non-null handle from whichever source has one. (Alternative, simpler: apply fix #1 and this falls out for free — the top-level keys will always be intact for a session that ever had a runtime.)
3. **Preserve the handle into archive too.** When the session is finally cleaned up and archived, include `runtimeHandle` / `tmuxName` in the archive record for post-mortem lookups.

The intent: the handle is the runtime's address, like an IP. A session transitioning to `terminated` does not invalidate the name; only tearing down the worktree does. Match that model.

## Suggested regression test

- Seed a session with a valid `runtimeHandle` and `tmuxName`.
- Simulate a probe disagreement that forces `sessionState = "terminated"`, `sessionReason = "runtime_lost"`.
- Assert top-level `runtimeHandle` and `tmuxName` are **still present** in the metadata file after the write.
- Assert `statePayload.runtime.handle` and `statePayload.runtime.tmuxName` are **still populated**.
- Then simulate a subsequent poll where `runtime.isAlive` returns true — assert the session rehydrates with the original handle, not a fabricated one.

## Related

- #1063 — intermittent orchestrator race marks session killed while tmux is alive. The upstream trigger for the kind of transient `terminated` transition this bug makes permanent.
- #989 — orchestrator immediately marked killed because `findClaudeProcess` hasn't seen the process yet. Same category — grace-period absent on probe.
- #1187 — zombie sessions from the opposite direction (process dies, `isProcessRunning` skipped). Same file, adjacent codepath.
- #1245 — sessions stuck in `working` with no recovery path. Also touches the "we lost track of the runtime" theme.
- #40 — MERGED PR that added `terminated` to `VALID_STATUSES`, so `terminated` is now a full terminal status in the state machine. That PR is fine on its own but makes this bug easier to hit because the state is no longer rewritten back to `spawning`.

Not a duplicate of any of the above — those cover the trigger (transient mis-labeling); this covers the irreversible data loss caused by the trigger.

title: RFC: self-improving orchestrator — end-to-end loop for self-diagnosis, issue filing, fix sessions, and verification
body:
## Vision

When a user tells the orchestrator "go self-diagnose" or "find and fix bugs," AO should be able to execute the full loop end-to-end, with the same rigor a human operator would apply, but without the 60+ minutes of manual cross-referencing it requires today:

1. **Self-diagnose from its own logs + live runtime.** Read correlated logs, session metadata, tmux/process state, and codebase source; identify inconsistencies, stuck sessions, probe flicker, missing events, lifecycle-worker gaps, handle loss, orphan worktrees, duplicate tmux sessions, etc. (The observability prerequisite — see #1457.)
2. **Report bugs** — file GitHub issues with high-quality evidence (file:line citations, log excerpts, reproducer state), cross-correlating against existing open/closed issues and linking prior art.
3. **Spawn worker sessions** for each confirmed bug, with anti-over-engineering briefs (small, surgical, scoped).
4. **Monitor and verify** — once a worker PR lands, the orchestrator session should independently verify the fix actually worked: re-run the specific diagnosis that found the bug and confirm it now passes. Not just "CI green."
5. **Close the loop** — mark fixed issues, recycle successful patterns into the orchestrator prompt / memory, and flag failed fixes for re-spawn or human escalation.

## Problem Statement — the motivating exercise

Today (2026-04-22) I was asked to audit codebase slop. The sequence I actually ran:

- 5 parallel Explore agents surveying different subsystems
- Codex second-opinion proofread (caught hallucinations in the first audit)
- 23 parallel sub-agents filing issues, each cross-correlating with existing GitHub issues
- `batch-spawn` of 23 worker sessions with anti-over-engineering briefs
- **60+ minutes of manual troubleshooting** for state-flicker and zombie-tmux bugs (#1454, #1456, #1458), cross-referencing by hand across:
  - `~/.agent-orchestrator/{hash}/sessions/{id}` flat metadata
  - `tmux list-sessions` / `capture-pane`
  - `ps`, `lsof` for daemon pids
  - codebase reads: `packages/core/src/lifecycle-status-decisions.ts`, `session-manager.ts`, `lifecycle-state.ts`

This exercise demonstrated both halves of the thesis:

- **What is possible today:** cross-agent debate, mass parallel issue filing, parallel worker spawn — the orchestrator pattern works.
- **What is structurally broken:** no correlated logs, no revive transition, handle loss on terminate, duplicate tmux spawn via synthesized handles, no unified probe of "what fault classes do we know exist?"

And the gap that motivates this RFC specifically: **the same orchestrator session that found these bugs cannot *verify* they were fixed**, because it has no ergonomic way to re-run the same diagnosis after a worker merges a PR. The loop has to be closed manually, which means in practice it does not get closed.

## Proposed Capabilities

### 1. `ao diagnose` — one-shot self-check

Scans metadata + logs + live runtime for the known fault classes:

- state flicker (terminated ↔ idle/ready oscillation) — #1454
- handle loss (runtimeHandle/tmuxName dropped on terminate) — #1458
- orphan worktrees (worktree on disk with no metadata, or vice versa)
- unpolled projects (spawn succeeds but no lifecycle worker is polling the project) — #1455
- stale terminated states (sessions marked terminated while tmux is still alive)
- zombie tmux (tmux session alive with no AO metadata)
- duplicate sessions (same task/issue, multiple live sessions; synthesized-handle double-spawn) — #1456

Output: structured findings with `severity`, `fault-class-id`, `evidence` (file:line, log excerpts, session IDs), and a stable `diagnosis-id` that can be re-run later.

### 2. `ao diagnose --fix` OR `ao triage`

Map findings to issue templates, query GitHub for duplicates, file issues with linked prior art. This is what I manually did today with 23 parallel sub-agents. The command should:

- dedupe against open + closed issues
- attach the `diagnosis-id` to the issue body (machine-readable block) so verification can find it
- apply a standard label (e.g. `ao-diagnosed`)
- default to `--dry-run`; require explicit `--file` to actually open issues

### 3. Orchestrator hooks for spawn & verify

Standardized protocol: "for issue #N, spawn a session with brief X, then when its PR merges, re-run diagnosis Y and report back."

Likely shape:

```
ao spawn --from-issue <N> --verify-with <diagnosis-id>
```

Stored in session metadata so the verifier knows what to run on PR-merge.

### 4. Verification workflow

After a worker PR merges:

- orchestrator automatically re-runs the diagnosis referenced by the session's `--verify-with`
- if the diagnosis still finds the fault → reopen the issue, post a comment with the new evidence, and either retry (bounded) or escalate for human review
- if clean → update a "fixes verified" log, close the issue with a verification comment

Verification must be distinct from "CI green." CI catches regressions in things tested. Verification here re-runs the *discovery* procedure that surfaced the bug.

### 5. Prompt / memory integration

Successful diagnosis → fix → verification cycles should feed back into:

- `packages/core/src/orchestrator-prompt.ts` (recycled patterns for future orchestrator sessions)
- the `memory/` directory (running list of known fault classes + their detection rules)

This is how the orchestrator improves itself across sessions rather than rediscovering the same bugs.

### 6. Safety rails (non-negotiable)

Self-improvement must **never** autonomously:

- force-push
- delete or `--force` worktrees
- kill tmux sessions
- amend/rewrite history

These remain human-gated. The existing memory rule ("NEVER force-remove worktrees, kill tmux sessions, or take destructive actions") applies to this system.

## Architectural Questions for Investigation

Not for this RFC to answer — for the worker(s) assigned to the design-doc phase:

1. **Where does `ao diagnose` live?** Core, CLI, or a new `packages/diagnose/` package? (Straw-man: CLI command with core helpers, so plugins can contribute fault-class detectors.)
2. **Diagnosis rule registry.** Each rule pairs a `detect()` and a `verify()` function. Where does that registry live, and how do plugins register into it? Is it a new plugin slot or a module-level export from existing plugins?
3. **How does verification know which diagnosis to re-run after a PR merges?** Likely via machine-readable metadata the orchestrator itself writes into the issue body + session metadata when it files the issue / spawns the worker. Spec the schema.
4. **Protocol between orchestrator and worker.** Today it is `ao send`. For verification, workers need to report "diagnosis-id-resolved" back — likely an `ao report` command writing into a structured status stream the orchestrator can tail.
5. **Loop / duplicate safety.** How do we prevent:
   - duplicate issues when `ao diagnose` runs repeatedly
   - zombie workers if a fix never lands
   - infinite re-spawn when a fix does not stick?
   Straw-man: attempt cap per issue, cooldown, hard escalation after N failures.

## Dependencies / Sequencing

**Explicitly downstream of #1457 (observability overhaul).** Without correlated, structured, persistent logs, `ao diagnose` has nothing to read. Do not start `ao diagnose` until the event stream from #1457 is in place (or at minimum stubbed with a stable schema).

Specific fault classes this system is designed to detect and verify (these are also the test corpus for the phase-1 MVP):

- #1454 — state flicker (terminated → idle/ready oscillation)
- #1455 — silent observability blackout when no daemon polls a project
- #1456 — duplicate tmux spawn from synthesized runtimeHandle
- #1458 — handle loss on lifecycle → terminated

Related prior art worth cross-referencing:

- #1252 — `ao doctor` already exists as a bug-report subject; scope/shape should be reconciled, not duplicated
- #1128 — RFC: multi-base-branch orchestrators (independent but the worker-spawn protocol overlaps)
- #1321 — RFC: reactive sync (replaces polling; `ao diagnose` over a push-based event stream is simpler)

## Out of Scope (explicit)

- Autonomous destructive actions (force-push, `worktree remove --force`, tmux kill). Human-gated, always.
- Replacing human review on worker PRs. Verification is a *post-merge* sanity check, not a substitute for review.
- Generalized "AI ops" beyond the orchestrator's own fault classes. This is **self**-diagnose, scoped to AO internals.
- Rewriting the lifecycle manager to support self-healing transitions — that is a separate follow-up if the RFC design surfaces it.

## Success Criteria

Done looks like:

1. **Design doc** answering the architectural questions above, merged either as this issue's resolution comment or as a `docs/rfcs/self-improving-orchestrator.md`.
2. **Phase-1 MVP `ao diagnose`** that detects at minimum the four known fault classes listed under dependencies, produces structured findings with stable `diagnosis-id`s, and has a `--dry-run` triage path that previews issue filing without executing it.
3. **One end-to-end demo** of the loop: `ao diagnose` finds a synthetic fault → `ao triage` files an issue → worker spawn fixes it → PR merges → verification re-runs the diagnosis → issue auto-closes with a verification comment.

Once 1–3 ship, the follow-ups (prompt recycling, attempt caps, escalation) are tractable increments.

---

Filed after today's manual self-diagnose exercise (23 issues filed + 60min handle-loss debug) — this RFC is the structural answer to "I should not have had to do that by hand."

title: fix(cli): refuse to spawn when daemon is not polling the project
body:
## Summary
closes #1455 

- Promote the `ao spawn` / `ao batch-spawn` "daemon not polling this project" warning at `packages/cli/src/commands/spawn.ts:73-81` to a hard error.
- No session is created in a state where the lifecycle manager will silently not run for it.
- Error tells the user exactly which `ao start` invocation fixes it.

## Why

Previously the warning printed but spawn proceeded anyway — sessions got full worktrees and tmux panes but no CI-failure routing, no review-comment routing, no revive transitions, and no event log. The dashboard looked normal; sessions were un-orchestrated. This is option 1 from the issue (the maintainer's recommendation): if the session can't be operated, don't create it.

Both `spawn` and `batch-spawn` already shared the warning helper, so a single-site change (now renamed `ensureAOPollingProject`) covers both commands.

## Test plan

- [x] New unit tests for both failure modes (no daemon, daemon polling a different project)
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli test` — 22/22 passing
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli typecheck` clean

title: fix(core): refuse ao send when runtimeHandle is missing
body:
## Summary

- Fixes #1456 — `ao send` could spawn a zombie tmux session running a second Claude on the same worktree when a session's metadata was missing its `runtimeHandle`.
- `prepareSession` in `session-manager.ts` used to synthesize a handle from the bare `sessionId`. But real tmux sessions are named `{projectHash}-{sessionId}`, so `restore()` would create a brand-new tmux session under the wrong unprefixed name — alongside the real one.
- Refuse to operate when the persisted runtime handle is missing and throw a descriptive error instead.

## Details

The fabrication check has to read the **raw persisted metadata** (`session.metadata["runtimeHandle"]`) rather than the enriched `session.runtimeHandle`, because `get()` → `ensureHandleAndEnrich` also fabricates a handle from the sessionId for liveness-check/display purposes. Using the enriched handle in `send`/`restore` is what corrupts state.

The error message points users at `ao session ls` to inspect or `ao session restore` to recover explicitly, rather than silently doing the wrong thing.

## Test plan

- [x] Updated existing regression test `refuses to send when runtimeHandle is missing…` in `packages/core/src/__tests__/session-manager/communication.test.ts` — asserts `send()` rejects with a `missing its runtime handle` error and never calls `runtime.sendMessage` or `runtime.create`.
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core test` — 808 tests pass.
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` — clean.
- [x] `pnpm lint` — 0 errors.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(core): preserve runtimeHandle and tmuxName across lifecycle writes
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1458 — a data-loss bug where `buildLifecycleMetadataPatch` (`lifecycle-state.ts`) and `buildTransitionMetadataPatch` (`lifecycle-transition.ts`) emitted empty-string values for `runtimeHandle` / `tmuxName` when the in-memory lifecycle had them null. `applyMetadataUpdates` treats empty strings as **deletions**, so a transient `terminated + runtime_lost` transition (from a probe disagreement — see #1063, #989) permanently wiped the session's routing address from disk while the tmux session was still alive.

- `ao send <id>` could no longer route (no handle)
- Dashboard terminal attach could not open (no tmux name)
- Even if the runtime came back alive on the next probe, AO had nothing to re-attach to

## The fix

Stop emitting the keys when the in-memory handle is null. Omitting the key in the patch leaves the existing disk value alone (`applyMetadataUpdates` skips `undefined`). Only explicit cleanup (archive) should ever delete the flat keys — and it already uses a different path.

No new handle-preservation subsystem, recovery layer, or rehydration logic. Just: if the handle is valuable metadata, stop destroying it.

## Changes

- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-state.ts` — `buildLifecycleMetadataPatch` emits `runtimeHandle`/`tmuxName` only when non-null
- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-transition.ts` — `buildTransitionMetadataPatch` same
- Tests updated to reflect the new contract
- New regression test: seeds a session with a valid handle, forces a `terminated + runtime_lost` decision, asserts the flat keys still exist on disk afterward and `readCanonicalLifecycle` rehydrates the original handle

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core test` — all 811 tests pass
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core typecheck` — clean
- [x] `pnpm lint` — no new warnings

## Related

- #1063, #989 — upstream triggers (transient mis-labeling) this bug makes permanent
- #1187 — zombie sessions from the opposite direction
- #1245 — sessions stuck in `working` with no recovery path
- #1454 — flicker issue; fixing this bug removes much of the visible damage
- #1456 — sibling to this one

Closes #1458

title: docs(rfc): self-improving orchestrator
body:
## Summary

Architectural RFC for #1459 — "self-improving orchestrator: end-to-end loop for self-diagnosis, issue filing, fix sessions, and verification".

- Proposes a **3-file, ~600-line** design: `core/diagnose.ts`, `core/diagnose-rules.ts`, `cli/commands/diagnose.ts`. No new plugin slot, no new package.
- `ao diagnose` scans for known fault classes and emits structured findings with a stable `diagnosis-id`.
- `ao diagnose --triage --file` files GitHub issues with a machine-readable marker (`<!-- ao-diagnose:{id}:{fingerprint} -->`) used for dedupe.
- `ao diagnose --verify <pr>` resolves the PR → issue, parses the marker, re-runs the rule's `detect()`, and closes / reopens accordingly.
- `ao spawn --verify-with <id>` stores the diagnosis id in session metadata so the verification step knows what to re-run.
- Phase-1 MVP targets the four fault classes from the motivating exercise: #1454, #1455, #1456, #1458.

## Non-negotiables

Autonomous destructive actions are **out of scope**: no force-push, no `worktree remove --force`, no `tmux kill`, no history rewrite, no autonomous issue closure without a verifying rule run. Aligns with the existing memory rule. Remediation is always a worker PR + human review.

## What this RFC is not

- Not a framework or plugin system — rules are entries in a plain array.
- Not a replacement for `ao doctor` (install health) or `ao verify` (human-driven verification). Composes with both.
- Not prescribing #1457's event-stream format — depends on it, does not decide it.
- Not auto-editing `orchestrator-prompt.ts` / `memory/` — promotion stays human-gated.

## Depends on

- **#1457** (correlated observability) — prerequisite for the detect() side of most rules.

## Next steps

1. Review and resolve the open questions in §9.
2. Phase-1 implementation as a follow-up PR once the contract is agreed.
3. Optional: minimal `ao diagnose` POC (single rule, no triage) after the design is settled.

## Test plan

- [ ] Reviewers confirm the rule contract (`detect` + `verify` on a `DiagnosisRule`) fits each of #1454, #1455, #1456, #1458 without extension.
- [ ] Reviewers confirm verification via marker parsing is the right dedupe/lookup mechanism (vs. a side-channel index).
- [ ] Safety rails in §6 are agreed before any implementation begins.
- [ ] Open questions in §9 are resolved or explicitly deferred.

Refs #1459 (design-only; closes on phase-1 implementation PR merge).

title: fix(core): stop single-shot dead probe from latching session to terminated
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1454. A single transient probe miss used to walk a session straight to `session.state=terminated` with `reason=runtime_lost`. There was no inverse transition — once terminated, subsequent probes showing the runtime alive and active activity could not flip the session back. The dashboard then flickered `idle → killed → ready` as different surfaces read different fields.

Two single-shot terminal latches removed:

- **`lifecycle-status-decisions.ts:resolveProbeDecision`**: `runtime=dead && process=dead && !recentActivity` now routes through `detecting`/`runtime_lost` instead of `killed`/`terminated`. The standard `detecting → stuck` escalation already handles persistence; `stuck` is recoverable, `terminated` was not.
- **`session-manager.ts:enrichSessionWithRuntimeState`**: a single `isAlive=false` observation no longer overrides `session.status` to `"killed"` or `session.activity` to `"exited"`. Lifecycle is set to `detecting`/`runtime_lost` and the legacy status is mirrored to `"detecting"` so the dashboard stays aligned.

Manual kills (`ao session kill`) and the explicit `done` path remain the only ways to reach a terminal state.

## Why this approach (vs. adding a revive subsystem)

The issue suggested two options: harden the probe OR add a revive transition (preferably both). I went with hardening alone — the simpler fix that addresses the root cause. Adding a revive subsystem would have been new infrastructure to compensate for a bad terminal decision; this PR removes the bad terminal decision instead. Net diff is mostly deletions.

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core test` — 809/809 pass
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core typecheck` — clean
- [x] New regression test asserts: probe N sees dead+dead → `detecting`, probe N+1 sees runtime alive → session walks back to `working` (the exact scenario from the issue's metadata artifact)
- [x] Existing tests that asserted single-shot kill behavior updated to assert single-shot detecting behavior

title: feat(core): always-on event log + ao logs CLI (phase 1 of #1457)
body:
## Summary

Phase 1 of the observability overhaul (#1457). Prerequisite for #1459.

Adds a project-level structured event stream that is written on **every** lifecycle tick, transition, reaction, and session action — not just while a daemon is polling. Exposes it through `ao logs`. Also tees `ao start`'s dashboard subprocess stdout/stderr to a rotated log file so the daemon's output is persisted.

### Philosophy — remove and simplify first

This PR deliberately does **not** build a logging framework, trace-span system, or pluggable sinks. The proposal in #1457 is a sketch; the actual surface that unblocks self-debug turned out to be:

1. **One JSONL per project**, appended to from any AO process
2. **One CLI** to filter / tail it
3. **One tee** for the dashboard daemon's output

Correlation-ids across subsystems, `ao doctor`, and sink pluggability are left for a follow-up once we know they earn their complexity.

### What's in it

- `packages/core/src/event-log.ts` — `appendEvent` / `readEventLog` / `followEventLog`, size-rotated to one `.1` rollover (default 10 MB, env `AO_EVENT_LOG_MAX_BYTES`), sensitive-key redaction, depth-bounded sanitization. Never throws.
- `packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts` — four emission sites:
  - status transitions (with probe details + fromStatus/toStatus)
  - `lifecycle.sync` probe ticks (no status change)
  - reactions (success / escalation / action)
  - `pollAll` cycle (success or failure)
- `packages/cli/src/commands/logs.ts` — `ao logs [target]` with `--follow`, `--kind`, `--since {5m,30s,2h,1d}`, `--limit`, `--project`, `--correlation-id`, `--json`, `--path`.
- `packages/cli/src/lib/tee-log.ts` + wiring in `commands/start.ts` — mirrors the dashboard child's stdout/stderr to `{observabilityBaseDir}/dashboard.log` (5 MB rollover) **and** to the parent terminal, so interactive use is unchanged.

### Location

Lives under the existing hash-based observability directory — `{observabilityBaseDir}/events.jsonl` and `{observabilityBaseDir}/dashboard.log` — so it's already isolated per config / per checkout.

### Overlap with #855

#855 proposes a durable event log for state rehydration. That concern is complementary (state source-of-truth), not duplicated — this PR is about debug trails. If #855 lands on the same file format we can merge the two streams later.

### Scope intentionally NOT in this PR

- Correlation IDs across subsystems (schema has the field; we're not threading yet)
- `ao doctor` command
- Plugging in session-manager `destroyAllForProject` paths (#1073) — deferred; lifecycle transition events will capture the downstream status changes
- Replacing `observability.ts` (the snapshot/trace module stays)

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core test` — 817 passing (includes 9 new event-log tests)
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli test` — 523 passing
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm lint` — 0 errors (35 pre-existing warnings untouched)
- [x] `pnpm build` — all packages
- [ ] Manual: run `ao start`, confirm `dashboard.log` gets written and mirrors to terminal
- [ ] Manual: run `ao logs --follow` during a spawn cycle, confirm transitions/probes/reactions appear

Refs #1457
Unblocks #1459

title: refactor(core): storage redesign — projectId-based paths, JSON metadata
body:
## Summary

### Core storage redesign

- **V2 path layout**: `projects/{projectId}/sessions/{sid}.json`, `projects/{projectId}/worktrees/` replacing hash-based `{hash}-{name}/` directories
- **JSON metadata**: Replaces key=value flat-file format with structured JSON and typed `SessionMetadata`
- **storageKey removal**: Identity is `projectId`; removed storageKey plumbing from global config and runtime paths
- **SessionMetadata type evolution**: `statePayload`/`stateVersion` moved into `lifecycle`; runtime/dashboard/report fields are structured

### Archive removal

- **No more archive directory**: Sessions stay in `sessions/` with `lifecycle.state: "terminated"` instead of being moved to `sessions/archive/`
- Removed `getProjectArchiveDir`, `getArchiveFilePath`, `compactTimestamp` from core paths
- Removed `readArchivedMetadataRaw`, `updateArchivedMetadata` from metadata
- Removed `listArchivedSessionIds`, `markArchivedOpenCodeCleanup` from session manager
- `deleteMetadata` simplified to permanent delete (no archive boolean)
- `kill()` checks terminated state via lifecycle instead of archive lookup
- `restore()` reads directly from sessions/ (no archive fallback)
- `cleanupSessions()` iterates terminated sessions instead of archive directory
- Migration flattens old archives into `sessions/` as terminated records

### Session lifecycle: dual-truth elimination

- Source of truth is **`lifecycle-state.ts`**: `state` + `reason` replace the old `SessionStatus` enum
- Canonical states: `not_started | working | idle | needs_input | stuck | detecting | done | terminated`
- Terminal reasons: `manually_killed | runtime_lost | agent_process_exited | probe_failure | error_in_process | auto_cleanup | pr_merged`
- Legacy `SessionStatus` is **derived** at read time via `deriveLegacyStatus(state, reason, prState)` — used only for display backward-compat, never persisted
- `previousStatus` arguments removed throughout the codebase
- **Stale runtime reconciliation**: `sm.list()` checks if the tmux/process backing each session is still alive during enrichment. Dead ones get persisted as `runtime_lost` → legacy status `killed`. Without this, sessions whose runtime died silently would show "active" forever.

### Cross-project CLI rework

#### `ao stop`
- `ao stop` (no args): kills **all** sessions across **all** registered projects, stops parent process + dashboard, writes `last-stop.json` with `otherProjects` for cross-project restore
- `ao stop <project>`: surgical — kills only that project's sessions. **Does not** kill parent process or dashboard. Calls `removeProjectFromRunning(projectId)` so that `ao start <project>` can restart without hitting the "already running" gate
- Always loads global config (`~/.agent-orchestrator/config.yaml`) to see all projects

#### `ao start`
- Reads `last-stop.json` on startup and prompts to restore sessions — including cross-project ones
- **`projectNeedsRestart` gate**: if `ao start <project>` is called after `ao stop <project>` removed it from `running.json`, the "already running" menu is bypassed. An `isProjectId` guard (`!isRepoUrl && !isLocalPath`) prevents false triggers on path/URL arguments
- Project picker offers "Add this project" when launched in an unregistered cwd
- Auto-registers a flat local config on first `ao start` if missing

#### `Ctrl+C` graceful shutdown
- Mirrors `ao stop` exactly: kills all sessions, writes `last-stop.json`, unregisters `running.json`
- Async IIFE inside sync signal handler (Node.js signal handlers remove default exit behavior — must call `process.exit()` explicitly)
- 10s hard timeout via `setTimeout().unref()` in case cleanup hangs
- Before this PR, Ctrl+C left tmux orphans

#### Tab completions
- Merge global + local config so tab completion shows every registered project

### Dashboard sidebar fix

- Sidebar always shows all sessions across all projects, regardless of which project page is active
- `useSessionEvents` called without project filter — sidebar gets unscoped sessions
- Per-project filtering applied client-side via `projectSessions` memo for kanban display

### Project identity redesign

- New registrations now use deterministic external IDs: `{sanitized-basename}_{10-char-sha256}`
- Hash input is `absoluteProjectPath + ':' + originUrl`, so same-basename repos get distinct IDs without ordering-dependent suffixes
- Existing projects keep their legacy config keys and storage directories; only the generation path changed
- `registerProjectInGlobalConfig()` now reads origin before locking, generates the hashed ID for new registrations, reconnects same-path re-registration to existing storage, and throws on true hash collision
- Removed `deriveAvailableProjectId()` and the CLI/web suffix allocation flow
- Deprecated `generateProjectId()` while preserving legacy read/path compatibility

### Migration (`ao migrate-storage`)

- Converts `{hash}-{name}/` and bare `{hash}/` directories to `projects/{projectId}/`
- Converts key=value metadata to JSON with type conversion
- Flattens old archives into `sessions/` as terminated records (no more archive directory)
- Supports active tmux session detection, `--dry-run`, `--rollback`, and `--force`
- Idempotent migration; re-running skips `.migrated` directories
- Rollback preserves post-migration sessions with safety checks
- Handles stray worktrees and repairs broken git worktree references after migration
- 21+ named edge cases handled (macOS case-insensitive collisions, partial failure rollback, concurrent migration locking, etc.)

### Bug fixes and hardening

- Atomic metadata writes (temp file + rename, never partial overwrites)
- V1 storage detection and upgrade warnings
- Graceful handling of malformed JSON metadata
- Session restore PR state reset to avoid immediate re-termination
- Restore command preserves permission flags
- V2 tmux name parsing allows hyphens in prefixes
- DELETE route guards missing storage directories
- `removeProjectFromRunning()` — surgically removes project from `running.json` during targeted stop (6 dedicated tests)
- `isProjectId` guard prevents `projectNeedsRestart` from false-triggering on filesystem paths or URLs

### New runtime artifacts

| File | Lifetime | Written by | Read by |
|------|----------|------------|---------|
| `~/.agent-orchestrator/config.yaml` | Persistent | `ao start`, `ao spawn`, manual edits | All CLI commands needing cross-project visibility, tab completions |
| `~/.agent-orchestrator/running.json` | Lives while `ao start` is running | `ao start` (register), `ao stop`/Ctrl+C (unregister), `ao stop <project>` (removes project) | `ao status`, `ao spawn`, dashboard, `ao start` (already-running + projectNeedsRestart gate) |
| `~/.agent-orchestrator/last-stop.json` | Cleared after restore prompt | `ao stop`, Ctrl+C | `ao start` |

### Documentation

- Updated `CLAUDE.md` with canonical lifecycle, CLI behavior, key invariants
- Added `handoff/pr-1466/` with architecture docs, review state, and checkout recipes for new contributors

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm build`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` (all 27 packages)
- [x] `pnpm lint` (0 errors)
- [x] `pnpm test` (all packages)
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core test`
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli test` (550+ passing)
- [x] `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-web test`
- [x] Stop command tests updated for all-sessions kill behavior
- [x] Targeted stop: 6 tests for `removeProjectFromRunning` + `projectNeedsRestart` gate
- [x] Ctrl+C graceful shutdown writes last-stop and unregisters
- [x] Dashboard sidebar shows all projects' sessions regardless of active project
- [x] Integration tests for metadata lifecycle and config-metadata service

**[PR #1466 Behavior Dashboard](https://theharshitsingh.com/static/pr-1466.html)** — open in a browser. Two tabs:
- **Behavior**: per-feature before/after comparison
- **Commit Story**: themed commit groups with descriptions

title: Enable tmux status bar in web terminal (currently forced off)
body:
## Problem

The tmux status bar is explicitly disabled when a web terminal PTY attaches to a tmux session. In `packages/web/server/mux-websocket.ts:288`:

```ts
const statusProc = spawn(this.TMUX, ["set-option", "-t", tmuxSessionId, "status", "off"]);
```

This hides useful session information that users (and agents) could see in the terminal — current session name, window list, datetime, etc.

## Proposed Fix

Change `"status", "off"` → `"status", "on"` in `mux-websocket.ts` so the tmux status bar is visible by default in the web terminal.

Optionally, configure a sensible status bar format (session name, active pane) via `set-option` for `status-right` / `status-left` to make the bar useful rather than just present.

## Context

Requested by @yyovil during design iteration on SubSession concepts. The status bar provides useful at-a-glance context when working with multiple tmux sessions/panes.

title: restore: session-level permissions lost when resuming from dashboard card
body:
## Summary

When a session is restored (via the dashboard card \"Restore\" action, or any other path that triggers \`session-manager.ts\`'s restore flow), the agent gets re-launched with **project-default permissions** instead of the **permissions the session was originally spawned with**. If the user ran the session under \`--permissions permissionless\` (or anything other than the project default), resume loses that setting and the agent starts requiring approvals again — or worse, vice versa.

## Affected agents

Any plugin whose \`getRestoreCommand\` reads \`project.agentConfig?.permissions\`:

- \`@aoagents/ao-plugin-agent-claude-code\` — \`packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts:830\`
- \`@aoagents/ao-plugin-agent-codex\` — \`packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts:736\`
- \`@aoagents/ao-plugin-agent-opencode\` — \`packages/plugins/agent-opencode/src/index.ts:~430\`
- \`@aoagents/ao-plugin-agent-kimicode\` — \`packages/plugins/agent-kimicode/src/index.ts:~575\`

(Aider + cursor are unaffected — they return \`null\` from \`getRestoreCommand\`.)

## Root cause

\`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:2764-2778\` resolves the effective launch config correctly:

\`\`\`ts
const agentLaunchConfig = {
  sessionId,
  projectConfig: projectConfigForLaunch,
  issueId: session.issueId ?? undefined,
  permissions:
    selection.role === \"orchestrator\"
      ? \"permissionless\"
      : selection.permissions,   // ← resolved per-session, not project default
  model: selection.model,
  subagent: selection.subagent,
};

if (plugins.agent.getRestoreCommand) {
  const restoreCmd = await plugins.agent.getRestoreCommand(session, projectConfigForLaunch);
  launchCommand = restoreCmd ?? plugins.agent.getLaunchCommand(agentLaunchConfig);
} else {
  launchCommand = plugins.agent.getLaunchCommand(agentLaunchConfig);
}
\`\`\`

The bug is on the second line: \`getRestoreCommand\` only receives \`(session, projectConfigForLaunch)\` — not the resolved \`agentLaunchConfig\`. So each plugin's restore path falls back to reading \`project.agentConfig?.permissions\`, which is just the project default. The per-session override (\`selection.permissions\`) is invisible to the plugin.

The \`--model\` and \`--subagent\` restore-time choices have the same issue — they're resolved on \`selection\` but the plugin can only see project-level defaults.

## Reproducer

1. In \`agent-orchestrator.yaml\`, set \`projects.<id>.agentConfig.permissions: suggest\`.
2. Spawn a session with an override: \`ao spawn <issue> --permissions permissionless\`.
3. Watch the agent run with auto-approvals (correct).
4. Kill or restart the orchestrator.
5. Resume the session (dashboard card \"Restore\" or \`ao session resume\`).
6. Actual: agent is now prompting for approvals (\`suggest\` mode) — the \`permissionless\` override was silently dropped.
7. Expected: agent resumes with \`permissionless\` — the original effective permissions.

## Fix direction

Change the \`Agent.getRestoreCommand\` signature in \`packages/core/src/types.ts:507\` to accept the full \`AgentLaunchConfig\`:

\`\`\`ts
getRestoreCommand?(
  session: Session,
  config: AgentLaunchConfig,   // ← new: carries resolved permissions / model / subagent
): Promise<string | null>;
\`\`\`

Update \`session-manager.ts:2774\` to pass \`agentLaunchConfig\` instead of \`projectConfigForLaunch\`, then update each plugin's \`getRestoreCommand\` to prefer \`config.permissions\` / \`config.model\` / \`config.subagent\` over the project defaults.

Keep \`project\` accessible via \`config.projectConfig\` so plugins don't lose anything.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] \`Agent.getRestoreCommand\` signature updated in core types
- [ ] \`session-manager.ts\` passes the full \`agentLaunchConfig\` on restore
- [ ] All four affected plugins (claude-code, codex, opencode, kimicode) read permissions + model + subagent from \`config\`, falling back to project defaults only when unset
- [ ] Unit test per plugin: restoring a session spawned with a non-default \`permissions\` emits the correct approval flag
- [ ] Regression test in \`session-manager\` that asserts \`getRestoreCommand\` receives the resolved permissions

## Out of scope

- Persisting the original spawn permissions on \`Session\` itself (we resolve via \`selection\` on every restore — the gap here is plumbing, not storage).
- Auditing what else on \`selection\` never reaches the plugin (model and subagent have the same issue, but at least model is often identical between project default and per-session override).

## Discovered in

Follow-up to #1384 / PR #1390 (kimicode plugin) while testing the restore-from-card flow on a real kimi-cli install.

title: feat: multi-repo PR lifecycle tracking — lifecycle manager skips PRs on repos that don't match project config
body:
## Problem

When a project uses git submodules (or spans multiple repos), the `repo` field in `agent-orchestrator.yaml` can only point to **one** repository. The lifecycle manager matches PRs to projects by comparing `pr.owner/pr.repo` against the configured `repo` field:

```javascript
// lifecycle-manager.js:180-182
const project = Object.values(config.projects).find((p) => {
  const [owner, repo] = p.repo.split("/");
  return owner === pr.owner && repo === pr.repo;
});
```

If an agent creates a PR on a different repo (e.g., config says `osac-project/fulfillment-service` but the PR is on `osac-project/osac-operator`), the lifecycle manager:
- Skips the PR during batch enrichment
- Never polls CI status, review decision, or merge state
- Never transitions the session to `review_pending`, `changes_requested`, `approved`, `mergeable`, or `merged`
- Never dispatches review comments or CI failure messages to the agent

The session stays stuck in `working`/`idle` forever despite the PR being open, reviewed, and eventually merged.

## Use Case

Our project (`osac-project`) is a superproject with 8 git submodules, each a separate GitHub repo:
- `osac-project/osac-operator`
- `osac-project/fulfillment-service`
- `osac-project/osac-aap`
- `osac-project/osac-installer`
- etc.

A single Jira issue may require changes in any of these repos. The agent spawns in the superproject worktree, works inside a submodule, and creates a PR on that submodule's repo.

## Proposed Solutions

### Option A: Accept multiple repos per project
```yaml
projects:
  osac-project:
    repos:
      - osac-project/osac-operator
      - osac-project/fulfillment-service
      - osac-project/osac-aap
    # or org-level match:
    repoOrg: osac-project
```

The lifecycle manager would match PRs against any repo in the list.

### Option B: Infer repo from PR URL in metadata
When the session metadata has `pr=https://github.com/osac-project/osac-operator/pull/193`, the lifecycle manager could extract `osac-project/osac-operator` from the URL and use the project's SCM plugin directly, bypassing the `repo` field match.

### Option C: Per-session repo override
Allow sessions to override the project's repo at spawn time or via metadata, so the lifecycle manager uses the session's repo instead of the project's.

## Current Workaround

We created a Claude Code PostToolUse hook that:
1. Captures PR URLs from `gh pr create` output → writes to session metadata
2. Polls `gh pr view` on a throttle → updates session status directly in metadata
3. Sends `ao send` messages to the agent on CI failure or review comments

This duplicates the lifecycle manager's logic in a bash script, which is fragile and misses features like batch enrichment, fingerprinting, and escalation.

## Related

- #1095 — Per-session worktree support for secondary repos (same multi-repo pain point, different symptom)

## Environment

- AO: latest (npm)
- OS: Linux (Fedora 41)
- Agent: Claude Code
- Tracker: Jira (custom plugin)

title: fix: reduce opencode session list churn
fix(core): prevent stale reaction dispatch on status oscillation
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1409

When `prEnrichmentCache` returns stale data that oscillates between CI failing/passing or conflicts/no-conflicts, the lifecycle manager was re-dispatching CI failure and merge conflict messages to agent sessions infinitely. The agent would dismiss them as "stale orchestrator noise" but they kept coming every 5 seconds.

## Root cause

Three reinforcing problems:

1. **Transition handler clears reaction trackers on status exit** (line ~1729): When status oscillates `ci_failed → working → ci_failed`, the `ci-failed` tracker is cleared on exit, creating a fresh tracker with `attempts: 0` on re-entry — resetting the retry budget every cycle.

2. **`maybeDispatchCIFailureDetails` clears tracker when leaving `ci_failed`** (line ~1338): Double-clears the tracker from a different code path, same effect.

3. **`maybeDispatchMergeConflicts` clears `lastMergeConflictDispatched` based on stale batch data** (line ~1531): When enrichment cache flips to `hasConflicts: false`, it clears the dedup flag. Next cycle when cache flips back to `hasConflicts: true`, the flag is gone and it dispatches again.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `lifecycle-manager.ts` | Transition handler: skip clearing `ci-failed` and `merge-conflicts` trackers on status exit |
| `lifecycle-manager.ts` | `maybeDispatchCIFailureDetails`: clear fingerprint metadata but preserve tracker when leaving `ci_failed` |
| `lifecycle-manager.ts` | `maybeDispatchMergeConflicts`: only clear dispatch flag when mergeability is from live API call, not stale batch enrichment |
| `lifecycle-manager.test.ts` | 2 new tests: CI failure oscillation and merge conflict oscillation |

## Test plan

- [x] New tests cover both oscillation scenarios
- [ ] Existing lifecycle tests pass (`pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-core test`)
- [ ] Manual verification: run a session with stale CI data, confirm no repeated dispatch

## Relationship to #1347

This is the companion fix to PR #1347 (issue #1290). That PR fixes the "CI signal never reaches dead sessions" gap in the webhook path. This PR fixes the "CI signal won't stop reaching live sessions" gap in the lifecycle polling path. Together they ensure CI signals are delivered exactly once to the right session.

Terminal should render the agent output visible in the tmux session.
