title: [Bug]: OpenCode  & Kilocode free mode is incorrectly reported as needs auth
body:
## Summary

AO reports installed OpenCode and Kilo CLIs as `unauthorized` / **Needs auth** when they have no provider credentials, even though both currently support credential-free use with public zero-cost models.

This blocks or discourages valid free-model usage. Since AO cannot prove that the user's selected model will work without credentials, the no-credential state should be advisory `unknown`, not `unauthorized`.

## Steps to reproduce

### OpenCode

1. Install OpenCode without adding provider credentials.
2. Ensure there is no provider API-key environment variable and no populated `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` or OpenCode account database.
3. Run OpenCode with one of its public free models.
4. Run `ao agent ls --refresh`.
5. Observe that OpenCode is reported as **Needs auth**.

### Kilo

1. Install the Kilo CLI without adding provider credentials or signing in.
2. Select an eligible free model such as `kilo-auto/free`.
3. Run `ao agent ls --refresh`.
4. Observe that Kilo is reported as **Needs auth** when `kilo auth list` reports `0 credentials` and `0 environment variables`.

## Expected behavior

For both adapters:

- Positively detected credentials or an active account: `authorized`.
- No detected credentials: `unknown`, allowing the user to continue with an advisory warning and use public free models at their own risk.
- Malformed or unreadable auth state: `unknown`.
- Missing binary: **Needs install**.
- Spawn remains the authoritative validation point for the selected model.

## Actual behavior

### OpenCode

The adapter treats an empty credential store/database or `opencode auth list` output containing `0 credentials` as `unauthorized`.

Relevant implementation: `backend/internal/adapters/agent/opencode/opencode.go`.

### Kilo

The adapter treats `kilo auth list` output containing both `0 credentials` and `0 environment variables` as `unauthorized`.

Relevant implementation: `backend/internal/adapters/agent/kilocode/auth.go`.

## Upstream behavior

### OpenCode

OpenCode's provider implementation supports the no-key case by retaining zero-cost models and using its public access path:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/dev/packages/opencode/src/provider/provider.ts#L166-L185

The official Zen catalog lists multiple free models:

https://opencode.ai/docs/zen

### Kilo

Kilo documents `kilo-auto/free` as requiring no configuration and documents anonymous eligible free-model requests with IP-based limits:

https://kilo.ai/docs/getting-started/using-kilo-for-free

https://kilo.ai/docs/contributing/architecture/cloud-security

https://kilo.ai/docs/gateway/usage-and-billing

Therefore, zero stored credentials describe provider-login state, not whether either CLI can run an eligible public free model.

## Proposed direction

Preserve positive credential detection as `authorized`, but normalize no-credential cases to `unknown` at each adapter boundary. Do not interpret zero credentials as proof that the CLI is unusable.

No frontend or API schema change should be necessary because `unknown` already exists and is handled as advisory readiness.

## AO version

Originally reproduced at commit `43b94c073`; fix work is based on current `upstream/main`.

## Environment

macOS/Darwin 25.5.0 arm64.

## Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing upstream issues for duplicates.
- [x] I removed secrets and tokens from this report.

title: feat(reviews): rework the Reviews tab and fix reviewer session handling
body:
## Summary

Reworks the session inspector's Reviews tab around what it can actually tell you, and fixes three reviewer-runtime bugs found while testing it against a real repo.

**Reviews tab**

- hide the tab entirely when the session has no pull request, instead of showing an empty shell
- drop the redundant panel heading and the repeated agent role label
- show each reviewer's logo next to its name, sourced from a small harness→logo registry
- keep every past review pass, grouped by the reviewer that ran it, with a tab per reviewer above the PR list
- pick the reviewer agent for a single pass from the panel, reusing the same picker as project settings rather than a second one that could drift
- collapse PR rows by default, including the first one, so a long review doesn't push the rest of the panel off screen
- lock the reviewer picker while a pass is running and say why — multi-harness isn't supported yet
- let each session opt out of handing findings back to its worker agent

**Stale verdicts**

A "changes requested" verdict from before the latest push was rendered as if it still applied. It now reads as a previous verdict, with the commit it was left against.

**Reviewer runtime fixes**

- a terminal that outlived its agent is no longer treated as a live reviewer
- each review pass gets its own agent session id rather than reusing the pane's
- the tmux foreground probe uses `list-panes` instead of `display-message`

## Why

The reviewer's liveness check asked tmux whether the session existed. It always did — a tmux pane survives the process that started it and falls back to a shell. So AO decided the previous reviewer was still running and delivered the next review prompt to it, which meant **typing prompt text into an interactive shell inside the worker's worktree**. Harmless in practice only because the prompt opened with `Read` and the target was a non-executable `.md`.

Fixing liveness surfaced the next layer: claude-code derives a deterministic `--session-id` from the AO session id, and the reviewer handle is stable per worker, so a second pass on the same worker collided with the first — `Session ID … is already in use`. Confirmed by reproducing the UUIDv5 derivation from the handle and matching the id in the error. Passes now carry the run id, so each gets its own session. codex and opencode take no session flag and were never affected.

The probe added for liveness then turned out to be inert. `display-message` resolves an exact session target (`=name`) to the session but reports nothing for a pane-scoped format, so it returned empty on every call — and empty means "cannot tell", which callers treat as "keep the pane". The check kept answering yes. `list-panes` resolves the same target correctly and is what the codebase already uses for pane pids.

## Validation

- `go build ./...` and `go test ./internal/...` — no failures
- `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx vitest run` — 1191 tests across 91 files pass
- `go generate ./internal/httpd/apispec/...` produces no diff, so the spec and the generated TS client are in sync
- tmux probe behaviour checked against the live server rather than assumed: `display-message` with `=name` returns empty, without it returns `zsh`, `list-panes` returns `zsh` either way
- reviews run end-to-end against a real GitHub repo in the desktop app

Not yet re-run end-to-end after the last commit: the `list-panes` fix is covered by a unit test and verified against live tmux, but a full claude-code pass on a restarted daemon hasn't been done since.

## Follow-ups

- a codex pass was observed posting its review successfully and then reporting `Conversation interrupted` — separate cause, still open

title: fix: allow OpenCode and Kilo free models without detected auth
body:
## Summary

OpenCode and Kilo can run eligible public free models without stored provider credentials. AO currently interprets those valid credential-free states as `unauthorized`, which surfaces as **Needs auth** and incorrectly implies the agents cannot be used.

This change:

- maps OpenCode and Kilo no-credential states to `unknown` instead of `unauthorized`
- preserves positive credential and account detection as `authorized`
- covers OpenCode `0 credentials`, empty `auth.json`, and an empty account database
- covers Kilo `0 credentials` together with `0 environment variables`
- keeps readiness advisory while leaving agent spawn as the authoritative runtime validation
- adds regression tests for the affected credential-free states

No frontend or API schema changes are required because AO already supports the `unknown` auth state.

Official references: [OpenCode free models](https://opencode.ai/docs/models/#free-models), [Kilo free model](https://kilo.ai/docs/getting-started/using-kilo-for-free), and [Kilo anonymous request handling](https://kilo.ai/docs/contributing/architecture/cloud-security).

title: Open first browser content automatically and badge background activity
body:
## What

Make the session Browser’s attention behavior reflect actual browser content and activity:

- Automatically open Browser when the session receives its first real content.
- Respect the user’s tab choice after that first reveal.
- Show the Browser glow when new preview or agent-browser activity occurs while Browser is hidden.
- Clear the glow when Browser becomes visible.
- Reset the lifecycle after the preview is cleared, allowing the next first content to auto-open again.
- Clear stale navigation state when switching sessions.

Users can now continue working in Summary, Reviews, or Files without Browser repeatedly stealing focus, while still receiving a meaningful indicator when background browser work occurs.

## Why

The previous glow was driven by terminal-output URL detection rather than browser state.

Any HTTP(S) URL printed in the terminal—including replayed terminal history—could activate the Browser glow even when the Browser had no page to display. At the same time, a legitimate first preview did not automatically reveal Browser.

This made the indicator misleading: it could appear with nothing to show and did not reliably guide users to actual preview content.

## How

Browser attention is now driven by authoritative session state:

- A non-empty `previewUrl` or browser navigation URL begins a content lifecycle.
- The first content in that lifecycle selects Browser and expands the inspector.
- Later `ao preview` revisions glow when the user is viewing another inspector tab.
- Agent-browser commands also glow while Browser is hidden, including commands that do not navigate.
- Opening Browser consumes the unseen state.
- Clearing all browser content resets both the reveal and unseen state.
- Explicitly clicking a terminal link still opens Browser immediately and persists the selected target.

### Removed

- Removed `detect-urls.ts` and its tests.
- Removed terminal output decoding through `useTerminalSession.onOutput`.
- Removed the `TerminalPane` watcher that treated printed URLs as Browser activity.

These paths existed only to power the passive URL glow. Clickable terminal links use the separate xterm link handler and remain supported.

## Testing

- `npm test -- src/renderer/components/SessionView.test.tsx src/renderer/components/SessionInspector.test.tsx src/renderer/components/TerminalPane.test.tsx src/renderer/hooks/useBrowserView.test.tsx src/renderer/hooks/useTerminalSession.test.tsx`
  - 5 test files passed
  - 158 tests passed
- `npm run typecheck`
  - Passed
- Manually verified the Browser auto-open, background glow, glow clearing, and tab-preservation behavior in the desktop app.

## Checklist

- [x] Branched from `main`
- [x] One focused change
- [x] Follows `AGENTS.md` conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added or updated for the user-visible behavior
- [x] Relevant local frontend checks pass

title: Add immutable Chat/TUI session modes and structured orchestrator Chat
body:
## Problem

AO currently has one interaction model for a running agent session: launch the provider's native CLI/TUI inside the selected terminal runtime, then deliver later messages by pasting text and Enter into that pane.

That model is valuable for broad agent compatibility, native provider workflows, and terminal escape hatches, but it is not a reliable substrate for a first-class chat product:

- a successful pane write is not an agent delivery acknowledgement;
- terminal bytes do not provide durable, typed conversation history;
- tool calls, diffs, plans, permissions, streaming deltas, usage, and errors must be inferred from terminal output or separate hooks;
- a keystroke intended as a prompt can land in a permission dialog or shell;
- a Chat UI backed by an SDK while a native TUI remains writable would create two independent conversation controllers that can diverge.

The unsafe design is:

```text
Chat UI -> Claude SDK / Codex app-server -> provider conversation A
Terminal -> native Claude/Codex TUI      -> provider conversation B (or a racing client on A)
```

Even if both clients start with the same provider conversation ID, concurrent writers can race on turns, permissions, compaction, model/mode changes, and reconnect state.

AO should instead let the user choose a **default session interface**:

- **Chat**: AO starts and owns a structured provider controller (Claude Agent SDK, Codex app-server, ACP, or another supported machine protocol). Chat is the default session surface. The Terminal option opens a plain shell in the same worktree, not a second native agent TUI.
- **Terminal UI (TUI)**: AO behaves as it does today. The provider's native TUI is the only conversation controller and the session opens in the existing terminal experience.

This must be a durable, immutable per-session controller mode, not merely a preferred tab. The global preference selects the mode for newly created sessions; every later spawn, send, restore, activity, permission, and UI decision uses the mode stored on the session.

## User outcome

As an AO user, I can choose **Chat** or **Terminal UI** as my default session interface.

When I choose Chat:

- newly created orchestrators open in a first-class Chat UI;
- workers spawned later use Chat when their selected harness has a production-ready structured driver;
- desktop, mobile, `ao send`, browser annotations, orchestrator coordination, and automated reactions all feed the same AO-owned conversation controller;
- I can open a normal shell in the session worktree without starting a second copy of the agent;
- messages, streaming output, tool calls, permissions, diffs, plans/todos, errors, and usage are represented as structured events;
- daemon/app restarts resume the same provider conversation.

When I choose Terminal UI:

- newly created sessions use the current native TUI workflow;
- the session opens in the current terminal view;
- existing terminal delivery, hooks, restore, and runtime behavior remain intact;
- no structured SDK/app-server controller is started for that session.

Changing the preference affects **future sessions only**. It never changes the controller of an existing session.

## Final architecture

```text
Daemon setting
defaultSessionMode = chat | tui
             ↓
Spawn resolves and persists immutable session.mode
             ↓
      ┌──────┴──────┐
      │             │
 mode=chat       mode=tui
      │             │
Conversation     Native Agent
Controller       + tmux/conpty
      │             │
Codex app-server Existing guarded pane delivery
over stdio
      │
Provider thread
```

For the project orchestrator, the durable human-facing conversation is project-scoped even though the runtime session is replaceable:

```text
Project conversation
├── ordered turns and items
├── durable actions
├── delegation records
└── current orchestrator binding
        ├── AO session ID
        ├── provider conversation ID
        └── controller generation
```

Worker conversations remain session-scoped.

The first production Chat provider is **Codex app-server over its default stdio transport**. Claude Agent SDK is the second structured provider after the provider-neutral contract and Codex vertical slice are proven. Chat mode does not use Codex remote TUI attachment, WebSocket transport, or a provider TUI as an approval fallback.

## Required invariants

These are load-bearing acceptance rules, not implementation suggestions:

1. **Exactly one controller per session.** A live session has one effective mode and one active conversation controller.
2. **Mode is immutable.** `session.mode` is chosen before controller launch, persisted with the session, and cannot be patched later.
3. **Settings affect only new sessions.** Changing `defaultSessionMode` never mutates existing rows or restarts existing controllers.
4. **Server-side enforcement.** The daemon dispatches from the persisted session mode. UI visibility alone is not a safety boundary.
5. **All senders share one dispatcher.** Desktop, mobile, CLI, browser annotations, lifecycle reactions, reviewer results, orchestrator notices, and internal coordination cannot bypass mode-aware routing.
6. **Chat mode never launches the native agent TUI.** Its Terminal action creates/opens only a session-scoped shell terminal.
7. **TUI mode never launches a structured chat driver.** It continues to use the existing runtime/pane path.
8. **No silent fallback.** If Chat is requested for an unsupported or unhealthy harness, creation fails with a typed error and the client may offer an explicit “Create as TUI” action.
9. **Explicit fallback is decided before creation.** Choosing “Create as TUI” produces a TUI session from birth; it does not start Chat and then switch.
10. **Existing sessions remain TUI.** The migration backfills every pre-feature session to `tui`.
11. **Wrong-generation events are ignored.** Events from a dead/replaced Chat controller cannot mutate the current session.
12. **Provider context has one owner.** AO controls provider input ordering; clients never invoke provider transports directly.
13. **PTY output is not chat history.** No code converts raw terminal bytes into canonical assistant/tool messages.
14. **Structured events are authoritative in Chat mode.** Existing native hooks/terminal markers remain authoritative in TUI mode and must not race Chat projections.
15. **Terminal availability does not imply conversation availability.** A Chat shell can outlive or fail independently from the structured provider controller, and vice versa.
16. **Orchestrator conversation identity is project-scoped.** Replacing the orchestrator changes the runtime binding, not the human-facing conversation ID.
17. **Orchestrator replacement preserves mode by default.** A clean replacement inherits the current orchestrator's persisted mode unless an explicit creation-time mode change is requested.
18. **Native-context discontinuity is explicit.** If a replacement cannot resume the provider conversation, AO appends a system boundary and never pretends native context survived.

## Current architecture affected

The implementation should preserve current daemon/API boundaries and work from these existing seams:

| Area | Existing seam and required change |
|---|---|
| `backend/internal/domain/session.go` | `SessionRecord` lacks controller mode; `SessionMetadata` runtime IDs describe the native-TUI path and cannot identify a structured stream. |
| `backend/internal/ports/session.go` | Add requested/effective mode to `SpawnConfig`. |
| `backend/internal/ports/agent.go` | Keep the native CLI contract; do not stretch it into the structured conversation protocol. |
| `backend/internal/ports/outbound.go` | Replace direct use of terminal-specific `AgentMessenger` at shared send call sites with mode-aware dispatch. |
| `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go` | Split `Manager.Spawn`/`Manager.Send` after persisted-mode resolution: native runtime for TUI, conversation controller for Chat. |

## Product behavior

### General setting

Add a daemon-backed setting:

```text
Default session interface
  Chat
  Terminal UI
```

Requirements:

- default to `tui` on upgrade for backward compatibility;
- explain that it applies to newly created sessions;
- expose a concise capability warning when Chat is selected;
- update through a daemon API so desktop, mobile, CLI, and headless spawns resolve one value;
- store under AO's existing `~/.ao` data boundary;
- do not use only Electron localStorage;
- do not mutate live sessions when changed.

Suggested copy:

> Controls how new orchestrator and worker sessions talk to their agent. Chat uses a supported structured agent connection. Terminal UI uses the agent's native terminal interface. Existing sessions are unchanged.

### Chat-mode session screen

The central session surface should be:

```text
Session
├── Chat (default and authoritative)
├── Terminal (plain worktree shell)
└── Inspector (summary, changes, PRs, files, browser, reviews)
```

Chat must support:

- initial prompt and follow-up user messages;
- streaming assistant content;
- stable message/turn identity;
- tool-call start/progress/completion;
- command, cwd, exit status, stdout/stderr, and duration where provided;
- file changes and diffs;
- plans/todos and progress state;
- permission/request-user-input cards with explicit decisions;
- interrupt/cancel;
- steering only when the driver declares it;
- queued follow-ups when steering is unavailable;
- structured errors and reconnect state;
- session resume/replay;
- token/cost/usage when provided;
- links, code blocks, copy actions, and accessible keyboard behavior;
- scroll anchoring that does not yank the user away from history;
- unread/new-output indication when the user is scrolled up;
- loading, empty, unsupported, crashed, reconnecting, and terminated states.

The Terminal action must use the existing session-scoped `shell_terminals` workflow. It must not attach to or launch the provider's native TUI.

### TUI-mode session screen

Keep the existing central terminal experience:

- native provider TUI remains the only conversation controller;
- existing shell/reviewer tabs continue to work;
- current send, terminal mux, hooks, activity, resume, and runtime safety remain intact;
- Chat is either hidden or replaced with a non-interactive explanation that this session was created in Terminal UI mode;
- no Chat driver process is started.

### Explicit one-off override

The first implementation may omit a per-spawn selector if the global setting is sufficient. The API/domain should nevertheless distinguish:

- no mode requested: resolve `defaultSessionMode`;
- explicit `chat` or `tui`: validate and persist that value.

This supports:

- “Create as TUI” after a typed unsupported-Chat failure;
- CLI/headless automation that needs deterministic behavior;
- future project/role defaults without changing session semantics.

An override is a creation-time input, never a live-session toggle.

### Unsupported Chat provider

Strict behavior is preferred:

```text
requested mode = chat
driver missing/unhealthy/incompatible
  -> reject before durable session/worktree creation where possible
  -> return typed capability error
  -> client offers explicit TUI creation
```

Do not silently create a TUI session. Silent fallback makes the setting untrustworthy and can put the user into a native terminal experience they deliberately disabled.

## Configuration resolution

Recommended precedence for a spawn:

1. explicit request mode, if present;
2. future project/role override, if introduced;
3. daemon-owned user `defaultSessionMode`;
4. compatibility default `tui`.

The effective mode must be resolved before the controller launches and written into the seed session record.

The harness and mode are separate decisions:

```text
harness = claude-code | codex | opencode | ...
mode    = chat | tui
```

A harness may implement:

- TUI only;
- Chat only in the future;
- both, selectable per session.

Do not encode modes as new harness names such as `claude-chat` or `codex-tui`; that would duplicate agent configuration and make capability discovery harder.

## Durable model and migration

Add a new SQLite migration; never edit an already-merged migration.

Minimum session facts:

```text
sessions.session_mode                  TEXT NOT NULL CHECK IN ('chat', 'tui')
sessions.provider_conversation_id      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
sessions.controller_generation         TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
```

Naming may change during implementation, but the concepts must remain explicit.

Migration rules:

- add `session_mode` with/backfilled to `tui`;
- existing `agent_session_id` compatibility must be audited before deciding whether to reuse, rename, or supersede it;
- do not conflate terminal `runtime_launch_id` with a Chat controller generation;
- include new fields in session insert/update/get/list queries;
- regenerate sqlc from query/migration sources;
- update storage round-trip and migration tests;
- update CDC session payloads only where clients need mode/controller state;
- use DB triggers for durable Chat event CDC rather than manual parallel store emission.

### Conversation persistence

Use a small stable durable core rather than a table or schema migration for every provider event subtype:

| Durable concept | Scope and purpose | Important identity |
|---|---|---|
| `conversations` | Project-scoped orchestrator narrative or session-scoped worker narrative | scope kind/id, current orchestrator binding, predecessor/boundary metadata |
| `conversation_turns` | One user/automation request and the agent work that follows | conversation, handling AO session, controller generation, provider turn ID, state |
| `conversation_items` | One ordered readable unit: message, activity, approval, delegation, summary, error, or system boundary | conversation sequence, revision, kind, origin, provider item ID |
| `conversation_commands` | Crash-safe provider-bound command/outbox row | conversation + client message ID, command state, provider request ID |
| `conversation_actions` | Crash-safe AO operation requested from Chat | idempotency key, request message, target, confirmation, state, typed result/error |
| `conversation_provider_state` | Provider binding, cursor, controller lease/generation, health | AO session + provider binding |
| `conversation_provider_events` | Dedupe for provider events that have stable native IDs | AO session + provider event ID |
| `session_delegations` | Orchestrator-to-worker assignment and action correlation | orchestrator session/turn, worker session, action, assignment |

```text

changed_files

```

Provider-specific detail stays inside typed item projections. Unknown native events may be retained as bounded diagnostics, but they do not automatically become timeline semantics.

Ordering rules:

- conversation item `sequence` is immutable and conversation-scoped;
- item `revision` increases when streaming changes one existing item;
- timestamps are display metadata, not primary ordering;
- provider events from an inactive controller generation/lease are rejected;
- provider event IDs deduplicate observations;
- private/raw reasoning is never accepted into the normalized model;
- message origin is a durable field: `human`, `worker`, `orchestrator`, `automation`, `daemon`, or `provider`;
- worker/automation identity is stored structurally, never inferred from text prefixes.

### Project-scoped orchestrator continuity

The orchestrator runtime is replaceable; the project conversation is not.

On clean orchestrator replacement:

1. refetch and lock the current active orchestrator;
2. preserve its persisted mode unless the caller explicitly requests a different mode before creation;
3. create the replacement session with a fresh controller generation;
4. update the project conversation's current orchestrator binding;
5. record the exact old/new AO session IDs;
6. resume the same provider conversation when the driver can prove safe continuity;
7. otherwise start a new provider conversation and append a visible system boundary explaining that provider-native context restarted;
8. never reinterpret AO's durable history as provider model context unless the provider protocol explicitly supports that operation.

Changing the global default alone must not change the mode of a replacement orchestrator.

### Durable global preference

AO currently lacks a general daemon-owned user-preferences model. Introduce the smallest typed solution that can safely serve desktop, mobile, and CLI.

Preferred properties:

- a typed singleton settings record/table or equivalent daemon-owned store;
- `default_session_mode` constrained to `chat|tui`;
- default `tui` when absent;
- GET/PATCH service and controller boundary;
- atomic writes;
- API validation and stable error envelope;
- no Electron default app-data paths;
- no renderer-only source of truth.

Avoid adding unrelated settings in the same change.

## Chat conversation domain

Add a provider-neutral domain that is separate from terminal runtime ports.

Illustrative contract:

```go
type ConversationConnector interface {
    Probe(ctx context.Context, cfg ChatStartConfig) (ChatCapabilities, error)
    Start(ctx context.Context, cfg ChatStartConfig) (ConversationConnection, ConversationRef, error)
    Resume(ctx context.Context, cfg ChatResumeConfig) (ConversationConnection, error)
}

type ConversationConnection interface {
    Snapshot(ctx context.Context) (ProviderConversationSnapshot, error)
    Watch(ctx context.Context, cursor string, sink ProviderEventSink) error
    SendTurn(ctx context.Context, msg UserMessage) (TurnRef, error)
    Steer(ctx context.Context, turn TurnRef, msg UserMessage) error
    Interrupt(ctx context.Context, turn TurnRef) error
    ResolvePermission(ctx context.Context, requestID string, decision Decision) error
    Close() error
}
```

Exact method grouping is open to implementation, but the port must not:

- expose provider DTOs outside its adapter;
- depend on frontend types;
- use terminal byte streams as semantic events;
- treat an empty user message as Enter;
- mix shell-terminal lifecycle with provider conversation lifecycle.

### Capabilities

The agent catalog should expose structured capabilities independently of installation/auth status:

```text
chat
history
resume
streaming
tools
permissions
diffs
plans
interrupt
steer
queue
usage
models
```

Each capability should have an explicit status where necessary:

- supported;
- unsupported;
- experimental;
- temporarily unavailable due to version/auth/preflight.

Define a minimum production Chat capability set before enabling the Chat setting for a harness. At minimum, an agent that can mutate the workspace should not be considered Chat-ready unless permissions, errors, completion, and resume/recovery are safely represented.

## Provider-neutral projection and live protocol

Provider adapters normalize native events into AO turns/items and a small semantic live protocol. Persist durable item state; do not persist every token as a standalone domain event.

Suggested live envelope:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "liveEventSequence": 291,
  "streamGeneration": "daemon-generation-id",
  "conversationId": "conv-project-ao",
  "sessionId": "ao-12",
  "provider": "codex",
  "providerConversationId": "thr_...",
  "controllerGeneration": "gen_...",
  "type": "item.upsert",
  "payload": {
    "itemId": "item_...",
    "sequence": 42,
    "revision": 7
  }
}
```

Initial semantic stream types:

```text
subscribed
turn.upsert
item.upsert
action.upsert
message.delta
capabilities
controller.state
resync_required
error
```

Durable item kinds and typed `detail_json` represent tools, commands, diffs, plans, permissions, usage, delegations, summaries, and errors without leaking provider DTOs into the renderer.

Rules:

- preserve provider-native IDs as opaque correlation metadata;
- AO live event IDs/sequences and durable item sequences are provider-neutral;
- **durable item sequence and live stream sequence are different counters**;
- provider-specific additions do not leak into shared rendering components;
- streaming deltas update one item revision in place instead of allocating new timeline positions;
- final turn/item state and provider cursor flush immediately;
- intermediate deltas may be coalesced in memory and persisted at bounded intervals;
- terminal ANSI/control sequences never enter this protocol;
- large raw output is bounded and references durable artifacts when necessary;
- secrets and raw credentials are redacted before persistence or UI delivery;
- private/raw reasoning is excluded from the normalized model.

### Snapshot/subscription boundary

The snapshot must expose both counters:

```json
{
  "conversationId": "conv-project-ao",
  "scope": { "kind": "project", "projectId": "agent-orchestrator" },
  "currentOrchestratorSessionId": "ao-12",
  "latestItemSequence": 149,
  "liveEventCursor": 291,
  "streamGeneration": "daemon-generation-id",
  "capabilities": {},
  "controller": { "state": "connected", "error": null },
  "turns": [],
  "items": [],
  "hasMoreBefore": false
}
```

Client bootstrap:

1. fetch the authoritative durable snapshot;
2. render the returned turns/items;
3. subscribe to the semantic mux channel **after `liveEventCursor`**, never after `latestItemSequence`;
4. apply revision-aware deltas/upserts;
5. refetch/resubscribe when stream generation changes or a revision/cursor gap is detected.

This closes the snapshot/subscribe race without misusing SQLite CDC as a token stream.

### CDC versus semantic mux

- DB triggers emit compact invalidation events for durable conversation/turn/item/action/provider-state changes.
- Existing `/api/v1/events` CDC continues to invalidate/refetch session, PR, review, check, workspace, and conversation facts.
- Existing `/mux` gains a conversation channel for high-frequency semantic deltas and authoritative upserts.
- CDC payloads never become chat prose.
- Terminal payload buffering remains separate from semantic conversation backpressure.

Suggested mux subscription:

```json
{
  "ch": "conversation",
  "type": "subscribe",
  "conversationId": "conv-project-ao",
  "streamGeneration": "known-generation",
  "afterEventSequence": 291
}
```

Backpressure rules:

- coalesce message deltas approximately every 16–50 ms;
- keep at most one replaceable pending delta per streaming item;
- never drop a final upsert, completion, approval, action transition, or error;
- include base/current item revision where needed;
- revision gaps require a snapshot resync;
- bound semantic queues independently per client;
- disconnect a slow client rather than blocking provider readers.

## Message ordering, idempotency, and delivery

Use a per-session serialized command path:

```text
client input
  -> validate session/mode/capability
  -> assign clientMessageId/messageId
  -> persist queued intent
  -> controller queue/lease
  -> provider send
  -> persist accepted/rejected outcome
  -> stream provider events
```

Requirements:

- all AO send surfaces accept or generate a stable client message ID;
- duplicate client retries do not create duplicate provider turns;
- only one dispatch operation mutates a provider conversation at a time;
- mid-turn messages follow declared driver semantics:
  - steer when supported and explicitly intended;
  - otherwise queue until idle;
  - never paste into a permission dialog;
- uncertain provider acknowledgement is surfaced as uncertain rather than automatically retried;
- controller restart reconciliation resolves queued/in-flight records conservatively;
- automated messages use the same queue and do not bypass user messages;
- provider-generated sequence gaps trigger replay/reconciliation where supported.

The provider conversation is authoritative for model context. AO's durable event ledger is authoritative for product ordering, rendering, delivery state, and orchestration. AO must not maintain a second independently writable model transcript.

## Chat controller ownership and recovery

Each Chat session needs a single daemon-owned controller actor/worker:

- one live owner per `session_id`;
- one provider conversation ID;
- one controller generation;
- serialized commands;
- cancellation and shutdown;
- bounded reconnect/backoff;
- stale-generation event rejection;
- explicit health/readiness state.

On daemon restart:

1. read the persisted session mode;
2. do not start a native TUI for a Chat session;
3. resume the stored provider conversation;
4. reconcile provider history/status where supported;
5. project any missing durable events idempotently;
6. mark an interrupted/unknown turn honestly;
7. resume queued work only when duplicate execution is ruled out.

Do not silently create a new provider conversation when resume fails. Surface a recovery state with user choices such as retry, inspect diagnostics, or create a new session.

### Process supervision

V1 launches a daemon-managed Codex app-server and communicates through the app-server's default JSONL stdio transport.

Why stdio:

- it is the stable/default transport;
- the Go daemon is the only interactive provider client in Chat mode;
- no remote native TUI must attach;
- no new Unix socket, WebSocket, TCP listener, capability token, or Windows loopback transport is required;
- it removes multi-client approval ownership and remote backpressure from the V1 architecture.

The V1 spike must decide whether one daemon-managed app-server multiplexes several AO/Codex threads or each Chat session gets an isolated app-server process. Compare resource use, failure blast radius, configuration consistency, approval routing, and restart behavior before locking this process topology. Either topology still has one writable AO controller per provider thread.

Claude Agent SDK is a later provider. Its integration requires a packaging decision because AO's daemon is Go while the Agent SDK is exposed through supported non-Go runtimes. The likely shape is a small daemon-owned provider bridge/sidecar with structured local IPC. Requirements:

- it is backend infrastructure, not Electron renderer logic;
- ship it through the canonical desktop distribution;
- keep all runtime state under `~/.ao`;
- version/protocol handshake before session creation;
- no network listener beyond existing allowed AO boundaries;
- prefer stdio or a protected local IPC endpoint;
- log safely and redact secrets;
- expose health and graceful shutdown;
- support deterministic integration tests with a fake bridge.

Evaluate provider-by-provider whether a reconnectable broker is needed to preserve in-progress turns across daemon restarts. Provider session resume may recover completed context but not an actively executing turn.

## Spawn architecture

Do not grow `session_manager.Manager.Spawn` into a large provider/mode conditional.

Refactor only as needed to establish real shared phases:

```text
resolve project/harness/mode/config
validate selected controller capability
create seed session with immutable mode
materialize/provision workspace
write attachments/system instructions
start exactly one controller:
  tui  -> existing Agent + Runtime path
  chat -> ChatDriver path
persist controller identity
mark lifecycle spawned
deliver initial prompt through the selected controller
```

Rollback must understand which resources exist:

- workspace created but no controller;
- TUI runtime created;
- Chat provider conversation created;
- shell terminal created independently;
- provider conversation created but AO persistence failed.

Chat rollback should not archive/delete provider history unless that destructive behavior is explicitly designed and tested. Prefer preserving recoverable provider context and recording an orphan/recovery fact.

## Restore, kill, cleanup, and reaper behavior

Every lifecycle operation must branch from persisted mode:

### Restore

- TUI: retain current native restore command/runtime behavior.
- Chat: resume the provider conversation through the Chat driver.
- never fall back across modes;
- rotate controller generation before accepting new events;
- preserve cleanup-generation fencing.

### Kill/terminate

- TUI: current runtime teardown.
- Chat: interrupt active turn, close driver/broker ownership, retain durable history according to provider policy, terminate session;
- shell terminals follow their existing cleanup semantics;
- a failed provider probe is not proof the session is dead.

### Reaper

- separate Chat controller liveness from shell terminal liveness;
- do not derive Chat death from a missing terminal handle;
- do not derive TUI death from a missing Chat driver;
- keep unknown probe results non-terminal;
- reconcile orphaned controller processes safely.

### Cleanup

- preserve current dirty-worktree safety;
- delete/archive chat event rows only under the session's explicit cleanup policy;
- avoid destructive provider-history deletion by default.

## Activity and status projection

Current activity derives from hooks and terminal/runtime observations. Add a mode-aware projector:

- Chat mode:
  - `turn.started` -> active;
  - permission/user-input request -> blocked/waiting input as appropriate;
  - completed turn -> waiting input/idle;
  - controller failure -> exited or a new durable fact feeding derived status;
- TUI mode:
  - preserve existing hook/activity behavior.

Rules:

- do not persist a second display status;
- continue deriving user-facing status from durable facts;
- disable or fence duplicate hook signals for Chat-mode provider processes;
- preserve SCM-derived status precedence;
- ensure a Chat permission resolution clears only the matching request;
- handle parallel/subagent tool events using stable IDs rather than tool-name heuristics.

Do not use the global preference to render an existing session. Always use the mode returned on that session.

### Chat workspace

Build composable components around normalized domain events, for example:

```text
ChatWorkspace
├── ConversationHeader
├── MessageTimeline
│   ├── UserMessage
│   ├── OriginMessage
│   ├── AssistantMessage
│   ├── ToolCallCard
│   ├── CommandCard
│   ├── DiffCard
│   ├── PlanCard
│   ├── PermissionCard
│   ├── UserInputCard
│   ├── DelegationCard
│   ├── CoordinationSummaryCard
│   ├── ActionCard
│   └── ErrorCard
├── ScrollToLatestControl
├── Composer
└── ChatStatusBar
```

Requirements:

- thin renderer: all lifecycle, ordering, capability, and permission decisions stay in the daemon;
- keyed incremental rendering without replacing completed items;
- markdown/code rendering with safe link handling;
- accessible focus movement for permission/input requests;
- keyboard submit vs newline behavior;
- initial spawn attachments may continue through existing safe workspace materialization; follow-up Chat attachments are deferred until MIME, quota, provider-input, and cleanup policy are designed;
- optimistic user message state reconciles by message ID;
- explicit queued/sending/accepted/uncertain/failed states;
- preserve draft per session;
- reconnect from durable history, not an in-memory-only transcript;
- virtualize/bound very long histories;
- no provider-specific `if (claude)` rendering in shared components.

For orchestrator Chat:

- composer copy and empty state make clear that requests are project-level coordination;
- human, worker, automation, daemon, and provider origins remain distinguishable;
- delegation cards are driven by durable `session_delegations` and authoritative session facts;
- worker cards show requested, provisioning, started, working, waiting, blocked, completed, failed, or terminated;
- changed files on worker turns come from git facts;
- orchestrator summaries describe coordination and never imply that the orchestrator directly edited worker files;
- destructive or ownership-changing AO actions render an object-specific confirmation and refetch preconditions before execution;
- ambiguous natural-language targets produce candidate cards and no mutation.

### Chat terminal

Reuse the existing session-scoped shell-terminal hooks and daemon service:

- Chat's Terminal button opens/selects a shell under the session;
- shell tab clearly says Shell/Terminal, not Claude/Codex;
- do not show the hidden provider conversation ID in copy-pasteable commands;
- warn in documentation that manually launching a provider CLI creates an unmanaged conversation;
- filesystem changes are immediately shared through the worktree, but shell command text/output is not automatically added to model context.

### TUI workspace

Keep current behavior and tests. Add only:

- mode badge/metadata where helpful;
- optional explanation that this session uses Terminal UI;
- explicit lack of Chat rather than a broken empty timeline.

### Settings UX

Add the General Settings control backed by daemon queries/mutations:

- initial loading and daemon-unavailable state;
- two options with concise descriptions;
- “Applies to new sessions” helper text;
- capability warning when Chat has limited harness coverage;
- mutation error feedback;
- do not optimistically change spawn behavior until the daemon confirms persistence.

### Spawn UX

- normal create uses the default without requiring an extra choice;
- typed unsupported-Chat error opens a confirmation offering “Create as Terminal UI”;
- confirmation retries with explicit `mode: tui`;
- do not silently retry;
- show the effective mode on success/navigate.

## Security and trust boundaries

- Keep the primary daemon listener loopback-only and unauthenticated as designed.
- The opt-in LAN listener continues to require bearer-password middleware and must not gain control-only routes.
- Chat history/events exposed through mobile must follow existing LAN route/auth policy.
- Do not create a new network-facing provider bridge.
- Provider bridge local IPC must not be reachable by arbitrary network clients.
- Treat provider event payloads and command output as untrusted display data.
- Sanitize markdown/links and never render provider HTML directly.
- Redact secrets, tokens, environment values, and sensitive paths from durable logs/events where required.
- Permission decisions must be explicit typed actions; never derive them from a generic Send/Enter.
- Shell terminal remains a powerful local escape hatch and should preserve existing user expectations.
- All Electron state remains under `~/.ao/electron`; daemon/provider state remains under `~/.ao`.

## Failure modes and product handling

| Failure | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| Chat selected for unsupported harness | Reject with typed error; offer explicit TUI creation |
| Driver binary/bridge missing | Fail before durable creation when possible |
| Auth missing | Report auth-required and offer setup/retry; do not silently open native TUI |
| Provider protocol version mismatch | Mark driver incompatible and keep TUI available for new explicit sessions |
| Provider process exits before first prompt | Roll back safely or park recoverable terminated session with clear reason |
| Provider accepts turn but AO loses connection | Mark delivery uncertain; reconcile history before retry |
| Duplicate client retry | Return existing message/turn outcome |
| Daemon restarts during idle | Resume same provider conversation |
| Daemon restarts during active turn | Reattach/reconcile if supported; otherwise surface interrupted/unknown without duplicate execution |
| Permission request arrives while user sends | Serialize actions; never interpret send as permission resolution |
| Old controller emits after restore | Reject by generation |
| Shell survives while Chat driver dies | Keep shell available; show Chat recovery state |
| Chat driver survives while shell exits | Chat continues; allow opening a new shell |
| User manually starts native agent in shell | It is unmanaged and not merged into AO Chat |
| Setting changes with live sessions | Live sessions unchanged |
| History is very large | Page/virtualize; do not load entire transcript synchronously |
| Unknown provider event | Retain bounded diagnostics; do not guess semantic UI |

## Testing plan

### Domain/config

- validate `chat|tui`;
- reject unknown mode;
- default to `tui`;
- precedence: explicit request over daemon default;
- setting changes affect only future resolutions;
- mode cannot be updated after creation;
- capability resolution per harness.

### Storage/migrations

- fresh database defaults correctly;
- upgraded database backfills existing sessions as TUI;
- session mode and provider conversation identity round-trip;
- controller generation rotates/persists;
- settings round-trip;
- project-scoped orchestrator conversation survives replacement;
- worker conversation remains session-scoped;
- turns/items preserve sequence and revision monotonicity;
- actions/delegations preserve correlation and idempotency;
- provider event/cursor update is atomic with its durable projection;
- trigger-backed CDC emits expected rows;
- no generated sqlc files are hand-edited;
- migration down/up behavior follows repository policy.

### Service/session manager

- TUI spawn follows existing runtime path and starts no Chat driver;
- Chat spawn starts Chat driver and creates no native agent pane;
- unsupported Chat fails before workspace creation where possible;
- explicit TUI fallback creates TUI from birth;
- initial prompt uses selected controller;
- send dispatches by persisted mode, not caller-provided/default mode;
- restore cannot cross modes;
- kill/cleanup resource ownership per mode;
- rollback at each spawn failure boundary;
- automated senders use the same dispatcher;
- concurrent sends serialize;
- stale generation events are ignored;
- uncertain acknowledgement is not blindly retried.

### Provider contract tests

Use deterministic fake protocol servers/bridges:

- handshake and capability negotiation;
- start/resume;
- streaming deltas;
- tool/command/diff/plan normalization;
- permission request/resolve;
- interrupt;
- error mapping;
- malformed/unknown events;
- process exit/reconnect;
- history reconciliation;
- snapshot/live cursor separation;
- duplicate events;
- out-of-order/gapped events;
- cancellation and shutdown;
- redaction.

No package should require live provider/network calls in normal unit tests.

### HTTP/API

- settings GET/PATCH;
- spawn omitted/explicit mode;
- session response includes effective mode;
- Chat/TUI send responses;
- history pagination;
- live event reconnect;
- stale permission/turn actions;
- typed unsupported/auth/incompatible errors;
- LAN listener auth coverage;
- OpenAPI route/spec parity;
- generated Go/OpenAPI/TypeScript drift checks.

### CLI

- `ao spawn --mode chat|tui`;
- invalid mode is usage error;
- omitted mode delegates resolution to daemon;
- typed unsupported Chat error is legible;
- `ao send` remains daemon-only and transport-neutral;
- daemon error envelope/request ID preserved.

### Frontend

- General setting loads/saves through daemon;
- helper text says new sessions only;
- Chat session renders Chat by `session.mode` even if current default is TUI;
- TUI session renders terminal by `session.mode` even if current default is Chat;
- unsupported Chat explicit fallback flow;
- Chat composer optimistic/reconciled states;
- streamed delta folding;
- snapshot then mux subscription does not lose or duplicate an item;
- revision gaps trigger resync;
- permission accessibility and stale state;
- reconnect/history replay;
- long-history behavior;
- shell terminal from Chat never mounts agent `TerminalHandleID`;
- existing terminal tests remain valid.

### Integration/e2e

- upgrade from a database with live/terminated TUI sessions;
- choose Chat -> spawn orchestrator -> send from desktop -> send from CLI -> observe one ordered conversation;
- clean-replace the orchestrator -> retain the project conversation -> show the old/new runtime boundary -> preserve Chat mode;
- orchestrator spawns/redirects a worker -> render one correlated delegation/action record;
- Chat orchestrator spawns supported Chat worker;
- unsupported worker prompts explicit TUI decision;
- Chat session opens shell, changes a file, agent later observes filesystem without shell text appearing in chat;
- restart daemon/app and resume same provider conversation;
- active permission survives/reconciles across reconnect;
- choose TUI -> current native workflow remains unchanged;
- change default while sessions are live and verify no controller changes;
- attempts to call wrong-mode permission/terminal paths fail closed.

### Race and resilience

- Go race tests around controller ownership/queues;
- concurrent restore/send/kill;
- controller exit during message acceptance;
- daemon shutdown while event persistence is in progress;
- stale process/events after generation rotation;
- CDC reconnect during high-volume streaming;
- bounded buffers/backpressure.

## Telemetry and observability

Add allowlisted, non-content telemetry:

```text
session_mode_selected
session_spawn_mode
chat_driver_preflight_failed
chat_controller_started
chat_controller_resumed
chat_controller_failed
chat_message_queued
chat_message_delivery_uncertain
chat_permission_requested
chat_reconciliation_result
explicit_tui_fallback_selected
```

Never include prompt, response, command output, file content, credentials, or provider tokens.

Operational logs should include:

- AO session ID;
- provider/harness;
- mode;
- controller generation;
- provider conversation/turn IDs where safe;
- transition/outcome;
- structured error code.

Avoid logging full event payloads by default.

## Documentation

Update:

- README quickstart/session explanation;
- `docs/architecture.md` with dual mutually exclusive controller modes;
- `docs/STATUS.md` with shipped provider coverage;
- `docs/agent/README.md` with Chat-driver vs native-agent adapter responsibilities;
- CLI docs for `--mode`;
- desktop/dashboard docs;
- mobile send behavior;
- agent capability documentation;
- troubleshooting for auth, resume, unsupported drivers, recovery, and unmanaged native CLIs.

Document clearly:

- Chat and TUI are creation-time session modes;
- changing the default affects new sessions only;
- Chat Terminal is a shell, not the provider TUI;
- manually running a provider CLI in the shell is not synchronized with Chat;
- current Chat-supported harnesses and capability limitations.

## Phased delivery / suggested PR sequence

Keep each PR independently testable and avoid combining all providers with the first UI change.

### Phase 0 — ADR and protocol decisions

- [ ] Record the immutable session-mode decision.
- [ ] Record project-scoped orchestrator and session-scoped worker conversation identity.
- [ ] Record strict unsupported-provider behavior and explicit TUI fallback.
- [ ] Record Codex app-server over stdio as the first provider transport.
- [ ] Define minimum Chat capability set.
- [ ] Define Conversation/Turn/Item/Command/Action/Delegation schema v1.
- [ ] Define separate durable item and live mux cursor contracts.
- [ ] Spike one shared Codex app-server versus per-session app-server process topology.
- [ ] Decide Chat history retention and reconciliation rules.

Exit gate: the immutable-mode, project-conversation, Codex-stdio, and semantic-stream architecture is recorded and the app-server process topology is selected.

### Phase 1 — Durable mode and settings foundation

- [ ] Add `SessionMode` domain enum.
- [ ] Add daemon-owned `defaultSessionMode` setting.
- [ ] Add migrations and sqlc query changes.
- [ ] Backfill existing sessions to TUI.
- [ ] Add mode to `SpawnConfig`, session read model, DTOs, OpenAPI, and frontend types.
- [ ] Add optional spawn mode to CLI/API.
- [ ] Add General Settings control.
- [ ] Keep default TUI and behavior unchanged.

Exit gate: all current tests pass and every existing/new omitted-mode session remains TUI.

### Phase 2 — Mode-aware lifecycle dispatcher

- [ ] Introduce the Chat driver port/capability registry.
- [ ] Split shared workspace provisioning from controller-specific launch.
- [ ] Dispatch spawn/send/restore/kill/reaper from persisted mode.
- [ ] Audit and route every internal sender.
- [ ] Add controller generation fencing.
- [ ] Implement strict unsupported-Chat errors.
- [ ] Add explicit TUI fallback API/client behavior.

Exit gate: fake Chat driver proves no TUI runtime is touched; TUI tests prove no Chat driver is touched.

### Phase 3 — Durable conversation/actions and fake end-to-end Chat

- [ ] Add conversation, turn, item, command, action, delegation, provider-state, and provider-event-dedupe storage.
- [ ] Add trigger-backed compact CDC.
- [ ] Add outbox/idempotent message delivery.
- [ ] Add project/session conversation snapshots and item pagination.
- [ ] Add the semantic conversation channel to `/mux`.
- [ ] Add permission/interrupt/action APIs.
- [ ] Implement controller actor, queue, restart, and reconciliation against a fake driver.
- [ ] Add status/activity projection.
- [ ] Prove the snapshot/live-cursor race, revision-gap resync, and slow-client backpressure.

Exit gate: fake-provider project-scoped orchestrator Chat works across daemon restart with ordered history, actions, delegation, permission handling, and resync.

### Phase 4 — Codex app-server production connector

- [ ] launch/supervise Codex app-server over stdio;
- [ ] capability/version/auth preflight;
- [ ] start/resume/send/stream;
- [ ] tools/commands/diffs/plans;
- [ ] permissions and interrupt;
- [ ] history reconciliation;
- [ ] controller/process restart and upgrade handling;
- [ ] provider-specific integration fixtures.
- [ ] verify that Chat mode never launches or attaches a Codex native TUI.

Exit gate: Codex orchestrator Chat satisfies the minimum production capability set across two turns and daemon restart.

### Phase 5 — Orchestrator Chat UI

- [ ] Add mode-aware session central view.
- [ ] Build timeline/composer/origin/activity/action/delegation/coordination cards and reconnect states.
- [ ] Reuse inspector and session shell terminals.
- [ ] Add explicit permission/input UX.
- [ ] Add mode badge and diagnostics.
- [ ] Verify desktop accessibility and long conversations.
- [ ] Show/demo through `ao preview` during implementation.

Exit gate: user can run an orchestrator entirely through Chat, use a worktree shell, restart AO, and continue the same provider conversation without a native agent TUI.

### Phase 6 — Supported Chat workers

- [ ] Apply default resolution to worker spawns from every source.
- [ ] Ensure orchestrator-spawned workers use daemon mode resolution.
- [ ] Add worker Chat UI and task attachment behavior.
- [ ] Validate parallel controller scaling/resource limits.
- [ ] Add explicit fallback for unsupported worker harnesses.

Exit gate: orchestrator and workers have consistent immutable modes and no cross-controller routes.

### Phase 7 — Second provider and ACP onboarding

- [ ] Implement the Claude Agent SDK bridge as the second structured provider.
- [ ] Add generic ACP driver.
- [ ] Probe agents individually; do not assume ACP capability parity.
- [ ] Publish live capability matrix.
- [ ] Keep unsupported agents TUI-only.

Exit gate: multiple providers render through the same event/UI model without provider branches in shared frontend components.

### Phase 8 — Hardening and default evaluation

- [ ] crash/active-turn recovery testing;
- [ ] resource/backpressure/load testing;
- [ ] security review and redaction audit;
- [ ] telemetry review;
- [ ] mobile parity;
- [ ] docs/troubleshooting;
- [ ] staged rollout/feature flag if needed;
- [ ] evaluate whether new installs should default to Chat only after coverage and reliability thresholds are met.

## Rollout strategy

1. Ship schema/settings with default `tui`; no workflow change.
2. Gate Chat option by driver capability and possibly developer/experimental flag.
3. Enable Chat for one orchestrator provider.
4. Observe spawn failures, resume success, uncertain delivery, permission completion, and crash recovery.
5. Enable supported workers.
6. Add providers incrementally.
7. Keep TUI as a permanent compatibility mode for long-tail agents and provider-native workflows.

Do not change existing users to Chat automatically. A future new-install default can be a separate product decision with evidence.

## Definition of done

- [ ] User can select Chat or Terminal UI as the daemon-backed default.
- [ ] Preference applies only to future sessions.
- [ ] Every session persists immutable `chat|tui`.
- [ ] Existing sessions are migrated to TUI.
- [ ] Chat creation is allowed only for a production-capable driver.
- [ ] Unsupported Chat never silently falls back.
- [ ] Chat sessions start no native agent TUI.
- [ ] TUI sessions start no Chat driver.
- [ ] Every external/internal sender dispatches through persisted mode.
- [ ] Chat has durable ordered history and structured streaming.
- [ ] Tool calls, commands, diffs, plans/todos, permissions, errors, usage, and completion are represented without PTY parsing.
- [ ] Chat permission decisions are typed and correlated.
- [ ] Restart resumes the same provider conversation.
- [ ] Stale controller events are fenced.
- [ ] Human-facing orchestrator history is project-scoped and survives clean orchestrator replacement with an explicit runtime/provider boundary.
- [ ] Replacement orchestrators inherit the current mode unless a new mode is explicitly requested before creation.
- [ ] Worker conversations remain session-scoped.
- [ ] Durable item sequence and live mux cursor are separate and snapshot/subscription races are covered.
- [ ] Conversation actions and orchestrator-to-worker delegations have durable IDs, state, targets, idempotency, and typed errors.
- [ ] Codex Chat uses app-server stdio and never launches/attaches a native Codex TUI.
- [ ] Chat Terminal is a plain session-scoped shell.
- [ ] TUI behavior and terminal safety regressions are covered.
- [ ] CLI, desktop, mobile, automated reactions, and orchestrator coordination remain consistent.
- [ ] Generated API artifacts are updated together.
- [ ] Architecture/status/agent/user documentation is updated.
- [ ] Focused unit, integration, race, frontend, and e2e suites pass.

## Non-goals

- Real-time concurrent control of one provider conversation by SDK/app-server and native provider TUI.
- Automatic switching of a live session between Chat and TUI.
- Parsing terminal ANSI output into canonical chat/tool events.
- Reimplementing every provider-native slash command in the first release.
- Enabling Chat for every AO harness before capability parity is verified.
- Moving daemon lifecycle/business logic into Electron.
- Replacing the existing shell terminal system.
- Changing primary/LAN listener security boundaries.
- Automatically importing arbitrary out-of-band native CLI conversations.

## Open decisions

The product architecture is settled by this issue. These bounded implementation decisions remain for Phase 0/spikes:

1. Does V1 use one daemon-managed Codex app-server with multiple threads or one process per Chat session?
2. What exact tested capability/version floor makes an installed Codex build Chat-ready?
3. What are the size/retention limits for command output, diffs, item detail, and conversation history?
4. Can an active Codex turn be reattached after daemon failure, or must some crash boundaries settle as interrupted/uncertain?
5. Can `/send` evolve compatibly for Chat acknowledgement, or should it delegate to a new canonical `/messages` response contract?
6. How long is AO Chat history retained after session cleanup, and is provider-owned history ever archived/deleted?
7. Is documentation sufficient for manually launching a provider CLI in a Chat shell, or should AO show a contextual warning?
8. What performance threshold triggers timeline virtualization beyond paginated history?
9. When, if ever, should Chat become the default for new installations? This is a later rollout decision, not part of V1.

The following are **not** open:

- Codex app-server is the first production Chat provider.
- V1 uses app-server stdio, not remote native TUI attachment.
- Chat/TUI is immutable per session.
- Chat-mode Terminal is a plain worktree shell.
- structured approvals are required for mutating Chat V1.
- orchestrator conversation is project-scoped and worker conversation is session-scoped.
- existing sessions remain TUI and are not reconstructed from terminal output.
- Claude Agent SDK follows the Codex vertical slice.

## Alternatives considered

### Chat UI plus writable native TUI for the same session

Rejected. Two independent provider clients can race and diverge even when initialized with the same conversation ID.

### Move a conversation back and forth between SDK and TUI

Not part of the initial design. Serialized ownership handoff is provider-specific, difficult to make crash-safe, and unnecessary when each session has a fixed mode.

### Treat Chat/TUI as a frontend tab preference

Rejected. CLI, mobile, internal reactions, restore, and reaper behavior would still use ambiguous controller paths.

### Use terminal output as the Chat transcript

Rejected. PTY bytes are ephemeral presentation data without stable message/tool/permission identity.

### Remove terminals entirely

Rejected. Chat mode retains a normal session-scoped worktree shell; TUI mode remains available for compatibility and provider-native workflows.

### Silently fall back from Chat to TUI

Rejected. It violates user intent and obscures provider capability gaps. Fallback must be explicit before session creation.

## Before submitting

- [x] Searched open issues for similar Chat UI / TUI / session-mode work.
- [x] Grounded the plan in the current Go daemon, SQLite/CDC, API generation, Electron renderer, terminal mux, session-scoped shell, CLI, and lifecycle boundaries.

title: ao-web next-server leaks zombie processes (~11/min) until the OS process-table cap; machine-wide fork failures
body:
## Summary
`ao-web`'s next-server (both the supervised `:3000` instance started by `ao start` and the `dist-server/direct-*` variant) does not reap the child processes it spawns. Zombies (`<defunct>`) accumulate at roughly **11/minute** under normal dashboard operation until the per-user process-table cap is reached, at which point every process on the machine starts failing with `fork failed: resource temporarily unavailable`.

## Environment
- `@aoagents/ao` 0.9.5 / `@aoagents/ao-web` 0.9.5 (global install)
- macOS (Darwin 25.5.0), node v22.21.0
- `kern.maxprocperuid` = 2666

## Observed incident (2026-07-28/29)
- `ao start <project>` supervises `ao-web` (wrapper → next-server). Within ~1.5-3h of uptime, `ps -axo stat | grep -c Z` reached **1,145 zombies**, all with the next-server PID as parent (verified via `ps -axo ppid=,stat=`).
- Combined with live processes (~750), the user hit the 2,666 process cap: unrelated tools began failing to fork (observed across shells, git, gh, and plausibly contributed to Docker Desktop and an Electron app dying the same day).
- `kill <next-server-pid>` reparented the zombies to launchd, which reaped them instantly (1,053 → 0), confirming the parent simply never `wait()`s.
- The ao daemon respawns ao-web after a kill, so the leak restarts (~3h to crisis per cycle).

## Ask
1. Reap spawned children in ao-web's server (SIGCHLD handler / `child.on('exit')` on whatever spawns the per-request work — the zombie births correlate with dashboard polling activity).
2. Optionally: a `--no-web` flag for `ao start` so headless operators can opt out of the dashboard entirely.

Happy to provide more diagnostics from a live leak if useful.

The generated llms.txt directly exposes only 3 of the site's 55 documentation URLs. The 52 omitted pages include installation, platforms, architecture, troubleshooting, migration, configuration, guides, and the full plugin reference.

Flattening all 55 pages into one peer list would obscure the distinction between 11 overview/index pages and 44 leaf pages.

title: fix(landing): apply Content-Signal to allowed crawler groups
body:
## Problem

The landing robots.txt route emitted Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=yes only after the Bytespider group. Because Content Signals are scoped per user-agent group, the directive applied to the blocked Bytespider crawler rather than the allowed crawler policies.

## Expected behavior

Apply the Content-Signal directive to the User-Agent: * group and every explicitly allowed crawler group. Explicitly welcome the documented GPTBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, Bingbot, meta-externalagent, and DuckAssistBot controls while preserving the CCBot and Bytespider blocks.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every allowed crawler group emits Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=yes.
- GPTBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, Bingbot, meta-externalagent, and DuckAssistBot are explicitly allowed.
- CCBot and Bytespider remain disallowed and do not receive Content-Signal permissions.
- Existing sitemap output remains unchanged.
- The landing app builds successfully.

title: fix(landing): apply content signals to allowed crawlers
body:
## Summary

- apply Content-Signal permissions to the wildcard and every explicitly allowed crawler group
- explicitly welcome GPTBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, Bingbot, meta-externalagent, and DuckAssistBot
- preserve the existing CCBot and Bytespider blocks and sitemap output

## Root cause

Content-Signal is scoped to its robots.txt user-agent group. Its previous placement after the Bytespider group associated the site-wide permissions with a blocked crawler, while named allowed groups did not inherit the wildcard directive.

## Validation

- landing production build: npm.cmd run build
- group-level assertion: every Allow: / group has Content-Signal and blocked groups do not
- git diff --check

Closes #3364

title: Drag-and-drop file/folder into terminal session should insert its path as text
body:
## Summary

When dragging and dropping a file or folder into a terminal session, AO should detect the dropped path and insert it into the chat input as text — matching the behavior of other coding agents (Cursor, VS Code, Warp, etc.).

## Current behavior

Dragging a file/folder into a terminal session does nothing useful — the path is not detected or inserted.

## Expected behavior

- Drag a file/folder onto the terminal area (or chat input)
- The absolute path of the dropped item is inserted as text into the chat input
- User can then edit/send it as part of their message

This is standard behavior across coding agents and would be a meaningful UX improvement for AO's terminal sessions.

## Context

xterm.js fires `drop` events with the OS file path(s). The frontend terminal component would need to listen for these and route the path into the chat input field.

**Reported by:** @Dhruv Sharma
