title: feat: discover agent models from safe local config files
body:
## Summary

Extend adapter-aware model selection with a safe configuration-file discovery source. AO should read only declarative model metadata from installed agents config files, merge it with isolated CLI discovery, and cache the normalized result.

This follows #3385 and depends on the model-catalog API/UI introduced by #3386.

## Motivation

CLI discovery is not sufficient for every adapter. Some agents expose user-added providers or models only through local configuration, while others have no reliable list command. Reading known declarative model sections gives users their configured models without maintaining a large hard-coded catalog or repeatedly invoking every installed agent.

The first high-value slice covers:

- Crush: provider/model catalog in providers.json
- Continue: configured models in config.yaml or config.yml
- OpenCode: selected and custom provider models in opencode.json or opencode.jsonc
- Qwen: default and configured provider models in settings.json
- Kimi: default and named model sections in config.toml

## Required behavior

1. Read only fixed, adapter-owned config paths for the selected agent and registered project.
2. Parse declarative JSON, JSONC, YAML, and narrowly scoped TOML model sections without executing plugins, commands, imports, or file references.
3. Enforce a file-size bound and reject symbolic links.
4. Extract only normalized model ID, label, provider, and default status. Never retain API keys, tokens, headers, endpoints, or raw config content.
5. Merge configuration models with CLI results and deduplicate by model ID, preserving richer labels/provider/default metadata.
6. If CLI discovery fails but configuration produced models, return and cache the partial catalog with a warning instead of discarding it.
7. If neither source produces a model and no previous cache exists, retain the custom text fallback.
8. Invalidate the cached catalog after a relevant config file changes using a non-sensitive metadata fingerprint.
9. Keep OpenCode CLI discovery isolated with --pure.
10. Add focused parser, security-boundary, merge, partial-fallback, and cache-invalidation tests.

## Out of scope

- Parsing all 23 adapters in one change
- Executing JavaScript or TypeScript configuration/plugins
- Reading arbitrary user-provided paths
- Storing credentials or full configuration documents
- Replacing CLI discovery or custom model input

## Acceptance criteria

- The five adapters above expose configured models through the existing searchable selector.
- Only selected agent catalog endpoints perform discovery; AO does not scan all adapters on settings load.
- The last useful cached/partial catalog remains available when CLI refresh fails, with a visible warning.
- Backend tests and repository lint pass.
- No API wire-shape change is required.

title: feat: discover models from safe agent config files
body:
## Summary

- discover configured models for Crush, Continue, OpenCode, Qwen, and Kimi
- merge config metadata with isolated CLI discovery and deduplicate model IDs
- retain useful config catalogs with warnings when CLI discovery fails
- invalidate cached catalogs after relevant config metadata changes
- bound config reads, reject symlinks, and never retain credentials or raw config

Closes #3462.

## Dependency

This is a stacked PR on top of #3386, which introduces the model-catalog service, cache, API, and searchable settings UI. It should remain draft until #3386 merges. After #3386 lands, the base diff will reduce to the configuration-discovery commit.

## Behavior

AO reads only known declarative files for the selected agent:

| Agent | Config source | Extracted metadata |
|---|---|---|
| Crush | providers.json | provider models and configured defaults |
| Continue | config.yaml / config.yml | configured model, label, and provider |
| OpenCode | global/project opencode.json or opencode.jsonc | selected model and custom provider models |
| Qwen | settings.json | default model and provider model entries |
| Kimi | config.toml | default model and named model sections |

The parser does not execute plugins, commands, imports, or file references. Reads are limited to 4 MiB regular non-symlink files. Only model ID, label, provider, and default state enter the normalized catalog/cache.

If both CLI and config sources succeed, the response source is cli+config. If the CLI fails but config yields models, AO returns and caches that partial catalog as stale with a warning. If no source yields models and there is no cache, the existing free-text fallback remains.

## Verification

- GOCACHE=/private/tmp/ao-config-model-go-cache go test ./...
- GOCACHE=/private/tmp/ao-config-model-go-cache npm run lint
- focused parser/service tests cover JSONC comments and trailing commas, YAML, narrow TOML sections, credential exclusion, size limits, symlink rejection, metadata merging, partial fallback, and config cache invalidation

## Out of scope

- config parsers for the remaining adapters
- executing dynamic configuration or plugins
- arbitrary config paths
- changing the API response shape or frontend UI

title: feat(frontend): add i18next foundation and Simplified Chinese UI
body:
## Summary

Adds the production localization foundation for the Electron renderer and a complete Simplified Chinese UI catalog.

- Uses `i18next` + `react-i18next` with typed English source keys and `zh-CN` resources.
- Keeps English as the default and fallback locale.
- Supports live locale switching in Settings, persists the selection under `~/.ao`, and restores it before the renderer mounts.
- Updates both `document.documentElement.lang` and `dir` when the locale changes.
- Uses standard i18next interpolation and CLDR pluralization.
- Extracts app-owned display and accessibility text across the renderer, with an automated coverage test to prevent new hardcoded English UI strings.
- Keeps user/repository/agent/SCM data, commands, product names, and external browser content untranslated by design.

The architecture and scope are documented in [`docs/plans/chinese-ui-i18n.md`](docs/plans/chinese-ui-i18n.md).

Addresses #2106.

## Prior work and credit

This PR was opened and developed by @AllBeingsFuture. The completed implementation preserves that contribution and its current-main catalogs, persistence, settings control, and broad renderer extraction.

#2503 by @Aakriti0207 independently established the same `i18next` / `react-i18next` direction. This PR adopts that library choice without stacking on the older, substantially divergent branch.

## Implementation details

- Isolated i18next instance factory plus an application singleton wired through `initReactI18next`.
- Compile-time translation-key typing derived from the English catalog.
- Exact EN / zh-CN key and interpolation-variable parity checks.
- Locale persistence shared across Electron main and renderer through a typed schema and existing IPC boundary.
- Startup, concurrent-load, stale-read, read-failure, and write-failure handling.
- Exhaustive maps for dynamic shortcut, session, PR, CI, and review display states.
- Embedded locale bundles for the current two-locale desktop scope; runtime locale backends can be added later without changing component call sites.

Native OS menus/dialogs, daemon-generated payloads, landing/mobile surfaces, CLI output, documentation, and agent terminal content remain separate product scopes rather than renderer strings.

## Verification

- [x] `npm run typecheck`
- [x] `npm run typecheck:e2e`
- [x] `npx vitest run` — 103 files, 1,356 tests
- [x] Main, preload, and renderer production Vite builds

title: Empty "Pinned" section in sidebar — no way to pin sessions
body:
## Summary The sidebar shows a **Pinned** section header (pushpin icon) that is always empty, and there is no way to pin any agent session to begin with. ## Repro 1. Open the desktop app. 2. Look at the left sidebar — the **Pinned** collapsible section appears below Search. 3. Expand it — body is empty. There is no pin affordance on any session row, project, or context menu. ## Root cause Shipped as a deliberate UI placeholder in **PR #3310** (`Feat/sidebar collapsible sections`). `frontend/src/renderer/components/Sidebar.tsx:300-310`: ```tsx {/* Pinned — collapsible; body empty until pin functionality lands. */}
} label="Pinned" open={pinnedOpen} onToggle={() => setPinnedOpen((v) => !v)} className="mb-1" /> {pinnedOpen ?
: null} {/* ← empty body */}
``` The inline comment is explicit: **"body empty until pin functionality lands."** There is no `is_pinned` / `IsPinned` / `pinned_at` field anywhere in the backend, no API route to pin/unpin a session, and no UI affordance to trigger it. The feature was never implemented — only the shell. - **Author:** @Annieeeee11 - **Merged by:** @codebanditssss — 2026-07-31 ## Impact Minor UX papercut: a dead affordance visible to every user. The section looks interactive but does nothing. Users (and now our own triage flow) assume sessions can be pinned and go looking for a control that doesn't exist. ## Suggested fix Pick one of: 1. **Hide the section** until pin functionality exists — remove the `Pinned` block (lines 300-310) from `Sidebar.tsx`. Smallest possible change; no user-visible feature regression because nothing was working. 2. **Implement the feature** — add `is_pinned` to sessions (backend migration + DTO + API route to toggle), a pin control on session rows, and wire the sidebar body to list pinned sessions. Larger; file as `enhancement` separately. Recommend **(1) now** to stop shipping a broken-looking UI, with **(2)** as a follow-up enhancement. ## Priority **P2** — cosmetic/UX dead affordance, not a functional break.

title: feat(chat): add Chat UI
body:
## Summary

This PR adds **Chat as a first-class interface for an AO session**, alongside the existing terminal UI. It does not replace AO's session model: projects, worktrees, branches, lifecycle state, issue/PR context, orchestration, and navigation remain shared. The difference is the controller and presentation used to interact with the coding agent.

- **TUI mode** keeps the existing runtime + tmux/terminal path.
- **Chat mode** talks to the provider through a structured native protocol or ACP connection and renders normalized messages, tools, plans, diffs, approvals, and usage.
- A compatible session can switch between the two interfaces while keeping its AO session and worktree. Only one agent controller is active at a time.
- Desktop and mobile both consume the daemon-owned conversation and transition APIs; neither client owns provider or lifecycle logic.

The final implementation is broader than the original Codex-only slice and includes Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Droid, desktop Chat, mobile Chat, and durable Chat/TUI handoff.

## Architecture

```text
AO session
├── shared: project, worktree, branch, role, lifecycle, issue/PR state
│
├── TUI interface
│   └── runtime controller → tmux/PTY → terminal renderer
│
└── Chat interface
    └── Chat controller → provider driver → normalized conversation events
                         ├── Codex app-server
                         └── ACP transport → Claude Code / OpenCode / Droid
```

The daemon remains the source of truth. `session_mode` is persisted on the session and is resolved by the daemon when omitted at creation. A user can explicitly select a mode for a new session, and an explicit interface transition can later change the persisted mode. Changing the global default does not silently rewrite existing sessions.

Chat sessions are runtime-less from the agent-controller perspective: they do not create a second tmux-hosted copy of the agent. The shell available from a Chat session is an ordinary shell in the same worktree and remains separate from the structured agent connection.

## Provider support

| Harness | Chat transport | Installation/auth behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | Native `codex app-server` protocol | Uses the user's installed and authenticated Codex CLI |
| Claude Code | `claude-agent-acp` bridge over the shared ACP transport | Uses the user's installed Claude Code executable, login, `~/.claude` configuration, settings, hooks, and MCP setup; AO does not bundle Claude Code itself |
| OpenCode | Native `opencode acp` command over the shared ACP transport | Uses the user's installed and configured OpenCode CLI |
| Droid | Droid's ACP daemon over the shared ACP transport | Uses the user's installed Droid CLI and account/API configuration |

The driver registry performs provider discovery and capability/preflight checks before durable creation. Unsupported, unavailable, incompatible, and authentication-required failures use stable typed API errors rather than generic 500s. Harnesses without a Chat driver continue to use the existing TUI path.

Codex has a dedicated adapter because its app-server exposes a richer native surface. The other integrations share one provider-neutral ACP client and event normalizer rather than duplicating a full Chat implementation for each CLI.

## Durable conversation model

Chat is backed by daemon-owned SQLite state rather than renderer-local transcript state. The model includes:

- conversations, turns, messages, activities, usage, provider session/thread identity, and controller generation;
- a raw provider-event archive plus normalized projections used by desktop and mobile;
- atomic archive + projection writes, event identity handling, and generation fencing so stale controllers cannot mutate the current conversation;
- paged historical snapshots with semantic invalidation for live updates;
- project-scoped orchestrator conversation identity, including rebinding across clean orchestrator replacement;
- import/deduplication of native provider history on resume and interface handoff;
- persisted standing role/system context for orchestrators and workers.

The HTTP surface covers conversation snapshots and paging, sending/queuing/steering, interruption, approvals, interactive input, rollback, title changes, skills, model/configuration options, MCP reload, and compaction where supported. API inputs are validated strictly and daemon error envelopes—including request IDs—are preserved by desktop and mobile.

## Chat ↔ TUI interface handoff

Interface changes are durable, serialized transitions rather than a renderer toggle:

1. AO records the requested transition and reserves a new controller generation.
2. The source controller is quiesced. TUI input is gated before the final idle barrier so new keystrokes cannot race with shutdown.
3. If work is active, AO waits for it to finish. The user can cancel while the transition is still safely reversible.
4. AO stops the source controller, preflights and starts the target controller, and changes the persisted mode through the lifecycle boundary.
5. Queued messages are durably delivered with stable idempotency once the target is ready.
6. Recovery logic handles daemon restarts, failed preflight, ambiguous source shutdown, rollback, and stale controller events.

Only one provider/runtime owns the session at any point. Completed native conversation history is reused or imported when the provider supports it. When exact native resume is unavailable, AO retains the durable transcript, reapplies the session's role/system context, and starts a fresh provider context with an explicit boundary. In-flight tool execution is drained or stopped; it is not transferred between protocol implementations.

## Desktop experience

`SessionView` renders the established terminal surface for TUI sessions and the Chat workspace for Chat sessions. The Chat surface includes:

- streamed assistant text and Markdown;
- compact tool/command activity, command output, plans, file changes, and diffs;
- approval and interactive-input cards;
- attachments, file mentions, skills, rollback, copy actions, and conversation titles;
- provider-supported model, reasoning/effort, permission, and configuration controls;
- stop, steer-current-turn, and queue-for-next-turn behavior;
- context usage, compaction markers, controller health, resume/recovery, and typed failure states;
- a reachable plain shell in the same worktree;
- non-blocking interface-transition status and cancellation in the top bar.

Reasoning and noisy bookkeeping events are hidden by default so the transcript prioritizes the conversation and meaningful agent activity.

## Mobile experience

Mobile uses Chat as the default session experience while retaining the terminal view where needed. It uses the same daemon contracts and persisted conversation as desktop, including:

- the Chat timeline, composer, streaming/invalidation, paging, and reconnection;
- skills, file mentions, attachments, approvals, and interactive input;
- provider configuration controls, stop/steer/queue, retryable errors, and request IDs;
- compact mobile layouts for plans, commands, diffs, failures, compaction, and transition state;
- buffered PTY bytes when the terminal WebView is temporarily unmounted.

No provider logic or lifecycle mutation is implemented in the mobile client.

## Storage and upgrade safety

- Chat migrations are numbered `0066`–`0079`, above the migrations already present on `main`.
- A compatibility repair handles development databases that previously recorded the Chat migrations under the collided `0052`–`0065` versions, then applies the real migrations from `main`.
- Existing TUI sessions remain valid and continue through the established runtime path.
- Controller shutdown is context-bounded, ACP interruption cancels the local blocked prompt as well as notifying the provider, and controller startup no longer holds the global Chat registry lock while importing provider history.
- Codex preflight enforces the tested app-server version/protocol floor before creating durable session state.

## Verification

Latest local verification on this branch includes:

- `go build ./...`
- full backend `go test ./...`
- frontend typecheck and the full renderer suite (`1,930` passing tests)
- mobile typecheck and test suite (`331` passing tests)
- focused migration/upgrade, provider-state, lifecycle, transition, ACP, and controller tests
- Electron launched against the real `~/.ao` data set, with projects, sessions, usage, and upgraded schema loading successfully
- manual Chat and interface-switch exercises for Codex and Claude Code, plus ACP probing/exercises for OpenCode and Droid where local credentials allowed

## Known limitations

- **First-class Compact is currently Codex-only.** ACP 1.2 has no standard compaction RPC, so AO returns `CHAT_COMPACTION_UNSUPPORTED` for ACP providers. Claude Code and OpenCode native `/compact` commands were manually verified to compact their native histories and allow a subsequent turn, but AO cannot yet normalize that into structured `compactedAt`/usage metadata or a semantic compaction marker. Droid compaction could not be exercised without an active subscription.
- Chat drivers currently ship for Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Droid. Other AO harnesses remain TUI-only until a native or ACP connector is added.
- A handoff preserves the AO session, worktree, durable transcript, role, and completed provider history; it cannot migrate an executing tool process or partially completed background task into another controller.
- Live updates currently use SQLite change invalidation plus paged refetch. A cursor-based semantic mux with gap recovery is not part of this implementation.

Agents can control the same live Electron browser view that the user sees, while users retain full visibility and control through tabs, DevTools, and browser activity indicators. ## What changed ### Browser automation - Added the `ao browser` CLI command and corresponding backend API routes. - Added support for navigation and common interactions: - Open, click, double-click, focus, fill, type, press, hover, drag, scroll, select, check, and uncheck. - DOM snapshots with stable element references. - Property reads, screenshots, waits, console logs, page errors, dialogs, and frames. - Added stable logical tab management: - List, create, select, and close tabs. - Capture popup windows as selectable AO tabs. - Preserve stable tab IDs across browser operations. - Added shared automation output and error handling across the CLI, backend service, and Electron runtime. ### Session isolation and runtime security - Integrated the pinned native `agent-browser` runtime. - Added runtime preparation, SHA-256 verification, packaging, and license handling. - Agents operate against the existing AO Electron browser instead of launching a separate browser or profile. - Added worker/session isolation using dedicated browser partitions and CDP targets. - Added a private loopback-only CDP bridge managed inside the desktop process. - Avoided exposing a global Electron debug port or returning private CDP endpoints to the daemon. - Prevented unsafe browser attachment, personal profile reuse, persistent state, arbitrary JavaScript execution, arbitrary file reads, and network-route changes. ### Detached Chromium DevTools - Added a user-facing detached Chromium DevTools window for the active browser tab. - Added toolbar, title-bar menu, and keyboard shortcut access. - DevTools can inspect Elements, Console, and Network activity while agent automation continues. - Added lifecycle handling for opening, closing, reopening, and cleaning up DevTools without orphaned processes. ### Network and diagnostics - title: fix(windows): correct pidAlive WaitForSingleObject check in ptyregistry
body:
## What
Fixes two Windows-specific bugs in daemon/worker process lifecycle:
1. `pidAlive` in the ConPTY registry adapter reported terminated processes as alive.
2. Daemon/worker teardown on quit used a POSIX process-group signal that is a no-op on Windows.

## Why
Fixes #3327. On Windows, killing a worker agent from the AO UI caused it to respawn repeatedly, and closing or killing the AO app did not fully stop the daemon — it kept restarting and reopening. Root cause analysis (see issue comments) traced this to two independent bugs stacking on top of each other.

## How
- **`backend/internal/adapters/runtime/conpty/ptyregistry/pidalive_windows.go`**: `defaultPidAlive` called `OpenProcess` and treated success alone as "process is alive." On Windows, a terminated process's kernel object persists until every handle to it is closed, so `OpenProcess` succeeds for recently-dead PIDs too. Added a `WaitForSingleObject(handle, 0)` check — `WAIT_TIMEOUT` means still running, anything else means exited. This mirrors the already-correct pattern in `backend/internal/processalive/process_windows.go::Alive`, which the ConPTY adapter's *other* `pidAlive` (`conpty/pidalive_windows.go`) already delegates to. `ptyregistry` had its own separate, unfixed copy — this brings it in line. Related: #3080.

- **`frontend/src/main.ts`** (`killDaemon` + the wedged-orphan takeover path): both used `process.kill(-pid, "SIGTERM")`, which relies on POSIX process groups. Windows has no equivalent, so the group-kill silently did nothing, and the fallback `child.kill("SIGTERM")` only reaches the direct child — not the `/bin/sh` wrapper's descendants or any ConPTY/pty-host grandchildren. Both now branch on `process.platform === "win32"` and use `taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F` (tree-kill, force) via `execFileSync`, since Windows processes largely ignore graceful term requests from Node and `process.on("exit")` handlers must stay synchronous.

**Intentionally not included**: the forced-kill timeout backstop suggested as fix-option #3 in the issue (kill the daemon if the supervisor pipe doesn't close within N seconds). The pidAlive fix is the primary root cause — the issue's own analysis states it "would likely resolve the respawning behavior" on its own — and the supervisor-link wiring (`connectSupervisor`, `establishSupervisorLink`) turned out to already be correctly implemented and tested, contrary to my initial read. Keeping this PR scoped to the two confirmed bugs; happy to follow up with the timeout backstop separately if reviewers want defense-in-depth.

## Testing
- `cd backend && go test ./internal/adapters/runtime/conpty/ptyregistry/... ./internal/adapters/runtime/... ./internal/lifecycle/...` — all pass
- `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- `cd frontend && npx vitest run` — 1359/1359 tests pass across 104 files, including `supervisor-link.test.ts` and `daemon-owner.test.ts`
- Not yet validated on an actual Windows machine — reviewers with Windows access, a manual repro of the original steps (kill worker from UI → confirm no respawn; close app → confirm daemon + workers fully exit; check Task Manager) would help close this out with confidence.



## Checklist
- [x] Branched from `main`
- [x] One focused change; links the related issue when applicable
- [ ] Follows AGENTS.md conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense
- [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go`, frontend)

title: Board loses all sessions: stale-PID group kill wipes tmux, misread probe archives everything, and skipped migration 0040 500s the session list
body:
Two independent defects both end with the user's sessions gone from the Board. They have different mechanisms and different fixes, but they are being tracked together here so one PR closes both. The migration half was originally reported in #3476.

Quick triage test to tell them apart:

| | Defect A | Defect B (#3476) |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/sessions` | 200, sessions returned | 500 `INTERNAL_ERROR` |
| UI | Board silently empty | `Could not load sessions.` banner |
| DB | sessions flipped to `is_terminated=1` | sessions untouched, `is_terminated=0` |
| Recovery | `ao session restore` | schema repair |

---

# Defect A: tmux server killed, then every session archived

Two bugs in a chain, both introduced by #3066. The first destroys the tmux server, the second turns that into a full board wipe instead of a recoverable outage.

## A1. Trigger: preview server group-kills a PID it no longer owns

The `previewserver` package has exactly one commit in its history: `3279c3a0b` ("Give every AO worker a live, session-owned browser", #3066, 2026-07-30). `manager.go` and `process_unix.go` have no prior history, so none of this code existed before that PR.

It introduced a process-group kill by raw PID:

```go
// process_unix.go
func forceKillPreviewProcess(cmd *exec.Cmd) error {
	err := syscall.Kill(-cmd.Process.Pid, syscall.SIGKILL)
	...
}
```

and calls it after the process has already been reaped:

```go
// manager.go:371
select {
case <-done:
	// The root may exit before descendants that ignored SIGTERM. Escalate
	// against the owned process tree even after Wait has completed.
	_ = forceKillPreviewProcess(cmd)
```

`run.done` is closed in `waitForExit` (`manager.go:495`) after `run.cmd.Wait()` (`manager.go:469`). Once `Wait` returns, the PID is released back to the OS and is no longer owned by the daemon. The negative argument makes this a process-group kill, so the blast radius is an entire group rather than one stray process.

Four sites do this:

- `manager.go:474` in `waitForExit`, immediately after `Wait()` returns, on any unexpected preview exit
- `manager.go:375`, the `case <-done` shown above
- `manager.go:797` and `:799` in `forceStopAfterGrace`
- `manager.go:829` in `reapPersistedProcesses`, the worst form: at daemon startup it reads the previous daemon generation's PIDs from `preview-processes.json` and group-kills each one, with no check that the PID still refers to a preview process

### Why it lands on tmux

A tmux server is always a process group leader, PGID equal to its own PID. Verified locally on two different servers (`14618/14618`, `4940/4940`), both `PPID 1`, own session. So a recycled PID landing on a tmux server means `kill(-pid, SIGKILL)` takes down the server and every session inside it at once.

Measured PID allocation on the affected machine is roughly 24/sec, so the PID space wraps about every 67 minutes. One affected tmux server had been alive 110 minutes. The same PR raises this rate by giving every worker a session-owned browser and preview, so the risky path now runs continuously instead of occasionally.

SIGKILL produces no crash report and no unified-log entry, which matches the forensics: the server vanished with the daemon still running and no trace in `DiagnosticReports`, `log show`, or `memorystatus`.

## A2. Amplifier: server-level probe failures misread as per-session death

`backend/internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/tmux.go:878`

```go
func sessionMissingOutput(out string) bool {
	s := strings.ToLower(out)
	return strings.Contains(s, "can't find session") ||
		strings.Contains(s, "no server running") ||   // server-level, not session-level
		strings.Contains(s, "error connecting") ||    // transient socket error
		strings.Contains(s, "session not found")
}
```

`IsAlive` (`tmux.go:497`) returns `(false, nil)` for these, so the reaper records a confident `ProbeDead` (`observe/reaper/reaper.go:166`) and `ApplyRuntimeObservation` sets `IsTerminated = true` (`lifecycle/manager.go:248`).

`no server running` and `error connecting` say nothing about any individual session. The first means the whole server is gone, the second is a transient socket failure that may not mean anything is dead at all.

The codebase already has the right guard and this path bypasses it:

- `ports/runtime_observations.go:9` : "`failed` means the probe errored or timed out and is never treated as a death conclusion"
- `observe/reaper/reaper.go:158` : "a transient tmux outage [must not] hide a really-dead session, and a transient adapter bug [must not] terminate a really-alive one"

## Observed

Local nightly `0.11.2-nightly.202608021445`. Filtering `change_log` to this signature (28 to 32 sessions terminated in one pass at a uniform 0.118 to 0.140s cadence, which is the per-session `tmux has-session` probe loop):

```
2026-08-02 05:05   28   0.123
2026-08-02 09:30   32   0.118
2026-08-03 03:14   28   0.118
2026-08-03 07:25   28   0.139
2026-08-03 09:16   29   0.140
```

Five occurrences, none before Aug 2, consistent with #3066 landing Jul 30 and shipping to the nightly channel. Earlier bulk terminations in the history are a different mechanism: they write at a 4 to 6 ms median gap, which is a single transaction and far faster than a probe loop that shells out per session.

The sidebar filters `isTerminated` (`renderer/components/Sidebar.tsx:476`), so the board reads as empty and the sessions appear lost.

`iitb-cli-1` confirms the 60s window is the only thing gating the sweep: it emitted an activity hook at 12:55:27.908 and was terminated at 12:56:28.014, 60.1s later, matching `defaultRecentActivityWindow` in `lifecycle/runtime.go:10`.

No data is lost. Worktrees, branches, and agent context stay intact, and `ao session restore` brings sessions back with full context.

---

# Defect B: skipped migration 0040 makes the session list 500

Originally filed as #3476 with full Windows reproduction, screenshots, and logs. Summary here so one PR can close both.

The daemon's generated queries select `sessions.diff_base_sha` and `sessions.diff_base_ref` (`storage/sqlite/gen/sessions.sql.go:138`, called from `store/session_store.go:191`). Those columns are added by `migrations/0040_add_session_diff_base.sql`.

On affected profiles `goose_db_version` already has version `40` recorded from an earlier shipped migration history, so goose skips `0040` and the columns are never created. Every session list then fails:

```
GET /api/v1/sessions -> 500 INTERNAL_ERROR
sqlite3 ~/.ao/data/ao.db "select diff_base_sha from sessions limit 1;"
Error: in prepare, no such column: diff_base_sha
```

`/healthz`, `/readyz`, and `/api/v1/projects` still succeed, so the daemon looks healthy while the core workflow is dead.

## Scope of the burned range is still unconfirmed

The collision is not conceptually limited to version 40. Once a version is recorded in `goose_db_version`, the real migration with that number is skipped silently, and the failure surfaces only later as an opaque 500 from a generated query.

The affected Windows profile has versions **40 through 46** recorded applied on 2026-07-23. Upstream currently ships migrations only up to `0040`.

**Correction to an earlier version of this issue:** I previously cited a macOS profile with versions 40 through 51 as a second independent reproduction. That was wrong. That machine burned 40-51 by running local `pipelines` feature branches, which define their own `0040_pipeline_tables.sql` through `0051_pipeline_run_number.sql`, with apply timestamps matching that branch work. It is self-inflicted by running unmerged branches and is not evidence about released nightlies. It has been retracted on #3476.

That leaves the load-bearing open question:

**How did a website-installed Windows nightly end up with versions 40 through 46 recorded?**

If that profile only ever ran released upstream nightlies, a released build shipped migrations in that range which were later renumbered or removed, which is a genuine release problem and P1 is right. If it also ran a fork or branch build, it is the same self-inflicted case and the priority changes substantially. This should be confirmed before the repair is designed, since it decides whether real users need a shipped repair migration or whether a guardrail plus documentation is sufficient.

Independent of that answer, the guardrail and the schema-verification work below are worth doing, because the failure mode is silent and the diagnostics actively mislead.

---

# Fix plan, one PR

## 1. Stop group-killing a PID the daemon no longer owns

A PID is only meaningful while the daemon still holds the unreaped child. After `cmd.Wait()` returns, the number is back in the OS pool and may already belong to something else. Because the kill is negative it targets a whole process group, so a stale number takes out an entire unrelated family.

- Delete the `case <-done` escalation at `manager.go:375`. After `Wait()` has returned there is nothing left the daemon legitimately owns, so this branch can only ever hit an unrelated process group.
- Same for the post-`done` calls in `forceStopAfterGrace` (`manager.go:797`, `:799`).
- `manager.go:474` in `waitForExit` runs immediately after `Wait()` returns and has the same problem.
- If orphaned descendants that ignored SIGTERM are a real concern, the group kill has to happen *before* the root is reaped, while the PID is still owned. Ordering is the fix, not an extra escalation afterwards.
- `reapPersistedProcesses` (`manager.go:829`) group-kills PIDs recorded by a previous daemon generation. Those are stale by construction. Either verify the PID still belongs to a preview process before killing, or drop the mechanism.

Invariant worth encoding: never pass a PID to `kill` unless the caller can prove the child has not been reaped.

## 2. Treat server-level probe errors as inconclusive

Split `sessionMissingOutput` (`tmux.go:878`):

- Keep `can't find session` and `session not found` as genuine per-session evidence.
- Map `no server running` and `error connecting` to `ProbeFailed` so the existing arbitration handles them.

This restores the behaviour the code already documents. The safety net exists and is correctly written, it is just bypassed before it can run.

`killSessionMissingOutput` delegates to the same helper. Being generous about "already gone" during teardown is fine, but it should not share a predicate with liveness probing.

## 3. Add a reaper circuit breaker

Fixes 1 and 2 close the two known doors. This one protects against causes not yet identified.

If a single reconcile pass concludes that every session, or nearly every session, is dead, that is not N independent deaths. It is one infrastructure outage. There is no realistic scenario in which 28 unrelated agents exit within three seconds of each other.

The reaper should refuse to act on a pass where the dead fraction exceeds a threshold, log at error level, and leave sessions untouched pending the next probe. A wrongly-skipped termination is cheap and self-corrects. A wrongly-applied mass termination archives the user's entire board.

Worth having on its own merits: during triage the original tmux death left no crash report, no unified-log entry, and no `memorystatus` record, so root-causing from forensics alone was not possible. A circuit breaker would have preserved the board regardless of cause.

## 4. Repair the schema and make the version checklist untrustworthy by design

- Add a forward repair migration numbered above any version plausibly burned, that adds `diff_base_sha` and `diff_base_ref` **only if absent**. It must be safe on profiles that applied `0040` correctly and on profiles already patched by hand, so a plain `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` will not do.
- Add a startup schema reconciliation that verifies the physical columns the generated queries depend on, rather than trusting `goose_db_version`. That table is known to lie on at least some real installs.
- Add a guardrail that rejects reuse of a version number already shipped in any nightly. Renumbering or deleting migration files after release is what produces this class of failure. Note that in-flight feature branches such as `pipelines` also claim numbers in this range, so branch and release numbering need to be reconciled.
- Surface migration and schema mismatches as a specific, actionable error instead of an opaque 500. Today `/healthz` and `/readyz` report healthy while the core workflow is dead.
- Triage note: a working `select diff_base_sha` does not prove a profile was never affected, since hand-patched databases resolve fine while the underlying burned versions remain.

## Regression tests

- `forceKillPreviewProcess` is never reached with a reaped `cmd`.
- A probe returning `no server running` yields `ProbeFailed`, not `ProbeDead`, and leaves `IsTerminated` unchanged.
- A reconcile pass where every session probes dead terminates nothing and logs an error.
- Session list succeeds against a DB whose `goose_db_version` contains 40 through 51 but whose `sessions` table lacks the diff-base columns.
- The repair migration is idempotent: it succeeds on a DB that already has the columns.

---

Both halves share one root pattern: trusting a stale identifier instead of checking reality. A PID that used to be a preview server, and a version number that claims a migration ran. In both cases the fix is to verify the thing in front of you rather than trust a number written down earlier.

title: Windows nightly: Board cannot load sessions when migration 0040 is skipped by prior goose version
body:
## Bug
The desktop Board can show only `Could not load sessions.` on Windows nightly because the daemon's session list endpoint fails with HTTP 500 when the local SQLite database has a previously-recorded goose migration version `40` but lacks the new `sessions.diff_base_sha` / `sessions.diff_base_ref` columns.

**Source:** Local device triage from a website-installed Windows nightly; screenshots supplied in Codex chat.
**Reported by:** @somewherelostt
**Analyzed against installed app:** `v0.11.2-nightly.202608021445` / tag `9159a0206a2e1d2a99333118bf9ebc5590b7404f`
**Current main checked:** `dd8f6e0b0321253b2e0a0ea18322c3de2397cf49`
**Confidence:** High
**Priority:** P1: core Board/session workflow is broken with no in-app workaround.

## Reproduction
On an affected Windows install/profile:

1. Install/run Agent Orchestrator nightly `v0.11.2-nightly.202608021445` from the website.
2. Use an existing `~/.ao/data/ao.db` whose `goose_db_version` already contains version `40` from an earlier shipped migration history, but whose `sessions` table does not contain `diff_base_sha` or `diff_base_ref`.
3. Open the desktop app Board.
4. Observe `Could not load sessions.`
5. Query the daemon directly:

```powershell
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\agent-orchestrator\resources\daemon\ao.exe" status
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\agent-orchestrator\resources\daemon\ao.exe" session ls
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/v1/sessions
```

Observed locally:

```text
AO daemon: ready
  pid: 30884
  port: 3001
  data dir: C:\Users\abuma\.ao\data
  healthz: ok
  readyz: ready

GET /api/v1/sessions -> 500 INTERNAL_ERROR
Internal server error (INTERNAL_ERROR) [request Somewherelostt/E4BRzyHpFn-000031]
```

The database has sessions and projects, so the board is not empty:

```text
select count(*) from sessions; -- 47
```

## Root Cause
The installed code's generated session queries select the new diff-base columns:

- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/gen/sessions.sql.go:132` defines `ListAllSessions`.
- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/gen/sessions.sql.go:138` selects `diff_base_sha, diff_base_ref` from `sessions`.
- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/store/session_store.go:191` calls the generated `ListAllSessions` query.
- `backend/internal/service/session/service.go:606` wraps that failure as `list all sessions: ...`, which the HTTP controller surfaces as an opaque 500.

The migration that should add the columns is:

- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/migrations/0040_add_session_diff_base.sql:3`
- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/migrations/0040_add_session_diff_base.sql:4`

However, the affected local DB already has goose versions `40` through `46` recorded from an earlier migration history, while the physical `sessions` table does not have the new columns:

```text
select * from goose_db_version order by id;
...
28|40|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
29|41|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
30|42|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
31|43|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
32|44|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
33|45|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
34|46|1|2026-07-23 19:46:19
...
46|39|1|2026-07-31 17:02:15
```

```text
pragma table_info(sessions);
-- highest relevant columns:
21|runtime_launch_id|TEXT|1|''|0
22|workspace_repo_path|TEXT|1|''|0
23|terminate_on_pr_merge|BOOLEAN|1|FALSE|0
```

Direct proof of the schema mismatch:

```text
sqlite3 ~/.ao/data/ao.db "select diff_base_sha from sessions limit 1;"
Error: in prepare, no such column: diff_base_sha
```

So goose skips `0040_add_session_diff_base.sql` because version `40` is already marked applied, and the daemon then ships code that assumes the columns exist. This is a migration version collision/regression for profiles that saw the older version-40+ migration history.

## Screenshots
![Board shows Could not load sessions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issue-assets-sessions-db-migration-0040-collision/.issue-assets/sessions-db-migration-0040-collision/board-could-not-load-sessions.png)

![Nightly version settings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issue-assets-sessions-db-migration-0040-collision/.issue-assets/sessions-db-migration-0040-collision/nightly-version-settings.png)

## Fix
Add a forward repair path with a migration version greater than any previously shipped version in affected DBs, or a startup schema reconciliation step, that ensures `sessions.diff_base_sha` and `sessions.diff_base_ref` exist before generated queries run.

Important: the repair must be safe for both profiles that already successfully applied `0040_add_session_diff_base.sql` and profiles where version `40` was already consumed by older migration history. A plain duplicate `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` will fail on users who already have the columns.

Also consider a guardrail so future migrations cannot reuse version numbers already shipped in nightly builds, even if migration files are later renumbered or deleted.

## Impact
- Desktop Board cannot load any sessions.
- `ao session ls` fails with `INTERNAL_ERROR`.
- `/api/v1/sessions` returns 500 while `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and `/api/v1/projects` still succeed, making the daemon appear healthy despite the broken core workflow.
- Affected existing profiles need a schema repair; reinstalling the app alone is unlikely to fix the existing DB.

title: feat(reviews): choose the reviewer agent per session, and show every pass in one place
body: First of three, splitting #3357 so each piece can be reviewed on its own. This one is the reviewer-selection slice. ## What **One reviewer picker, two callers.** The picker was private to `ProjectSettingsForm`. It is now a shared `ReviewerSelect`, used both for the project default and for a per-session choice, so the two read as the same control rather than two lookalikes. **Choosing a reviewer for one session cannot affect another.** `Trigger` takes an optional harness override. An empty one keeps the project's configured reviewer; a known one runs that pass under it without editing project config. Nothing is persisted, so the choice is scoped to the pass that used it. **Every pass in one place.** `ListReviewsResponse` now carries `runs`, every recorded pass for the session, newest first. `reviews` only held the current and previous run per PR, which cannot answer what a different reviewer said once a third pass has run, so there was no single place to summarise findings across reviewers. The trigger and the picker sit in the panel actions; the summary is its own surface below them. Deliberately separate. ## Not in this PR - the review-delivery toggle (`review_auto_inject_off`, the migration and its endpoint) - reviewer terminal tabs and their persistence `types/workspace.ts`, `useWorkspaceQuery.ts` and `api-client.ts` are untouched here because their changes in #3357 are entirely toggle-related. ## Worth a look in review The OpenAPI spec is generated, so the optional trigger body needed `specgen` to stop marking every request body required. Previously every body was forced required, which would have told clients the trigger body was mandatory when the whole point is that it is optional. That is the `optionalReqBody` flag in `build.go`. ## Verification Backend builds, all backend tests pass. Frontend typecheck clean, 1322 tests pass. Ran the app against a daemon built from this branch and confirmed the override path end to end: posting an unknown harness to the trigger route returns 422 from the validation added in `override_test.go`.

title: fix(desktop): clamp sidebar and inspector drags at min width instead of auto-collapsing
body:
## Summary

Dragging the left sidebar or the right inspector rail narrower used to shrink the panel past a usable width and then auto-collapse it entirely. Both drags now hard-stop at a minimum-width floor; collapsing remains available only through the explicit controls (⌘B / titlebar toggle for the sidebar, topbar button / ⌘⇧B for the inspector).

### Root causes

- **Sidebar** — `useResizable` had a `collapseBelow` threshold set to `SIDEBAR_MIN_WIDTH` (200px), so the instant a drag crossed the min it fired `onCollapse` and hid the panel.
- **Inspector** — the react-resizable-panels v4 panel was always `collapsible`, and rrp snaps a collapsible panel to 0% once a drag passes halfway below `minSize` (22%).

### Fix

- `useResizable` drops the `collapseBelow`/`onCollapse` drag path; the existing `min` clamp in `apply()` is the floor (200px, the same clamp convention as #1385). Persistence and the collapsed-rail drag-to-expand are unchanged; the drag-clamped width now also persists on pointer-up.
- The inspector panel is `collapsible` only while closed, so an open-panel drag clamps at the existing 22% `minSize`. Opening drives `resize()` to the persisted split (rrp's `expand()` no-ops on a non-collapsible panel); closing repeats `collapse()` on the next animation frame because rrp only derives the re-registered collapsible constraints one commit after the prop flips (a same-commit `collapse()` no-ops against the stale non-collapsible constraints).
- Drag-to-reopen of the collapsed inspector via its separator still works and is covered by e2e.

### Tests

- Unit: `Sidebar.test.tsx` / `SessionView.test.tsx` updated — drags assert the clamp (and never close the store); explicit toggles still collapse/reopen.
- E2E (new `e2e/resize-clamp.spec.ts`, real pointer drags over the real rrp + CSS pipeline): sidebar drag to the window edge stays expanded at 200px and persists; inspector drag to the group edge clamps at its 22% floor, the topbar button still collapses it, and the collapsed rail drags back open.
- Repaired `e2e/inspector-toggle.spec.ts`, which referenced the stale `refactor-mux` mock fixture (dataset is now `ao-demo`/`demo-working`) and could not run.

Verified visually against `dev:web` by dragging both rails to their extremes (screenshots checked): each stops at its floor instead of disappearing, and the explicit collapse controls still work.

`npm test` (renderer suite), `npm run typecheck`, `npm run typecheck:e2e`, and the `@T0|@P0` renderer smoke suite pass. The only failing file is the pre-existing, unrelated `src/landing/scripts/generate-markdown-twins.test.mjs` (fails identically on a clean tree in this environment).

Related: #1385 (min/max width clamp convention for the web project sidebar).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat(spawn): add --model for per-session model override
body:
Closes #3331

## What

Adds `ao spawn --model <model>` for a per-session model override, plus the matching `model` field on `POST /api/v1/sessions`. The override is scoped to the spawned session only — it never mutates project config.

## Precedence

Mirrors the chain from the issue, folded into the existing `effectiveAgentConfig` merge:

```
spawn --model > role agentConfig.model > project agentConfig.model
```

The resolved model is pinned on the durable session record at spawn so `ao session get` reports what the session actually launched with (new `model` field on `session get`, human + `--json`), and a later restore keeps the same model even if the project config changes.

## Changes

- **CLI** (`spawn.go`): `--model` flag, validated as a single token (rejects spaces/quotes so it can't smuggle launch args), forwarded as `model` in the spawn request. `session.go`: `model` in `session get` output.
- **Daemon** (`dto.go`, `sessions.go`, `ports/session.go`, `manager.go`): `SpawnSessionRequest.model`, `SpawnConfig.Model`, precedence folding in `effectiveAgentConfig`, pinned via `seedRecord`.
- **Persistence** (`0041_add_session_model.sql`, `queries/sessions.sql`, sqlc gen, store): `sessions.model` column, round-trip tested.
- **API**: OpenAPI spec + `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` regenerated (`npm run api`), sqlc regenerated (`npm run sqlc`).

## Tests

- DTO-drift e2e: `--model` arrives intact through the real HTTP round trip (`dto_drift_e2e_test.go`)
- CLI: `--model` rejects whitespace/quoted values (`spawn_test.go`)
- Precedence: spawn model wins over role override and base config for both worker and orchestrator (`provision_test.go`)
- HTTP: spawn request decodes `model` and echoes it on the session read model (`sessions_test.go`)
- Store: `model` column insert/update/get round trip (`store_test.go`)

`go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `npm run lint`, and `npm run frontend:typecheck` all pass (three unrelated flaky agent-adapter timing tests fail intermittently on clean `main` too).

title: fix(codex): prefer system-prompt file over inline -c arg (fixes #3326)
body:
## What
Codex orchestrator/worker launches now pass the system prompt to Codex via a temp file instead of inlining it as a `-c` command-line argument.

## Why
Codex's adapter inlined the full assembled system prompt (often several KB — role instructions, project rules, workspace context, skill pointer) as a `-c developer_instructions=...` CLI argument on every launch, even though `session_manager.Manager` already staged the same content to a file (`SystemPromptFile`) that every other adapter with the same problem (Aider, Agy, Auggie, Kiro, OpenCode, Copilot, Vibe) already uses. On Windows in particular this pushed the aggregate command line (system prompt + AO's other `-c` hook/session flags) past Codex CLI's own argument limits, surfacing as an opaque "prompt too long" error — even for a ~25-line task prompt nowhere near AO's real 4096-byte API limit.

Fixes #3326

## How
- `codex.go`: `GetLaunchCommand` and `GetRestoreCommand` now check `SystemPromptFile` first and only fall back to inline `developer_instructions` if no file was staged.
- `manager.go`: added `codex` to `systemPromptFileRequired`, so a staging failure surfaces as a clean spawn error instead of silently falling back to the inline path that caused this bug.
- `manager.go`: `Spawn()` now returns the real `promptBytes`/`systemPromptBytes` on every error path (previously hardcoded `0, 0`), and logs both sizes at debug level on every spawn — makes an oversized assembled prompt diagnosable instead of surfacing only as a bare CLI error.
- No changes to the HTTP/API layer (`sessions.go`) — the returned byte counts are available to callers but nothing new is wired into the error response yet; flagging in case a reviewer wants that as a fast-follow.

## Testing
- `go build ./...` — clean
- `go vet ./...` — clean
- `go test ./internal/adapters/agent/codex/... ./internal/session_manager/...` — passing
- Updated `TestGetLaunchCommandBuildsCrossPlatformArgv` and `TestGetRestoreCommandReadsAgentSessionID`, which had previously asserted the buggy inline-wins priority as expected behavior (test name literally used the string `"inline wins"`); both now assert the file-wins priority.
- **Not yet done: an actual manual repro against a real Codex binary** — spawning a Codex orchestrator with a large `OrchestratorRules`/workspace repo list on Windows, confirming the previous "prompt too long" no longer fires. Unit tests confirm the argv construction is correct; they don't confirm Codex CLI actually accepts it end-to-end.

## My take
Went with file-over-inline instead of just bumping the 4096-byte limit — that limit's on the task prompt, not the system prompt, so raising it wouldn't have actually fixed anything. File delivery is already how 7 other harnesses handle this, so this just brings Codex in line.

Confident in the core fix + test updates, both backed by real build/test output.

Less sure about: `domain.HarnessCodex` is a guess based on naming convention, never actually saw that file. Also haven't run this against a real Codex binary — only unit tests, so someone should manually repro on Windows before merging.

Left out on purpose: `sessions.go` still doesn't surface the byte counts to the API response on error. Didn't want to touch DTOs in the same PR as the crash fix — good follow-up though.


## Checklist
- [x] Branched from `main`
- [x] One focused change; links the related issue when applicable
- [x] Follows [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/blob/main/AGENTS.md) conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense
- [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go`, frontend, etc.)

title: Docs TOC active section indicator does not highlight bottom heading on scroll

When scrolling down to the bottom of a documentation page, the sidebar Table of Contents ("On this page") active indicator stays stuck on earlier headings (e.g. "Install") and does not highlight the bottom section ("Troubleshooting").

title: Fix URL editing in macOS maximized browser view
body:
## What

Keep the browser URL field selectable and editable when the browser panel is maximized on macOS.

## Why

The macOS shell uses a hidden native titlebar with a traffic-light drag region. The maximized browser is portaled to `document.body` and originally rendered from `y=0`, allowing its URL toolbar to overlap that native drag region. Electron treated pointer input there as window dragging instead of delivering it to the URL input.

Windows is unaffected because its Window Controls Overlay safe area is already applied.

## How

- Reserve the existing 40px macOS titlebar band in windowed mode.
- Mark the maximized browser surface and toolbar controls as `-webkit-app-region: no-drag`.
- Skip the inset during native macOS fullscreen, where traffic lights are hidden.
- Add regression tests for URL editing and fullscreen/windowed overlay behavior.

## Files affected

- `frontend/src/renderer/components/SessionView.tsx`
- `frontend/src/renderer/styles.css`
- `frontend/src/renderer/components/BrowserPanel.test.tsx`
- `frontend/src/renderer/components/SessionView.test.tsx`

title: feat(landing): record marketing analytics, with replay scoped to the design-partner page
body:
## The problem

The marketing site has been instrumented in code for a while: a `track()` helper with Reddit-pixel forwarding, a consent banner, `capture_pageview`/`capture_pageleave`/`capture_exceptions`, and a `download_clicked` event already wired to the download button.

**It has recorded nothing.** Verified against PostHog: **0 marketing events and 0 pageviews across 90 days.**

Two independent deployment blockers, either of which alone made it silent:

**1. `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` was never passed to the build.** `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is inlined at build time, so on the deployed site the key was `undefined` and `instrumentation-client.ts` skipped `posthog.init` entirely. The code even documents the symptom: *"which happens whenever NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY is unset."*

**2. `api_host` was `"/ingest"`.** That needs a Next rewrite, but `next.config.ts` sets `output: "export"` and states rewrites are *"intentionally omitted"*. Every capture request would have 404'd against GitHub Pages even once the key was set.

Fixing only the first would have looked successful and still sent nothing.

## What changed

- Deploy workflow passes `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`. A repository **variable**, not a secret: the value ships to every visitor in the JS bundle so it is not secret, it is a write-only ingestion key, and the desktop app already commits the same value in `shared/posthog-config.ts`.
- `api_host` is now absolute, overridable via env so a managed reverse proxy can be swapped in later without code changes.
- **Autocapture and session replay enabled**, which is deliberately the opposite of the desktop app. The app disables both because its DOM contains user source code, agent prompts, terminal output, and local paths. This site is public marketing copy, so click heatmaps and replay are the signal rather than a data-handling problem. Replay masks all inputs, with `[data-ph-no-record]` and `[data-ph-mask]` escape hatches.
- `download_clicked` now carries `platform`, `placement`, `is_mobile`, `size`. It previously sent no properties at all, so every download click looked identical.
- `section_viewed` via `IntersectionObserver`, fired at most once per section per page load. A single-page marketing site shares one URL, so scroll depth is the only way to see whether visitors reach the download section. The once-only guard matters: an unguarded observer re-fires on every scroll past, which is the shape of stream that caused the original PostHog bill.
- Config extracted into a pure builder so the invariants are testable.

## Validation

Built the static export both ways and grepped the output, rather than trusting the config:

```
build with no env  (today's deploy) -> KEY ABSENT from bundle
build with the env this PR passes   -> KEY PRESENT in bundle
                                       api_host = us.i.posthog.com
                                       "/ingest" no longer present
```

Also `npx vitest run src/landing` → 12 tests passing, covering the absolute-host invariant, autocapture and replay staying on, input masking, and consent staying opt-out by default.

## Still required after merge, and not code

- **Enable the project-side recording toggle.** `session_recording_opt_in` is currently `false` on project 475752, so the client change alone will not produce replays.
- **Set a replay sample rate.** `sampleRate` and `minimumDurationMilliseconds` are server-side config, not client options. The `session_replay` cap is already $250 with usage at 0; 5,000 recordings/month are free.
- **Add an `app_name != 'marketing'` filter to existing insights.** Landing events land in the same project as the app (the code already registers `app_name: "marketing"`), which is what makes a landing → install funnel possible, but existing DAU and volume charts will jump the day this ships and look like growth.

## Known limits, stated plainly

- **Download attribution is aggregate-only.** The installer carries no token and the site is a different origin, so a visitor cannot be joined to a specific install. Landing `download_clicked` versus GitHub installer counts gives you the split; nothing gives you per-user.
- **GitHub download counts must not be summed.** For v0.11.2, 7,137 of 7,925 "downloads" were `latest-*.yml` update polls, not installs. Real installer downloads were roughly 700.
- **Consent-gated.** `opt_out_capturing_by_default: true` stays, so only consenting visitors are captured. Correct posture, but landing numbers will read lower than raw traffic.

Independent of #3401. Different branch off `main`, no overlapping files.

title: fix: stop stale-PID group kills, misread liveness probes, and burned-migration 500s from wiping the board
body:
Fixes #3475 (and the migration half originally filed as #3476).

Three distinct failures, one shared root pattern: trusting a stale identifier (a PID, a tmux exit message, a goose version number) instead of verifying the thing in front of us.

## A1: preview server group-killed PIDs it no longer owned

Once `cmd.Wait()` returns, the PID is back in the OS pool; `kill(-pid, SIGKILL)` on that number targets a whole process group, and a tmux server is its own group leader, so one recycled PID wiped every tmux session at once. Every escalation site had the flaw (`stop`, `waitForExit`, `failAndStop`, `forceStopAfterGrace`), and `reapPersistedProcesses` group-killed PIDs recorded by the previous daemon generation with no check at all.

**Fix:** every preview root's kernel start time is captured at launch (`ps -o lstart=` on unix, `GetProcessTimes` on Windows) and persisted in the process registry. No group/tree kill is sent unless the number is positively re-verified:

- live process whose start time mismatches: recycled, never signalled;
- reaped root whose group still has members: those are our orphaned descendants (POSIX reserves a live group's PGID), which is exactly what escalation exists to reap, so the intended "descendants ignored SIGTERM" behavior is kept rather than deleted;
- registry entries with no recorded identity (older builds): skipped;
- identity capture failed: fall back to signalling only the direct child via `os.Process`, which refuses to signal a reaped child and can never hit a recycled PID.

## A2: server-level probe failures misread as per-session death

`sessionMissingOutput` matched `no server running` and `error connecting`, so `IsAlive` returned a confident "dead" for every session the moment the server was gone, and the reaper archived the whole board, even though the agents were still alive as orphans of the killed server.

**Fix:** the predicate is split. `can't find session` / `session not found` stay definitive per-session evidence. Server-level output now wraps a new `ports.ErrRuntimeUnavailable` sentinel, which the reaper reports as `ProbeFailed`, and the existing LCM arbitration (which was always correct, just bypassed) never terminates on it. Teardown (`kill-session`) keeps tolerating server-level output as already-gone. Restore, boot reconcile, and reconcile-reap map the sentinel back to their intended recovery semantics, so `ao session restore` after a dead server and the post-reboot boot pass both still work.

**Plus a reaper circuit breaker** for doors not yet found: if a single pass concludes that most of the board (>50%, minimum 5) is dead at once, that is one infrastructure outage, not N independent exits. The pass is downgraded to inconclusive and logged at error level; a skipped termination self-corrects on the next probe, a mass termination does not.

## B: burned migration versions 500 the session list

Profiles whose `goose_db_version` already records version 40 (written by a fork/branch build; a field Windows profile has 40-46) make goose silently skip the real `0040_add_session_diff_base.sql`. Generated queries then fail with `no such column: diff_base_sha`, so `GET /api/v1/sessions` returns an opaque 500 while `/healthz` stays green.

**Fix:** startup no longer trusts `goose_db_version` for these columns. After `goose.Up`, a schema reconciliation verifies the physical columns the generated queries depend on and adds any that are missing. It is idempotent (healthy and hand-patched databases untouched) and failures surface as a specific, actionable startup error. A versioned repair migration was deliberately not used: a burned version number is the exact mechanism that caused the skip, so it cannot be the delivery vehicle for its own fix (a profile burned past the repair's number would skip it too).

**Guardrail:** a new ledger test freezes every shipped migration version to its exact filename and rejects burned numbers: 22 (shipped in #2412, then reverted) and 41-51 (claimed by branch builds, observed recorded in the field). New migrations start at 52. Renumbering, renaming, or deleting a shipped migration now fails the build with an explanation instead of surfacing months later as an unexplainable 500.

## Regression tests

- reap refuses a live process whose identity mismatches the recorded preview, and skips legacy registry entries with no identity; verified kills still work; the post-reap escalation still reaps orphaned group members (real processes, not stubs)
- `no server running` / `error connecting` surface as `ErrRuntimeUnavailable`, and the reaper reports `ProbeFailed` for probe errors (existing test)
- a pass where every session probes dead terminates nothing; a minority-dead pass still concludes; small boards never trip the breaker
- session list succeeds against a DB whose `goose_db_version` records 40-51 but whose `sessions` table lacks the diff-base columns (built through the real migration path, listed through the real store); repair is idempotent
- migration version ledger test as above

## Verification

- `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` for darwin and windows
- full `go test ./...`: green except `TestWorkspaceFilesIncludeWorkspaceProjectChildRepoDiffs`, which fails identically on a clean `upstream/main` checkout on this machine (pre-existing, environment-dependent)
- `go test -race` on every touched package: green
- `golangci-lint v2.12.2 run --path-mode=abs`: 0 issues

## Known risks / follow-ups

- Identity verification shells out to `ps`/`pgrep` at preview start and kill time; on a system where those fail, teardown degrades to root-only signalling (descendants may leak, innocents never die).
- The verify-then-kill pair is not atomic; without pidfd-style primitives a recycle inside that microsecond window is theoretically possible. It replaces a window that was effectively unbounded.
- After this change a dead tmux server leaves sessions visible (probes keep failing) instead of archiving them; the boot-time reconcile still tears them down with restore markers on the next daemon start. That trade is deliberate per the issue.
- Whether a released nightly ever shipped migrations 41-46 (the open question in the issue) is unanswered here; the reconciliation repairs affected profiles either way.

title: feat(settings): settings modal with sectioned nav
body:
Converts settings from full-page routes to a modal dialog. Instead of navigating away, clicking Settings anywhere in the app opens a modal that stays over the current view.

## What changed

**SettingsDialog** — new modal component with a sidebar nav. Global settings has four sections: General, Updates, Developer, Help. Project settings has four: General, Agents, Workflow, Intake. Switching sections swaps only the right-hand content; the dialog stays open.

**GlobalSettingsForm / ProjectSettingsForm** — both now accept a `section` prop so the dialog can render one section at a time without re-mounting the whole form.

**Route redirects** — `/settings` and `/projects/:id/settings` still work. They now open the modal and immediately redirect back, so any bookmark or deep-link that lands on those URLs gets the dialog experience instead of a full page.

**DevSettingsSection** — dev-mode-only panel for controlling board fixture count and activity spread (replaces the inline inputs that were scattered around).

**ThemeStyle** — adds the type and `readStoredThemeStyle` / `applyDocumentThemeStyle` helpers to `lib/theme`, and wires `themeStyle` + `setThemeStyle` into the ui-store. The General section shows a palette picker that persists across reloads. Actual palette tokens come in a follow-up PR.

**ui-store** — adds `settingsModal`, `openGlobalSettings`, `openProjectSettings`, and `closeSettings`. Also adds `devSettings` and `setDevSettings` for the dev panel.

**Cleanup** — removes `SettingsPageShell` and `SettingsPanel`, which were the old full-page wrapper components. Nothing imports them after this change.

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

title: feat(session): surface harness context pressure on sessions and doctor
body: > tldr ; > real quick in my own words; when a worker runs out of context it doesn't die, > it just keeps sending cheap replies while dropping the actual work, and from > AO's side that looks identical to a worker thats being lazy on "active". poking > it again is the worst move bc it just burns more context. so this PR only > ferries the harness's context % to where you can actually see it, nothing > smarter. didn't add auto-respawn or a banner parser on purpose, those feel like > separate calls. > > the one thing i actually worried about is pressure reports bump updated_at and i > didn't want that tripping the reaper, checked by hand, reaper reads > lastActivityAt not updated_at so we're fine.90/10 thresholds are guesses from > the issue, easy to tweak. if anything the lifecycle bit in manager.go is what > i'd want eyes on most. ## What Add an optional, best-effort context-pressure reading to the session read model, carried alongside agent activity signals. A worker that has run out of context can now be distinguished from one that is refusing work — without touching the `activity_state` enum. Surfaces added: - `ao session get` → renders `contextPressure: used=N% untilAutoCompact=N% source=… observedAt=…` (human + JSON) - `ao session ls` → compact `ctx N%` tag - `ao doctor` → harness-agnostic **WARN** when any active worker has `usedPercent >= 90` or `untilAutoCompactPercent <= 10` ## Why When a worker is at the end of its context budget it is indistinguishable from a worker actively refusing work: `activity_state=active`, cheap text keeps flowing, expensive outputs (commits, gate runs) silently drop. The intuitive fix — re-nudging — burns more of the one resource it's out of, making it worse. The orchestrator needs to *read* context pressure so an operator can reap-and-respawn instead of nudge. Closes #3322. This PR implements **pieces 1 and 3** of the issue (session DTO + operator-facing surface) plus the **carrier path** (piece 2: the activity endpoint accepts the reading). It does **not** add a harness-specific banner parser — see "Intentional omissions" below. ## How - **`domain.ContextPressure`** (`{usedPercent, untilAutoCompactPercent, source, observedAt}`) added to `SessionRecord` as a `*` pointer. **Nil means the harness has not reported — never zero, never an error** (acceptance #1). DTOs use `omitempty`. - **Carrier path:** the existing `POST /sessions/{id}/activity` payload optionally accepts `contextPressure`. Edge validation rejects out-of-range percentages (0–100), sanitizes `source`, defaults `observedAt` to now. - **Lifecycle:** a pressure-only update persists the reading **without changing `activity_state` or `FirstSignalAt`** (acceptance #4) and **never blocks activity recording** — pressure is folded in alongside the activity write, nil is a no-op (acceptance #5). A small `contextPressureEqual` check prevents repeated identical readings from churning `updated_at` or fanning out CDC. - **Persistence:** new additive migration `0041` adds a nullable `context_pressure` JSON TEXT column and extends the `sessions_cdc_update` trigger so the UI refetches on a change. sqlc queries/store mapping (de)serialize JSON; corrupt stored JSON degrades to nil (best-effort). - **Generated artifacts regenerated and committed:** `sqlc/gen/*`, `openapi.yaml`, `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` (code-first contract; CI fails on drift). ### Behavioral note for reviewers (not a risk, flagged for transparency) Pressure-only hook writes now bump `updated_at` and emit a CDC `session_updated` event, where before a no-state/no-agent-session-id hook was a complete no-op. I verified this introduces **no change to orchestrator decisions**: - Reaper (`observe/reaper`) does not read `updated_at` → kill decisions unaffected. - Activity staleness gate (`observe/activity/observer.go:104`) keys off `Activity.LastActivityAt`, which pressure writes never set → unaffected. - Nudges (CI/review/merge-conflict) are PR-observation-driven and deduped via `GetPRLastNudgeSignature`, not `updated_at` → unaffected (the worker-idle nudge was already removed in #3040). The only consumer of `updated_at` is the `ExpectedUpdatedAt` reconciliation fence (`manager.go:316`); a pressure write landing between the terminal-idle observer's read and apply drops that one signal, which retries on the next 30s tick. This is the **same behavior class as the existing agent-session-id metadata write** (already bumps `updated_at` at the same code path) — no new failure mode. ### Heads-up: CDC/write volume A harness that reports pressure on *every* hook with a drifting value (87→88→89…) adds one write + one `change_log` row per drift. The equality check handles *identical* values. If this is a concern on a chatty harness, two cheap follow-ups (neither required here): rate-limit in the adapter, or drop `context_pressure` from the CDC trigger clause. ### Intentional omissions (vs. issue scope) - **No harness banner parser.** No adapter currently extracts Claude Code's statusline/banner metric into a pressure reading. This is deliberate: the issue's non-goal is "the harness detects and reports; AO carries the reading." A vanilla `ao start` will therefore not emit a reading on its own — the evidence below simulates the adapter's report via the real activity endpoint. An adapter hookup is a separate, harness-specific PR. - **No auto reap-and-respawn policy.** The orchestrator/operator decides what to do with the reading; this PR only makes the data available (issue non-goal). - **No `activity_state` enum change.** Additive only. ## Testing Validated locally with the new focused tests, which exercise the **real HTTP controller → real lifecycle manager → real SQLite store** pipeline against an in-memory DB and map 1:1 to the issue's acceptance criteria: Acceptance-criteria coverage: | Test | Acceptance criterion | | ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | `TestSessionPersistsContextPressure` | round-trips through the store; absent when not reported | | `TestSessionsAPI_ActivityAcceptsContextPressureOnly` | pressure-only POST succeeds, no `state` required | | `TestSessionsAPI_ActivityRejectsInvalidContextPressure` | validation rejects 101%, and never blocks activity recording (#5) | | `TestActivity_ContextPressureOnlyDoesNotChangeActivity` | **#4** — `activity_state` + `FirstSignalAt` untouched | | `TestSessionGet_RendersContextPressure` | **#2** — human line + JSON, with `source` + `observedAt` | | `TestSessionList_RendersContextPressure` | **#1/#2** — `ctx N%` in `ls` | | `TestDoctorWarnsOnHighContextPressure` | **#3** — WARN at ≥90%, harness-agnostic | Also ran: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `golangci-lint run` (clean), `go test -race ./...` (only failure is `TestWorkspaceFilesIncludeWorkspaceProjectChildRepoDiffs`, **pre-existing on `main`** — worktree SHA/ref, unrelated), and `npm run frontend:typecheck` (clean). ## Checklist - [x] Branched from `main` (or continuing an existing PR branch) - [x] One focused change; links the related issue when applicable - [x] Follows [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/blob/main/AGENTS.md) conventions and PR hygiene - [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense - [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go`, frontend, etc.)
