title: feat: update copy now AO Mobile is live on both stores
body:
AO Mobile is live on the App Store and Google Play, so every surface that
described a beta needed to change. Most of this is subtraction: the pre-launch
copy existed to explain multi-step workarounds that no longer exist.

**34 files, +674 / −1133.**

## Landing

The download page had two install funnels to explain — TestFlight (install
Apple's app, accept an invite) and an Android closed test (join a Google Group,
opt in, then install). Both are now one tap on a public listing, so the
walkthroughs are deleted rather than reworded, along with their phone-specific
sheets: a sheet whose job was to say "tap this other button" is pure friction
once the button goes straight to the store.

One shared `StoreQRDialog` replaces all five components. On a phone the badge
links directly to the listing; on a desktop it opens a QR, because the app
cannot install on the machine the visitor is reading this on. That handoff is
the only part of the old flow worth keeping.

The badges are Apple's and Google's own artwork, which their identity
guidelines require — the hand-drawn recreation this started with violated both
while also losing the recognition that makes a badge worth using. Their wording
differs ("Download on the" vs "Get it on") because each guideline fixes its
own; that mismatch is deliberate, not an oversight.

## Desktop — Connect Mobile

The iOS side still described a TestFlight beta. Pointing it at the App Store
made it identical to the Android side, which let the two branches collapse into
one and set off a chain of simplifications:

- **The platform dropdown is gone.** It never reached the pairing QR — the
  payload is built with `platform: ""`, and that field carries the desktop's OS,
  not the phone's — so all it selected was which of two store links to show.
  Step one now names both, each with its own hover QR.
- **The LAN step is gone.** `qrIsReady` withholds the code until the tunnel
  resolves, precisely so a scannable code always carries a tunnel endpoint, and
  the phone races every advertised endpoint. "Put your phone on the same Wi-Fi"
  contradicted a guarantee the panel already enforces, and the case where it is
  true (no cloudflared) has its own notice. Tailscale keeps its step — there,
  installing it really is a prerequisite.
- **`mobile.description` loses "over your LAN"** for the same reason, with no
  replacement qualifier: "from anywhere" would be wrong whenever the connector
  is missing.

All eight locales updated, mirroring each one's existing Google Play phrasing.
Store names stay untranslated as brand marks; the storefront name survives in
the aria labels for screen readers.

## Mobile app

The push-registration failure named an internal cause the person holding the
phone can do nothing with ("this build has no push entitlement") and sent them
to TestFlight. It now names the fix. `openStore`'s `itms-beta://` fallback
points at the real listing.

## Needs a decision before merge

**The connection-method picker (LAN/Tailscale) is commented out, not deleted**,
in three linked places so it restores as one unit. This also takes the
**secure-pairing toggle** off-screen, which iPhone-over-Tailscale requires —
iOS refuses cleartext to `100.x` addresses, and the TLS MagicDNS host is
deliberately not in the QR. LAN and tunnel paths are unaffected. The seven
tests that reached Tailscale through that picker are skipped with a matching
note rather than rewritten to bypass the UI, so they restore alongside it.

## Verification

- `tsc --noEmit` clean
- 15 suites, 99 passed / 7 skipped; mobile lib 70 passed
- Rendered on iPhone 13 and Pixel 7 viewports: no horizontal overflow, correct
  per-device badge behaviour (own store = direct link, other store = QR)

## Noted separately

On a phone the **cookie consent banner covers the store badges** on first load
— it buries the primary CTA on the page people arrive at to download the app.
Pre-existing and out of scope here, but worth its own fix.

title: rethink the complete mobile application flow
[Cloud][P0] Real-time terminal typing: SSH-parity latency for cloud sessions
body:
## What

Typing in a cloud session's terminal (orchestrator or worker, agent TUI or workspace shell) must feel the same as SSHing directly into the same NodeOps sandbox. Three workstreams:

1. **Duplex terminal stream (implement now).** Replace the polled, store-and-forward hot path with persistent sockets end to end (worker ⇄ control plane ⇄ client). Target: ≤10ms server-added latency, down from ~130ms today. Gated behind `AO_CLOUD_TERMINAL_STREAM` (off = byte-identical current behavior).
2. **Predictive local echo in the renderer (implement now).** mosh/VS Code-typeahead style: printable keys and backspace render instantly in the terminal and are reconciled against the authoritative echo when it arrives; auto-disabled when the terminal is in the alternate screen buffer (agent TUIs like claude/codex redraw aggressively). Makes typing feel ~0ms at any distance.
3. **Direct-to-sandbox live bytes (extensive design below — build only if 1+3 leave a perceptible gap).** Serve the live terminal WebSocket from the worker itself over NodeOps per-port HTTPS ingress, so client↔sandbox is the exact SSH network path; the CP keeps replay/history via async row shipping.

## Why

Cloud terminals today feel laggy compared to SSHing into the same sandbox from the NodeOps GUI. Measured from a client in India against staging: **~300ms per keystroke echo** (10 samples: 290–309ms). Direct SSH to the same region is ~175ms — so AO adds ~130ms of machinery on top of geography. The goal of the cloud offering is that users never *want* the raw sandbox; terminal feel is the most visceral part of that.

## Evidence

**Measured (probe: real WS client typing single chars into a workspace shell, timing each authoritative echo):**
| Path | median echo |
|---|---|
| Staging, client in India | 299ms (min 290 / max 309) |
| Raw network RTT India↔CP (Stockholm) | ~170ms (TCP connect timing, 5 samples 163–180ms) |
| Local Docker stack, poll path | **99ms** (pure server machinery, ~0 network) |
| Local Docker stack, duplex prototype | **5ms** (same binaries, flag on) |

**Where today's ~130ms machinery comes from (all in the hot path of every keystroke):**
- Keystroke: WS frame → `QueueTerminalInput` → **Postgres INSERT**, then waits for the worker's next `POST /worker/transport/claim` poll — a **100ms ticker** (`cloud/internal/workertransport/supervisor.go:79`) against an immediate-return claim endpoint (no long-poll).
- Echo: PTY output → `POST /worker/terminals/{id}/output` → **Postgres row append**, then waits for the CP's WS writer, which polls `ListTerminalOutput` every **50ms** (`cloud/internal/httpapi/terminal_handlers.go:296`).
- Sum: ~75ms average poll waits + 2 Postgres round trips + hops ≈ observed 99ms local / 130ms share of staging.

**Prototype:** branch [`proto/duplex-terminal-stream`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/tree/proto/duplex-terminal-stream) (commit `686ec9fa7`, ~650 lines). Worker holds one authenticated WS per terminal to the CP; input pushed down (bypasses queue+poll), output persisted server-side first (replay rows verified identical to poll path) then broadcast. 99ms → 5ms measured on the same binaries. Known prototype gaps: in-memory bridge is single-replica; no sequence-resume on stream flap; fast-path input not durable.

**SSH-parity framing:** direct SSH from India to the sandbox region (Hetzner Falkenstein) is itself ~175ms/keystroke — SSH has zero machinery, not zero latency. So parity = network RTT + ~0, and *beating* SSH requires local echo (this is exactly why mosh exists).

## Plan

### 1) Duplex stream — production hardening of the prototype
- **Multi-replica correctness** (staging runs 2 CP tasks): fan out via Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY keyed by terminal id — input pushed as NOTIFY payload to whichever replica holds the worker stream; output persisted (rows stay the single source of truth for replay) and NOTIFY wakes the client-serving replica instead of the 50ms poll. Same-replica fast path stays in-memory.
- **Reconnect/ordering:** DB-assigned sequences remain authoritative; worker redials with last-acked sequence; single writer per terminal enforced by worker epoch.
- **Backpressure & degradation:** bounded per-terminal buffers; any failure degrades to the existing poll path (correct, just slower). Flag off = current behavior, byte-identical.
- **Auth:** stream dial authenticated like other `/worker` routes; epoch bump terminates the socket.
- **Telemetry:** echo-latency histogram + stream-vs-poll path counters.

### 2) Direct-to-sandbox live bytes — design (build later only if needed)
- Enable NodeOps per-port ingress on AO sandboxes (currently disabled — deliberate surface-area decision to revisit); worker serves `wss` on an ingress port.
- Auth: the CP keeps minting single-use terminal tickets; the worker validates them via a CP introspection call (or CP-signed ticket verifiable with the worker's key material), so the trust anchor stays the CP.
- Data: client dials the sandbox directly for live bytes (network path identical to SSH: client↔Falkenstein, no Stockholm hop, ~25ms saved for EU↔India asymmetric routes); worker ships output rows to the CP asynchronously for replay/history/multi-viewer.
- Fallback: CP-relayed duplex stream (workstream 1) whenever ingress is unavailable — same client protocol, different dial target.
- Risks to resolve in review: TLS terminates at NodeOps' edge (threat model change); per-sandbox ingress exposure; CSP/connect-src for `*.app.sb.createos.sh`; ticket replay hardening; billing/limits of ingress.
- Verdict so far: most invasive per millisecond gained (~25ms over workstream 1); hold unless 1+3 leave a perceptible gap.

### 3) Predictive local echo (renderer)
- Typeahead in the cloud terminal component: printable chars + backspace render immediately (pending style), reconciled/rolled back against authoritative output; scoped v1 to workspace shells and normal-buffer contexts — **auto-disable when `terminal.buffer.active.type === 'alternate'`** (agent TUIs).
- Composes with either transport; pure renderer work; per-user toggle.

## Acceptance

- Flag on, EU-class client: staging echo ≤60ms; server-added overhead ≤10ms (probe echo minus TCP RTT).
- Flag on, India-class client: echo ≈ network RTT + ≤15ms — **SSH parity**; with local echo, printable keys paint locally in <16ms (one frame) at any distance.
- Flag off: current behavior byte-identical; any stream failure degrades to poll path with no data loss in replay.
- Replay/reconnect integrity: sequence-contiguous output rows across stream flaps; terminal reconnect resumes from cursor.
- Verified by: Go unit tests, Docker smoke assertions, before/after probe measurements in the PR, and a live run on hosted infra.

title: bug(projects): same-basename folders at different paths collide on derived project id — desktop creation dead-ends on ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED
body:
## Bug
Registering two projects whose folders share the same basename (e.g. `~/work/api` and `~/clients/api`) fails on the second registration with an **ID conflict** — the desktop UI shows a generic "create failed" error with no path forward.

**Source:** Discord #bug-triage (Vansh), 2026-09-01 | **Reported by:** Vansh
**Analyzed against:** `Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator@9997248c4` (origin/main tip)
**Confidence:** High — exact code path traced end-to-end
**Priority:** high — core flow (project creation) dead-ends in the UI with no in-product workaround

## Reproduction
1. Register a project for a git repo at `~/work/api` (desktop: Create Project flow, or `ao project add --path ~/work/api`). Succeeds; project id = `api`.
2. Register a second project at `~/clients/api` (same folder basename, different parent).
3. Desktop: creation fails with a generic error — no explanation, no suggested id, no retry path. Raw daemon response is `409 ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED`.

## Root Cause

Two layers combine to produce the dead-end:

**1. Daemon — project ids are derived from the folder *basename*, not the full path.**

`defaultProjectID` (`backend/internal/service/project/service.go:867` at `9997248c4`; was `:835` at `ed52364e3`):

```go
func defaultProjectID(path string) domain.ProjectID {
	id := strings.ToLower(filepath.Base(path))
	id = strings.TrimSpace(id)
	id = strings.ReplaceAll(id, " ", "-")
	return domain.ProjectID(id)
}
```

Two distinct paths → identical derived id. `Add()` then rejects the second registration at `service.go:204`:

```go
} else if ok && existing.ArchivedAt.IsZero() && existing.Path != path {
	return Project{}, apierr.Conflict("ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED", "A project with this id is already registered for a different path", map[string]any{
		"existingProjectId":  existing.ID,
		"suggestedProjectId": string(m.suggestID(ctx, id)),
	})
}
```

The daemon already computes an escape hatch — `suggestID` (`service.go:734`) returns `api1`-style suffixed candidates and returns it in `suggestedProjectId` — but it is only embedded in the error details.

**2. Desktop UI — the suggestion is dropped and no custom-id input exists.**

- `createProject` in `frontend/src/renderer/lib/shell-context.ts:11` accepts only `path`, agents, tracker intake, `asWorkspace` — **there is no field to pass a `projectId`**, so the UI can never avoid or resolve the collision.
- `projectSheetError` (`frontend/src/renderer/components/CreateProjectAgentSheet.tsx:65`) has tailored cases for `PROJECT_PATH_NOT_REPO_ROOT`, `PROJECT_BARE_REPOSITORY`, `UNSUPPORTED_GIT_REPO` — `ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED` (and `PATH_ALREADY_REGISTERED`) fall through to the generic "createFailedTitle / tryAgain" default. Grep of `frontend/src` for `ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED` / `suggestedProjectId`: **zero matches**.

So the user hits a hard dead-end: the daemon knows the fix (`api1`), the UI never shows it, and the UI has no id field to apply it manually.

## Workaround
CLI supports explicit ids (desktop does not):

```bash
ao project add --path ~/clients/api --id api2
```

(`--id` flag: `backend/internal/cli/project.go:268`.)

## Fix Direction
Two candidate approaches (can combine):

1. **UI (minimum viable):** add an `ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED` case to `projectSheetError` that surfaces "a project named X already exists" + the `suggestedProjectId` from the error details, with a one-tap "use `api1`" retry. Mirror for `PATH_ALREADY_REGISTERED` (see #4403).
2. **Daemon (structural):** make collision resolution automatic — on `ID_ALREADY_REGISTERED` for a derived (not user-supplied) id, transparently register under `suggestID()`'s candidate instead of erroring (display name still defaults to the basename, so both projects *display* as "api" but have distinct ids). User-supplied ids should keep the explicit conflict error.

## Impact
- Any user with same-named folders at different paths — common with `api`, `frontend`, `backend`, client/project dirs.
- Desktop flow is a dead-end; only CLI users who know about `--id` can escape.
- Same-basename dirs also collide with display assumptions elsewhere (session prefixes derive from id — `sessionPrefix`, `service.go`).

## Related
- #4403 — the mirror conflict: same *path* re-import dead-ends on `PATH_ALREADY_REGISTERED` with no "go to that project" option. Same UX gap class, different trigger.
- #4479 — dotted-basename project ids (`memron.ai`) rejected by ConPTY on Windows; same `defaultProjectID` derivation, different failure mode.

title: feat(chat): keep ACP providers alive across daemon restarts
body:
Code changes: +1927 -276  
Tests: +2320 -112  
Others: +231 -35  

## Summary

Make detached ownership the default for **all eight ACP Chat providers**: Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Droid, Kimi, Kimchi, Pi, and OMP. Updated against main through `24e101914`.

The root problem was both process and protocol ownership: the daemon owned each ACP child and its in-flight JSON-RPC state. Killing/updating it lost the provider, request correlation, pending permissions, and active prompt. Retaining only a PID or reconnecting a fresh SDK to a raw byte bridge is insufficient.

## Architecture

- **One shared ACP implementation:** the per-session host owns process lifetime, connection setup, request IDs, pending interactions, and bounded prompt replay. The existing shared ACP driver owns typed normalization; provider bindings keep their launch/configuration/permission quirks. No per-provider persistence switches.
- **Services own durable state:** replay starts only after restoring the AO turn/controller fence. SQLite deduplicates host-stable events. Completion is acknowledged only after all preceding projections commit, before dispatching the next queued turn.
- **Stable ownership, lazy launch:** reconnect matches harness/worktree/provider scope and protocol, not mutable model/environment/binary paths. Adoption precedes installation/auth probing and credential preparation. The surviving process retains its original environment and process-fixed permission policy.
- **Explicit lifecycle boundaries:** daemon-wide shutdown detaches; explicit Stop/Kill/handoff destroys the host, including after its controller disappeared. Failed fresh setup/branch publication releases newly created hosts; ambiguous live adoption preserves the possible owner. Short-lived catalog discovery remains ephemeral.
- **One updater safety fact:** the UI consumes daemon-derived `chatProviderPreserved`, replacing the frontend provider allowlist. Missing/unknown ownership remains conservatively warned.

## Replay and teardown hardening

- Give event/interaction IDs a random host-lifetime namespace so replacement hosts cannot collide with already-projected events.
- Retain successful **and failed** prompt receipts until acknowledgement; reject a new prompt while the previous one remains active/unacknowledged.
- Preserve causal order when providers reuse JSON-RPC request IDs.
- Retry failed event transactions in order; detach on sustained projection or ACK failure without losing the journal or dispatching queued work.
- Keep accepted permission/input commands idempotent across attachment loss.
- Share Unix/Windows host argument construction and bound Windows process-tree cleanup.
- Remove obsolete launch/environment fingerprint helpers and provider-gating code; condense the research note into current decisions and explicit evidence limits.

## Verification and evidence

Credential-free tests exercise real local host/provider processes under every ACP harness identity, repeated attachment, no-native-resume adoption, unavailable replacement installation, changed launch inputs, permission fences, failed setup, replay/ACK crash windows, transaction rollback, queued dispatch, and explicit teardown.

Authenticated tests exercise the actual daemon → detached host → ACP provider → model boundary. They wait for a tool-created acceptance marker, replace the daemon during the tool, require the **same host PID, AO turn ID, and provider turn ID**, verify the answer belongs to that turn, send a **fresh post-restart follow-up**, and verify explicit Kill removes the host.

- Fresh Claude and OpenCode runs passed both forced (`SIGKILL`) and graceful replacement, followed by new work and cleanup.
- The earlier Claude/Cursor screen recordings remain in PR comments as historical UI evidence.
- A fresh Cursor attempt stopped during its **initial** credentialed turn with `Upgrade your plan to continue`; no fresh Cursor live-pass claim is made.
- Droid previously returned HTTP 402. Droid/Kimi/Kimchi/Pi/OMP are now on the shared implementation, but are **not claimed authenticated-E2E-verified**. Pi's extra daemon topology and platform coverage remain distinct validation limits.

Local checks: full backend tests; affected-package race suites; `go vet ./...`; golangci-lint v2.12.2; Windows source cross-build; generated API drift check; frontend typecheck, 59 focused updater/board tests, and renderer production build. Exact commands, revisions, and outcomes are recorded in the accompanying evidence comment. Hosted CI is separate.

## Recovery boundary

This preserves a live provider and active prompt across daemon replacement, not provider/host/machine death. Actual provider loss still requires its native load/resume support; lost operations are not falsely reported as surviving. Existing TUI↔Chat eligibility and provider permission/version rules are unchanged. Persistent ACP support is shared by default; vendor E2E coverage is reported separately rather than encoded as another lifecycle allowlist.

Fixes #4526

## CI follow-up — `4b52b622e`

The failing `RestartToUpdateDialog` test still assumed that any Codex session was restart-safe. The production guard intentionally uses the daemon's `chatProviderPreserved` fact. This test-only fix (+24/-1) marks genuinely preserved Codex/Claude/Cursor fixtures explicitly and checks that Codex with false or unknown ownership still warns and never installs without confirmation. No production guard was weakened.

Verification on this revision:

**All 12 hosted CI checks passed**, including the [full Go race suite](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/34404469645/job/102644006071), lint, API drift, Windows checks, CLI native/container checks, renderer smoke, update helper, and secret scanning.

- Reproduced the original failing assertion locally on Node 24 before the fix; the focused dialog/risk suites passed afterward: **22 tests**.
- [Hosted frontend suite](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/34404469628/job/102644014511): **291 files passed; 4,129 tests passed, 6 skipped**, including all 16 merged-main restart-dialog tests. Hosted renderer smoke also passed.
- Local frontend and E2E typechecks, cloud-client tests (21), product-ui tests (126), package build/pack checks, generated API drift, Go build/vet, golangci-lint v2.12.2 (0 issues with an isolated cache), and CLI E2E tests passed.

Local validation limits: the first full frontend run had 4,014 passing tests, 2 failures, and 6 skipped; the reduced-concurrency rerun could not complete after dependency files became unavailable. Renderer smoke had 56 passing tests and 2 startup timeouts (the captured UI was still “Agent Orchestrator is starting”). Full local Go race validation hit disk-full errors and then missing toolchain/cache files. Docker was unresponsive, and Windows-native checks cannot run on this Mac. None of these incomplete/failed local runs are counted as passes; hosted checks provide separate evidence.

This CI-only follow-up does not resolve the separate lifecycle/replay findings from the architecture review.

title: fix(desktop): Open in editor (IDE ↗) finds no editors on Windows — PATH-only detection, no %LOCALAPPDATA%/App Paths fallback
body:
## Bug

On Windows, the "Open in editor" (`IDE ↗`) topbar control cannot open the session workspace in Cursor, VS Code, or any other editor — even when those editors are installed. The control reports no supported editors found, so the primary button is permanently disabled.

**Source:** reported in Discord `#bug-triage` | **Reported by:** @Vaibhaav-Tiwari | **Analyzed against:** `9997248c4` (origin/main, 2026-09-01)
**Confidence:** Medium — mechanism traced in code and consistent with the report; the reporter's machine has not been probed (see "Open questions").

## Reproduction

1. Windows 10/11, AO desktop ≥ v0.12.10 (feature landed in d2fec68c2, Aug 23 — shipped in v0.12.10).
2. Install Cursor and/or VS Code with default installer options (User Installer — the default on Windows — does **not** add `bin` to PATH unless "Add to PATH" is checked; the `cursor`/`code` shims live under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\...`).
3. Open any local session → look at the topbar `IDE ↗` control.
4. Actual: primary button disabled; dropdown shows no editors; guidance: *"No supported editor found. Use File Explorer or Command Prompt, or install Cursor."* — despite Cursor/VS Code being installed.
5. Expected: Cursor / VS Code detected and clickable.

## Root Cause

Editor detection on Windows is a **PATH-only scan with no fallback probing** — while macOS gets an explicit app-bundle fallback and Linux gets hardcoded extra dirs.

`frontend/src/main/editor-handoff.ts`:

- `commandSearchDirs()` (lines 92–96): for `win32` it returns **only** `env.PATH` split entries. Compare: darwin appends `/opt/homebrew/bin` etc., linux appends `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin`. There is no Windows equivalent.
- `resolveEditor()` (lines 112–128): after the PATH scan misses, the `.app` bundle fallback (lines 122–127) is gated behind `if (deps.platform !== "darwin") return undefined;` — so on Windows detection ends at "not installed."
- `EDITOR_CANDIDATES` (lines 27–47): each candidate has exactly one `commands[]` entry (`cursor`, `code`, `windsurf`, …). The standard Windows install locations are never probed:
  - VS Code / VS Code Insiders / Cursor / Windsurf user installs: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\{Microsoft VS Code,Cursor,Windsurf}\bin\{code,cursor,windsurf}.cmd` (also `{version}\bin` layout for VS Code)
  - System installs: `%ProgramFiles%\...\bin`
  - JetBrains Toolbox: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\JetBrains\Toolbox\scripts\` (`idea.cmd`, `webstorm.cmd`, …)
  - Windows `App Paths` registry (`HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\App Paths\code.exe`) — the OS-blessed lookup that `ShellExecute`/`start` use
- On Windows the CLIs are `.cmd` shims, not `.exe` — `executableNames()` (lines 86–90) does handle PATHEXT expansion for names *within a search dir*, so this is not the failure; the failure is that the *dirs themselves* are PATH-only.
- Additionally, `createEditorHandoff()` (lines 163–165) resolves the editor list **once at module construction** (wired at `frontend/src/main.ts:699`). If PATH/environment differs at launch (e.g. app auto-started, or user installs an editor later and doesn't restart AO), the list is stale for the entire app lifetime.

Renderer behavior when detection finds nothing — `frontend/src/renderer/components/TopbarOpenEditorButton.tsx`:

- Line 88: `const mainDisabled = busy || !workspaceAvailable || !preferred;` — with `editors.length === 0`, `preferred` is `undefined` → primary button permanently disabled.
- Lines 96–99: shows `editor.noEditorGuidance` → *"No supported editor found. Use File Explorer or Command Prompt, or install Cursor."* — misleading on a machine where Cursor **is** installed.
- Note `DEFAULT_EDITOR_ID = "cursor"` (`frontend/src/main/editor-settings.ts:6`), so the default preference is also among the "not found" set.

Not the cause (verified): the launch path handles Windows shims correctly — `frontend/src/main/launch-command.ts` `spawnSpec()` wraps `.cmd`/`.bat` via `cmd.exe /d /s /c` with `windowsVerbatimArguments`. The gap is purely **detection/resolution**, and secondarily the misleading guidance.

This mirrors the class of issue the feature's own spec called out (#3118 acceptance criteria: *"Failures are visible (not silent); works when app launched from Dock"* — the Windows analog, "works when app launched without the editor's shims on PATH," is unmet).

## Fix Direction

1. Add Windows fallback search roots in `commandSearchDirs()` / `resolveEditor()`:
   - `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\*` per-candidate `bin` dirs (match on `{code,cursor,windsurf,...}.cmd`), `{Version}\bin` for VS Code family
   - `%ProgramFiles%`, `%ProgramFiles(x86)%` install roots
   - `%LOCALAPPDATA%\JetBrains\Toolbox\scripts`
   - Optionally `App Paths` registry lookup via `reg query` (keeps it dependency-free)
2. Keep PATH-first ordering so an explicit PATH install wins over a probed one.
3. Re-resolve editor targets per `getState()` call (or cache with TTL) instead of freezing at app start, so a mid-session install or environment change is picked up.
4. If zero editors are detected on win32 after probing, keep the File Explorer/Terminal fallbacks but improve guidance (e.g. "Open {worktree} in File Explorer" is already there; the "install Cursor" line should not be the only hint when the editor may merely be off-PATH).
5. Add `win32` coverage to `frontend/src/main/editor-handoff.test.ts` (currently zero win32 cases) covering: shim in PATH, shim only in `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, PATHEXT expansion, and none-found.

## Impact

- All Windows users whose editor CLI shims are not on the GUI process's PATH (default User Installer path for VS Code; common for Cursor when "Add to PATH" was skipped) cannot use the `IDE ↗` feature at all — the feature is effectively macOS/Linux-only for them.
- The error guidance blames a missing install, sending users to reinstall editors that are already present.

## Open questions (from the reporter's machine)

- Exact AO version and whether the dropdown shows *some* editors or none (distinguishes "PATH miss for all" vs "partial detection").
- Whether Cursor/VS Code were installed per-user (`%LOCALAPPDATA%`) or system-wide.
- Terminal/File Explorer targets (which don't depend on PATH for file-manager, and use `ComSpec` for terminal) presumably still work — worth confirming the report is editor-specific.

## Related

- #3118 — feature spec: "Open session worktree in external IDE (`IDE ↗` + target menu)"
- #4571 — cloud-session gating for the same control (d2a134db7)
- #4607 — Neovim target request (same surface)

title: feat(cloud): real-time terminal — duplex stream + predictive local echo (#4763)
body:
Closes #4763.

## What

Two of the three workstreams from #4763, both flag-gated and measured end to end:

1. **Duplex terminal stream** (`AO_CLOUD_TERMINAL_STREAM`, default off = byte-identical current behavior). Workers hold one WebSocket per open terminal to the control plane (`GET /worker/terminals/{id}/stream`). Keystrokes still land in the durable queue, but the insert now fires a Postgres `NOTIFY` that the stream-holding replica claims-and-pushes down the socket immediately — lease semantics make the worker's transport poll a safe fallback, never a double delivery. Output frames are persisted first (`AppendTerminalOutput` rows stay the replay source of truth), and the commit fires a `NOTIFY` that wakes the client WS writer instead of its 50ms poll. All cross-replica coordination rides Postgres — nothing assumes the client and worker landed on the same CP task.
2. **Predictive local echo** in the renderer: a pure `TerminalLocalEchoController` wrapped around the cloud terminal mux — printable keys/backspace render instantly, reconciled against the authoritative echo (longest-prefix strip; mismatch or 2s timeout → exact-column rollback + cooldown), auto-disabled on the alternate buffer (agent TUIs) and for local sessions.

Workstream 3 (direct-to-sandbox via NodeOps ingress) stays a design in #4763 — only worth building if these two leave a perceptible gap.

## Measured

| Environment | Polled (today) | Duplex stream |
|---|---|---|
| Local Docker stack (network ≈ 0; pure machinery) | 99ms median | **9ms median** (30 samples, 4–13ms) |
| Live: India client → dev env (2 CP replicas) → NodeOps sandbox | 299ms median | **248ms median** (30 samples, 244–262ms) |

Live-run integrity: 31/31 pushed keystrokes' queue rows `succeeded` with **15.1ms avg completion** (vs ~86ms polled); zero CP errors; cross-replica NOTIFY exercised for real (two dev CP tasks). Local-run integrity: output sequences contiguous (no gaps/dupes), zero input rows left to the poll, flag-off coexistence in the same DB unchanged at 99ms. Remaining live overhead above the ~180ms network RTT ≈ 45–65ms: CP↔sandbox hop (~25ms) + 4 RDS transaction commits in the hot path (~20ms) + bridging — batching/relaxing those commits is the next optimization if wanted. With local echo on top, perceived typing latency is ~0 regardless of distance.

## Testing

- Go: 5 new unit tests (input push→PTY, output prefer/fallback, permanent-rejection stop, registry replace/subscribe, input drain complete/fail) — module green under `-race`, vet clean.
- Renderer: 22 controller tests + 3 integration tests through `useTerminalSession` (predict+strip, alt-buffer gate, local sessions untouched); 210/210 terminal-suite; typecheck clean.
- Smoke: `test-cloud-local.sh` honors the flag and asserts push-completed input rows and no stream errors.
- Reproduction tooling included: `cloud/cmd/terminal-echo-probe` (env-driven, supports ALB host-override dialing).

## Notes for review

- `Close` vs `CloseNow`: coder/websocket's `Close` runs a 5s close handshake; abandoned worker sockets use `CloseNow`.
- Pushed input adopts the SSH contract: a keystroke in flight when the worker dies is lost from the PTY (the row is completed) — identical to what SSH does, and the queue path remains for everything else.
- The deploy-script changes (env knobs + dev deploy wrapper) duplicate PR #4750's hunks; identical content merges cleanly whichever lands first. The CVE allowlist addition mirrors the staging integration branch.
- Renderer local echo currently activates for cloud agent panes only (the only cloud terminals the renderer dials today); agent TUIs on the alternate buffer self-disable, so its visible payoff arrives with cloud workspace-shell tabs — the wiring seam is ready.


---

## Follow-up: latency optimizations (added in this PR)

**Near-term (done here):**
- **1. Async DB write — same-replica fast path.** When the CP task serving a client's terminal WS also holds the worker's terminal stream, keystrokes are handed to it in memory (`terminalStreams.pushInput`), skipping the durable queue's insert + NOTIFY + claim round trip — **~15-20ms of intra-region Postgres latency off the hot path** for co-located terminals (~1/N of traffic with N replicas). Falls back to the durable queue when the worker stream is elsewhere/absent/buffer-full, so delivery is never dropped; adopts the existing push path's SSH contract. Unit-tested.
- **2. Connection affinity — code foundation.** `terminalRoutingKey(sessionID)` gives each session a stable consistent-hash shard (exposed as `routingKey` on the terminal-ticket response) so an affinity-aware entry can co-locate the client socket and worker stream on one replica, making the fast path the norm rather than a ~1/N coincidence. **Inert until the entry routing is wired** — an ALB cannot co-locate two independent connections by a shared key, so activation needs a consistent-hash proxy in front or ECS Service Connect / Cloud Map forwarding + a load test to tune. That infra step is deferred.

**Deferred pointers (design captured, not built):**
- **Scale hardening** (do when concurrent *active* terminals reach the hundreds): replace the Postgres `NOTIFY` message-bus with Redis/NATS pub/sub keyed per terminal (NOTIFY's global lock + every-replica fan-out is the ceiling); batch/async the durable output-row writes so Postgres is the record, not the bus; sequence-stamped reconnect/resume on stream flap; backpressure tuning on per-terminal buffers.
- **Workstream 3 — direct-to-sandbox** (the ~25ms true-SSH path via NodeOps per-port ingress): needs ingress enabled on sandboxes, worker-side ticket validation, CSP `connect-src` for `*.app.sb.createos.sh`, and a TLS-terminates-at-provider-edge threat review. Most attractive at scale.
- **Multi-region** to attack the *geographic* RTT floor (India ≈ 170ms): Fly.io Mumbai driver / NodeOps self-host / EC2 ap-south-1, with a CP presence near the sandboxes.
- **Renderer local echo**: extend to cloud workspace-shell tabs (agent-pane only today; seam ready); line-wrap prediction edge case.

**Testing note:** the two items above are covered by build + vet + race unit tests (fast-path deliver/fallback matrix, routing-key stability). **Not E2E-tested** — NodeOps has no credits left; the async fast path's real-world win and the affinity routing both need a live multi-replica load test before enabling in production.

title: Cloud session trash action calls local daemon and cannot delete the sandbox
body:
## Bug
Deleting a session from a cloud project in the Electron UI does not delete or terminate the cloud session. The route remains usable and the Coder workspace continues running.

**Source:** live product test in the AO desktop app  
**Reported by:** Prateek  
**Analyzed against:** `0ceec2416eb97323a953d8d1e9a42b999a2de5ac` ([PR #4624](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4624))  
**Priority:** high — cloud sandbox cleanup is unavailable from the product UI and running workspaces continue incurring cost  
**Confidence:** high

## Reproduction
1. Run the Electron app against an AO cloud control plane.
2. Create and open a cloud session backed by Coder.
3. Press the session trash button and confirm termination.
4. Observe that the control-plane session remains active and its workspace remains running.

## Root Cause
`frontend/src/renderer/hooks/useTerminateSession.ts` unconditionally invokes the local daemon route `POST /api/v1/sessions/{sessionId}/kill`. Cloud sessions are marked by `WorkspaceSession.cloud` and must instead invoke the cloud control-plane client’s `DELETE /orgs/{orgId}/sessions/{sessionId}` endpoint.

The UI’s shared trash surfaces all use this hook, so the cloud session is optimistically navigated away from without ever receiving a control-plane deletion request.

## Fix
Branch by session authority in `useTerminateSession`:

- Local session: retain the current local-daemon kill request.
- Cloud session: create the renderer cloud client from the configured control-plane URL and call `deleteSession(session.cloud.orgId, session.id)`.
- Invalidate both local workspace and cloud-session query keys on success.
- Add regression tests proving cloud and local sessions route to their respective authorities.

## Impact
- Cloud sessions cannot be deleted from the desktop app.
- Coder/NodeOps workspaces may continue consuming resources after the user believes they deleted them.
- The same shared termination hook affects topbar, sidebar, and board trash actions.

title: fix(chat): refresh ACP history during TUI-to-Chat transition
body:
Fixes #4681

## Problem

ACP-backed sessions could fail immediately when switching from TUI to Chat if the first native-history replay had not yet reached the transition checkpoint. ACP exposed only a history reader, so the controller treated the snapshot as non-refreshable and returned `TARGET_HISTORY_UNSETTLED`.

## Root cause

During TUI-to-Chat transition, the session manager stops the source TUI, commits the target controller epoch, and asks Chat to resume the same provider conversation with native history required. ACP's `Resume` opens the target connection and performs one `session/load`; the adapter captured that replay into an immutable slice. If Claude Code's durable transcript had not yet exposed AO's latest completed-turn checkpoint, `controller.readNativeHistory` correctly rejected the stale prefix. Because ACP did not implement `ChatHistoryRefresher`, the capability-based retry path from #4123 failed immediately instead of making another provider observation.

ACP `session/load` is repeatable for the same session ID: it resolves the existing session and replays that session's durable history again. The live adapter retains the connection and full load request needed to repeat that observation safely. The checkpoint remains proven only by the existing completed-turn/high-water matching in the Chat controller.

This differs from:

- #4120, which corrected which AO turn states may anchor the replay high-water mark;
- #4123, which introduced capability-based refresh and intentionally fast-failed ACP while its snapshot was considered immutable;
- #4424, which concerns unscoped checkpoint provenance/recovery and is unchanged here.

## Fix

Return a small `refreshableConversation` wrapper only for ACP agents that advertise `session/load`. It stores the exact initial load request and serializes repeated loads on the already-resumed ACP connection. `RefreshHistory` issues a new `session/load`, captures the new provider replay, and then exposes that snapshot to the existing controller checkpoint logic.

This is not polling the cached `historyEvents` slice: every refresh crosses the ACP protocol and causes another provider transcript observation. Resume-only ACP agents remain non-refreshable.

## Safety

- preserves history-completeness and checkpoint checks unchanged
- keeps the source TUI session intact through the existing rollback path on failure
- reloads the existing provider session; it does not create a replacement conversation
- regenerates stable provider event IDs, so identical replay prefixes remain idempotent and the existing projector deduplication remains effective
- uses the existing bounded controller retry/timeout and propagates context cancellation
- creates no target Chat controller until native history is accepted
- adds no harness-name conditional to service code and changes no Codex behavior

## Tests

Passed:

- regression-first proof: `go test ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/acp -run TestACPDriverRefreshesHistoryWithAnotherSessionLoad -count=1` failed before implementation because ACP did not advertise refreshable history
- `go test ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/acp/... -count=1`
- `go test ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/acp/... ./internal/service/chat/... ./internal/session_manager/... -count=1` (ACP and Chat packages passed; session-manager Windows baseline failures noted below)
- `go test ./internal/session_manager -run InterfaceTransition -count=1`
- `go test -race ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/acp/... ./internal/service/chat/... -count=1`
- `go test -race ./internal/session_manager -run InterfaceTransition -count=1`
- `go vet ./...`
- pinned golangci-lint against the diff: `... golangci-lint@v2.12.2 run --path-mode=abs --new-from-rev=origin/main --timeout=10m` — 0 issues

The final test-only assertion proving a third identical replay performs another wire `session/load` passed in the normal ACP suite. A post-assertion race rerun could not start after Windows cleaned the temporary checksum-verified Go/MinGW toolchain; the race suite above passed with the same production implementation.

Repository-wide Windows limitations:

- `npm run lint` and its `go test ./...` step encounter existing POSIX-path, shell/tmux, symlink-privilege, `/tmp`, and environment-sensitive test failures on Windows.
- The representative session-manager failures were reproduced in a clean `origin/main` worktree at `9aadfc8ae` with the same results.
- Running pinned golangci-lint globally on Windows reported 1,033 baseline findings (1,022 repository-wide goimports reports plus existing Windows errcheck/gosec findings) and timed out; diff-only lint reports 0 issues.

No live Claude Code/ACP provider validation was performed; coverage is deterministic fake-provider replay plus code-path verification.

## Intentional omissions

- No change to #4424's unscoped-checkpoint behavior.
- No controller timeout, replay-completeness, error-mapping, migration, frontend, or Codex app-server change.
- No retry by rereading an immutable cached snapshot and no arbitrary sleep.

[Bug]: codexappserver conformance test fails when the installed Codex is older than the pinned ProviderVersion
body:
### Summary

`go test ./...` fails on a clean checkout when the Codex installed locally is older than the version the checked in protocol file was generated from. Nothing in AO is actually broken. The test cannot tell the difference between "someone added a method that does not exist" and "this developer has an older Codex build".

`TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider` compares the generated method table in `codexproto/protocol.gen.go` against the schema that the `codex` binary on PATH emits. It treats the two directions differently:

| Direction | Handling | Line |
|---|---|---|
| Installed provider has methods the generated file lacks | `t.Logf`, test passes | `conformance_test.go:202` |
| Generated file has methods the installed provider lacks | `t.Errorf`, test fails | `conformance_test.go:209` |

Failing on the second case is correct when the generated file has genuinely drifted, because calling a method the provider does not have breaks at runtime. But the same condition is also true when the generated file is fine and the developer simply has an older Codex, which is not a defect.

The test is already tolerant of an unusable environment. It skips when `codex` is not installed (`conformance_test.go:169-171`) and when the provider refuses to emit a schema (`conformance_test.go:176-177`). Being strict only in the "installed Codex is older" case looks like something that was missed rather than a decision.

`protocol.gen.go` pins `ProviderVersion = "codex-cli 0.146.0"` and has been regenerated once, in [PR #3472](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/3472). Codex keeps releasing, so the distance between the pinned version and whatever a contributor has installed grows over time.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install a Codex CLI older than the pinned `ProviderVersion`. I have `codex-cli 0.142.5` and the file pins `codex-cli 0.146.0`.
2. Clone the repo and check out current `main`.
3. From `backend/`, run the documented local gate:
   ```
   go test ./...
   ```
4. Or run just the one test:
   ```
   go test ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver/ -run TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider
   ```

### Expected behavior

A contributor whose Codex is simply an older build should not get a red suite. The test should separate the two causes. One way is to compare the installed provider version against `codexproto.ProviderVersion` and skip or log when the installed build is older, the same way the test already skips when Codex is absent, while still failing when the versions line up and the generated file has actually drifted.

### Actual behavior

The test fails at `conformance_test.go:209`:

```
--- FAIL: TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider (0.84s)
    conformance_test.go:209: generated protocol declares 5 method(s) the installed
    provider does not: [externalAgentConfig/import/recordHistory
    thread/environment/connected thread/environment/disconnected
    app/installed app/read]
FAIL
FAIL	github.com/aoagents/agent-orchestrator/backend/internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver	0.843s
```

![conformance test failing against codex-cli 0.142.5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mukulkatewa/agent-orchestrator/issue-assets-codex-conformance-older-provider/.issue-assets/codex-conformance-older-provider/conformance-fail.png)

`go test ./...` is what `docs/development.md` and `docs/STATUS.md` present as the local gate, and `npm run lint` runs `go test ./...` as well. So a new contributor running the documented command for the first time sees a failure that has nothing to do with their changes.

### AO version

`0.10.3`, commit `92990fd3`, current `main` at time of filing.

### Environment

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS x86_64, kernel 6.14.0-37, Go 1.26.5, `codex-cli 0.142.5`

### Logs / extra context

```shell
$ codex --version
codex-cli 0.142.5

$ grep "ProviderVersion =" internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver/codexproto/protocol.gen.go
const ProviderVersion = "codex-cli 0.146.0"

$ go test ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver/ -run TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider
--- FAIL: TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider (0.84s)
    conformance_test.go:209: generated protocol declares 5 method(s) the installed provider does not: [externalAgentConfig/import/recordHistory thread/environment/connected thread/environment/disconnected app/installed app/read]
FAIL
FAIL	github.com/aoagents/agent-orchestrator/backend/internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver	0.843s
FAIL
```

The method names print in a different order on each run because Go iterates a map. The set itself is stable.

title: test(codexappserver): tolerate a provider older than the generated protocol
body:
## What

Makes `TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider` version aware. When the installed Codex is older than the build `protocol.gen.go` was generated from, the missing methods are reported with `t.Logf` instead of failing the test. When the installed build is not older, the existing `t.Errorf` is unchanged.

Fixes #4773.

## Why

`go test ./...` fails on a clean checkout for anyone whose Codex predates the pinned `ProviderVersion`, and nothing in the checkout is wrong.

The test compares the generated method table against the schema the installed `codex` emits, then splits the result two ways. A provider that declares methods the generated file lacks is only logged, because AO does not have to use everything. A generated file that declares methods the provider lacks is failed, because calling one of those breaks at runtime.

That second rule is right when the generated file has drifted. The problem is that an older provider produces exactly the same condition without anything having drifted: every method a later Codex added is a method the older build does not declare. The test could not tell the two apart, so it reported a version gap as a defect.

The test is already deliberate about not failing on an environment it cannot use. It skips when `codex` is absent and when the provider refuses to emit a schema. Failing only in the "your Codex is older" case was the gap.

This is not a rare state. `protocol.gen.go` pins `codex-cli 0.146.0` and has been regenerated once, in #3472, while Codex keeps releasing. My machine has `codex-cli 0.142.5` and reports five methods. `go test ./...` is what `docs/development.md` and `docs/STATUS.md` present as the local gate, and `npm run lint` runs it too, so this is the first command a new contributor runs.

## How

Test-only change. No production code is touched.

The comparison already exists in this package, so nothing new was introduced: `parseCodexVersion` and `codexVersion.less` in `driver.go` do the work. The new `providerOlderThanGenerated` helper only joins them and decides the one question the test needs answered.

Unparseable output on either side returns false and keeps the strict comparison. A version that cannot be read is not evidence that the gap is benign, so the safe direction is to keep failing rather than to quietly pass.

The version is read with `exec.Command(bin, "--version")` to match how this file already invokes the provider, rather than `installedCodexVersion`, which carries the driver's process environment that a schema comparison does not need.

The two `len(extra) > 0` arms are a `switch` rather than a nested `if` so the strict path stays visible at the same level as the tolerant one.

## Testing

```
go test ./internal/adapters/chatdriver/codexappserver/ -run TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider -v
```

Before this change, on `codex-cli 0.142.5`:

```
--- FAIL: TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider (0.84s)
    conformance_test.go:209: generated protocol declares 5 method(s) the installed provider does not: [...]
FAIL
```

After:

```
=== RUN   TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider
    conformance_test.go:220: installed provider (codex-cli 0.142.5) predates the generated "codex-cli 0.146.0", so it does not declare 5 method(s) this file has; update codex or regenerate to compare them: [...]
--- PASS: TestGeneratedProtocolMatchesTheInstalledProvider (0.91s)
```

`TestProviderOlderThanGenerated` covers the decision directly: older, equal, newer, and unreadable version output on either side.

I could not verify the strict path against a real Codex at or above `0.146.0`, since the only build available to me is older. The equal and newer cases are covered by the table test, and that path is unchanged from the current behavior.

Also run: `gofmt -l` clean, `go vet` clean, full `go test ./...`.

## Checklist

- [x] Branched from `main` (or continuing an existing PR branch)
- [x] One focused change; links the related issue when applicable
- [x] Follows [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/blob/main/AGENTS.md) conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added/updated for user-visible behavior where it makes sense
- [x] Relevant CI checks pass for the area touched (`go`, frontend, etc.)

title: [Bug]: Reboot leaves TUI sessions as live zombies until legacy tmux socket exists
body:
### Summary

After a hard Linux host reboot while TUI sessions are live, AO can keep those sessions as isTerminated=false / idle|working even though the tmux runtimes and Qwen processes no longer exist. _Tasks are undeleteable "Stuck in Limbo" and the Orchestrator gets no fresh Session / is unusable_

AO's normal reconciliation remains stuck while the legacy/default tmux socket is absent. Creating an otherwise-empty default tmux server immediately lets AO's own reaper recognize the stale sessions as dead, move them to Archive, and makes `ao session restore <id>` usable again. 

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start AO on Linux with multiple live TUI sessions (reproduced with Qwen workers and an orchestrator).

2. Reboot the host while those sessions are still live, so AO does not get a graceful shutdown.

3. Start AO again.

4. Observe that affected sessions are still reported as non-terminated, for example:

   ao session get <session-id> --json

   returns states such as:

   activity.state = idle
   isTerminated = false

   even though no corresponding tmux runtime or agent process exists.

5. Confirm the runtimes are actually gone:

   pgrep -af tmux
   tmux ls

   The default tmux socket reports that it does not exist / cannot be connected to.

6. Try to close the stale session from the desktop UI or with:

   ao session kill <session-id>

   This returns:

   Internal server error (INTERNAL_ERROR)

   and the session remains non-terminated.

7. Without modifying AO's database, create a harmless session on the legacy/default tmux server:

   tmux new-session -d -s ao-recovery-probe 'exec sleep 3600'

8. Wait for AO's normal reconciliation/reaper (about 20 seconds in my reproduction).

9. Re-check the stale AO sessions. AO now marks the missing-runtime sessions terminated and they appear in Archive.

10. Restore one normally:

    ao session restore <session-id>

    The runtime is recreated successfully. With Qwen, the persisted native Qwen session identity was used and the original Qwen conversation resumed.

11. Remove the temporary probe:

    tmux kill-session -t ao-recovery-probe

### Expected behavior

After a real host reboot where the recorded TUI runtime no longer exists, AO should reconcile the durable session with runtime reality without requiring a dummy tmux server or database modification.

If both AO's private tmux server and the legacy/default tmux server are absent, that should be treated as a definitively unavailable runtime for this reconciliation case, not leave the session indefinitely live-looking.

The stale session should become recoverably terminated/archived so `ao session restore <id>` can recreate the runtime and use provider-native resume where available.

`ao session kill <id>` should also be idempotent when the runtime is already gone rather than returning INTERNAL_ERROR.

### Actual behavior

After the reboot, AO preserves the durable session row as non-terminated even though the tmux runtime and Qwen process are gone.

The desktop shows a disconnected/re-attaching terminal, while `ao session get` may still report idle or working. **Tasks are "stuck" in Limbo and the orchestrator can not be used.**

`ao session kill <id>` returns INTERNAL_ERROR and makes no durable state change.

The important additional observation is that simply starting an empty tmux server on the legacy/default socket fixes reconciliation:

tmux new-session -d -s ao-recovery-probe 'exec sleep 3600'

Once the default socket exists and can answer AO's probe, AO's own reaper marks the stale sessions terminated without any SQLite edit. They move to Archive and `ao session restore <id>` works normally.

This strongly suggests that "legacy/default socket absent" is being treated as an inconclusive runtime probe, while "legacy/default server exists but session is missing" is correctly treated as definitive absence.

This appears closely related to #4481 / PR #4482, but the observed failure is also in automatic post-reboot reconciliation, not only the explicit Kill path.

### AO version

0.12.10

### Environment

Ubuntu 26.04 amd64

### Logs / extra context

```shell

```

### Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues for duplicates
- [x] I removed secrets / tokens from logs and screenshots

title: fix(cloud): clear stale signed-in UI after terminal token refresh failure

## Problem

When a stored WorkOS access token expires and refreshing it fails terminally (for example, the rotating refresh token was already consumed), the main process deletes `cloud-auth.bin` but does not broadcast the signed-out state. Renderer hooks can therefore retain the old account and React Query cache: the sidebar still shows cloud projects/sessions, while control-plane calls return 401 and opening the cached orchestrator renders “Session not found.”

Terminal refresh failure immediately publishes a null cloud session to all renderer windows. The stale cloud rows disappear and the existing “Sign in to AO Cloud” entry point is shown.

## Reproduction

Observed in the isolated Coder desktop preview: `cloud.getSession()` returned null and CP requests returned `401 no_token`, while the sidebar still showed the previous account, project, and orchestrator session.

title: feat(browser): support action postconditions
body:
Fixes #4708

## Problem

`ao browser act` previously proved only that AO matched an element and dispatched provider input. It could not tell callers whether the application produced an observable effect, and retrying after dispatch could duplicate a consequential action.

The first implementation added postconditions, but three correctness gaps remained:

- URL/text waits could report `satisfied` when the expected value was already present before dispatch.
- DOM/dialog observations polled a process-backed runtime every 25 ms and did not bound each native call to the remaining deadline.
- guarded navigation was covered only by invoking a mocked Electron listener, not by a real page executing `beforeunload`.

## Runtime trace and compatibility

The existing path remains intact: CLI flags -> browser HTTP command -> broker -> Electron browser host -> agent-browser runtime. `act` still snapshots and matches through the existing provider adapter, performs the existing stale-reference retry only before dispatch, dispatches input once, and then observes a postcondition. No daemon logic moved into the renderer and no provider/harness special case was added.

The merge with current `main` preserves the new browser-history store: main-frame navigations update both action-correlation generations and top-level history, while iframe history changes update neither.

## Fix

- capture URL/text satisfaction before dispatch and return `already-satisfied` when no correlated page effect makes the condition attributable to the action
- preserve separate `matched`, `inputDispatched`, `navigation`, and `postcondition` facts
- poll unavoidable DOM/dialog observations at 200 ms and give every process-backed observation only the remaining deadline
- propagate genuine provider failures; map only the pinned native wait-timeout message to an unmet timeout
- use a dialog result returned by the action as immediate evidence instead of polling
- prefer a committed navigation over an earlier blocked attempt, recognize an activated popup as navigation, and ignore iframe-only history changes
- reject invalid direct API timeouts instead of silently clamping them
- add a local HTTP fixture with a real `beforeunload` handler and dispatch real Chromium mouse input through the DevTools input domain
- run that fixture in frontend CI under Electron/Xvfb with bounded process-tree cleanup

## Safety

- no action is redispatched because a postcondition is unmet, cancelled, or unknown
- pre-existing URL/text state is never credited to the action
- each observation is bounded and cancellation-aware; a provider that ignores cancellation cannot extend the API deadline or create an unhandled rejection
- no application state or history check is weakened
- no new provider conversation/session is created
- existing behavior is unchanged when no postcondition is requested
- Chromium's native `beforeunload` behavior is observed, not overridden

This follows the same broad synchronization principle used by Playwright/Puppeteer: arm observation around the action and require browser evidence, rather than treating dispatch completion as application success. Electron's documented `will-prevent-unload` event remains the source of guarded-navigation cancellation evidence.

## Tests

Passed on the final merged head unless noted:

- `cd frontend && node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/main/browser-view-host.test.ts --pool=forks --maxWorkers=1` — 141 passed
- `cd frontend && node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/main/agent-browser-runtime.test.ts --pool=forks --maxWorkers=1` — 22 passed, 2 existing skips
- `cd frontend && npm run test:browser-postcondition-integration` — passed repeatedly on Windows, including after merging current `main`
- `cd backend && go test ./internal/cli -run TestBrowser` — passed
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed
- full TypeScript `tsc --noEmit` passed after the production changes; the final integration-only edits also bundled successfully with Vite and executed in Electron

title: fix(tmux): treat absent tmux server as definitive session death (#4776)
body:
Fixes #4776

## Problem

After a host reboot with live TUI sessions, AO kept those sessions as
isTerminated=false / idle|working even though the tmux server (private or
legacy/default) and the agent processes no longer existed. Tasks were stuck in
Limbo and ao session kill returned INTERNAL_ERROR. Reconciliation only worked
after creating a dummy tmux server on the legacy/default socket
(tmux new-session -d -s ao-recovery-probe 'exec sleep 3600'), which flipped the
probe from inconclusive to a definitive can't find session.

## Root cause

socketForSession already inspects both the session's private socket and the
legacy default socket for a migration candidate, and its comment says:

> Both known sockets definitively lack the session. Return the private target
> so IsAlive's ordinary exact-session handling reports false.

But IsAlive mapped 
o server running to ports.ErrRuntimeUnavailable (an
inconclusive probe). The reaper therefore reported ProbeFailed forever, the LCM
never terminates on failed probes, and the session stayed live-looking with
nothing to make it die.

## Fix

In IsAlive, treat 
o server running as definitive server absence and return
(false, nil) — a session cannot be alive without the server that owns its pane.
This matches the intent already documented in socketForSession.

Safety against a board-wide misread of a server outage (#3475) is preserved:
- transient failures (error connecting, protocol mismatch, server exited
  unexpectedly) still wrap ports.ErrRuntimeProbeInconclusive and are never
  per-session death;
- for a migration candidate, socketForSession has already inspected BOTH the
  private and the legacy default socket before IsAlive sees this output, so the
  evidence is definitive;
- the reaper's mass-death circuit breaker (#3491) remains in place.

## Testing

- TestIsAliveReportsNoServerAsDefinitivelyDead replaces
  TestIsAliveReportsNoServerAsRuntimeUnavailable with the new expectation.
- go test ./internal/observe/reaper/ ./internal/lifecycle/ passes.
- With this change, post-reboot stale sessions are reconciled by AO's own
  reaper within one tick, appear in Archive, and ao session restore <id>
  recreates the runtime with provider-native resume — no dummy tmux server or
  database edit required.

bug(review): CC ≥ 2.1.257 read-block permission prompts hang the headless claude-code reviewer — verdict never recorded; Write-tool ban blocks the payload-file workaround
body:
## Bug

Starting with **Claude Code v2.1.257** (2026-09-01), the headless `claude-code` reviewer hangs forever on a permission prompt when it tries to record its review verdict — and it cannot use the documented workaround (write the payload to a file, submit via stdin redirect), because the `Write` tool is blanket-disallowed in the reviewer launch policy.

Claude Code 2.1.257 introduced `permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`: any Bash command the built-in shell analyzer cannot statically verify (code on stdin, heredocs, nested `$(...)`, operand strings that resemble brace/subscript expansion) forces a permission prompt. Explicit allow rules do **not** bypass it — rule matching requires a clean static parse, so flagged commands prompt before allow rules are ever consulted. Verified live: `Bash(printf:*)` and `Bash(ao review submit:*)` were both in the reviewer's `--allowedTools`, and `Bash(cat:*)` in the user's global allow — all three still prompted.

The claude-code reviewer is launched headless (no human attached to the pane) with `--permission-mode auto` + a read-only allowlist + `--disallowedTools Edit,Write,NotebookEdit,Bash(git push:*),Bash(git commit:*)` — `backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/claudecode/claudecode.go:47-69, 90-92`. Its code comment assumes *"allow rules auto-approve without prompting … without stalling"* — that assumption broke with 2.1.257.

Observed prompts (live, 2026-09-03, Claude Code 2.1.258, AO `dev`):

1. `printf '%s' "$payload" | ao review submit --session X --reviews -` →
   *"printf operand '…' contains array subscript with expansion — zsh arith-evals %d/%i operands (may run $(cmd))"* — the payload is a plain review-body string (Cyrillic prose, no actual expansions).
2. `cat > /tmp/review.json <<'EOF' … EOF` + submit →
   *"Contains brace with quote character (expansion obfuscation)"* — quoted-delimiter heredoc with a static JSON literal.
3. Environment-inspection compounds: `bash scripts/check.sh`, `pip3 show pkg | sed …; cat "$(pip3 show pkg …)" || python3 -c "…"` → un-analyzable → prompt.

Nobody answers in a headless session: it parks at `waiting: permission prompt` (visible in agent view) and the verdict is never recorded — `ao review submit` never runs.

**Source:** chat, reported by @axisrow | **Analyzed against:** `c4b37af9d` | **Confidence:** High (exact code path traced; reproduced live across several review cycles)

## Reproduction

1. Claude Code ≥ 2.1.257 with `permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories: true` (reporter's user settings).
2. Run an AO review cycle with the claude-code harness on any PR.
3. Reviewer posts the GitHub review, then tries to record bookkeeping via `ao review submit` (printf-pipe or /tmp heredoc) → permission prompt fires → session parks at `waiting: permission prompt`; `ao review submit` is never executed.

## Root Cause

Two AO-side facts combine with the new upstream analyzer:

- `reviewerAllowedTools` / `reviewerDisallowedTools` (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/claudecode/claudecode.go:47-69`) were designed pre-analyzer: allow rules were expected to auto-approve `printf |` pipes *"without stalling"*.
- The reviewer has **no file-write tool at all** (`Write` blanket-disallowed as defense in depth), so the statically-safe CC pattern — write the JSON to `/tmp` with the Write tool, then `ao review submit --reviews - < /tmp/file.json` (a redirect from a known path parses cleanly) — is unavailable to it.

Live verification of the fix direction: after adding `/tmp` to `permissions.additionalDirectories` (user level), the exact same heredoc-write + redirect-submit passed **without prompting** across two subsequent review cycles — the flags are path-scoped (target outside working dirs), not content-scoped.

## Fix (options, need a decision)

**Design constraints (reporter's position):** the reviewer is read-only **by design** — granting it any file-write capability (the `Write(/tmp/**)` idea) violates the contract and is rejected; the same reasoning covers merge: the reviewer must never merge, yet `reviewerAllowedTools` currently grants blanket `Bash(gh:*)`, which includes `gh pr merge`.

- **Preferred — make the GitHub review the verdict channel:** the reviewer already posts the GitHub review via `gh` (this works today), and AO lifecycle already reads PR reviews. Drop the local `ao review submit` bookkeeping step from the headless reviewer entirely — then the reviewer needs no write path at all, and the whole class of stdin-payload prompts disappears.
- **Tool-policy tightening (independent of the above):** scope `Bash(gh:*)` down to what the reviewer actually needs — `gh pr view/list`, GET-only `gh api`, `gh pr review` — and add `Bash(gh pr merge:*)` to `reviewerDisallowedTools`. An explicit merge denial also removes the hang-or-merge ambiguity under the new analyzer.
- **Fallback if local bookkeeping must stay:** submit in argv form (`ao review submit --reviews '<json>'`) instead of a stdin pipe — needs a live analyzer test first (content flags fired on printf operands regardless of path scope); or a `PermissionRequest`-hook auto-allow for statically-describable safe patterns (AO already installs that hook in every workspace).
- **Secondary (separate class, same symptom):** env-inspection compounds (`pip3 show … ; cat "$(pip3 show …)" || python3 -c "…"`) stay un-analyzable regardless of `/tmp` scope. For headless sessions consider a `dontAsk`-style deny-and-retry so they degrade into a clean denial the agent can route around, instead of an infinite hang.

Note: "Always allow" from the prompt does not help — by design, allow rules never match un-analyzable commands.

## Impact

- Every AO user on Claude Code ≥ 2.1.257 with the read-block enabled: review cycles stall; the verdict is recorded only if a human notices the parked prompt and answers it manually.
- Workaround today (user-side, payload class only): `permissions.additionalDirectories: ["/tmp", "/private/tmp"]` in user settings. Does not cover the env-inspection class.
- **Interim workaround (until this is fixed): switch the reviewer harness to `codex`** (`domain.ReviewerCodex`) — the Codex reviewer adapter is unaffected by Claude Code's analyzer/permission changes.

## Related

- [#3745](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/3745) — Hardening: enforce read-only tool access and reliable cancel-stop for all reviewer harnesses (same subsystem; this is the too-strict flip side)
- Upstream: Claude Code changelog v2.1.257 (2026-09-01) — "Added a one-time prompt in auto mode before the first file read outside the working directories, with the option to block such reads (`permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`)"; the same release fixed worktree sessions refusing heredocs as "too complex to verify" — the area is actively changing upstream, so a launch-side mechanism (B/C) is preferable to hard-coding around today's analyzer quirks.

title: feat(claude): add account management and hot switching
body:
## Summary

- Stacked on [PR #4722](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4722), reusing its account-management architecture without changing the Codex credential contract.
- Adds macOS-first Claude Code subscription account login, reauthentication, local logout, deletion, and device-global hot switching.
- Adding account B uses isolated Claude configuration and secure-storage paths, so it does not activate B or modify the current account A.
- Switching replaces the canonical Claude credential safely without forking, stopping, or restarting running Claude sessions.
- Adds durable switch phases, idempotency, active-account revision fencing, crash recovery, admission gates, SSE updates, generated API contracts, and a Claude-specific Settings UI.

## Architecture

- AO stores only redacted account metadata under `~/.ao/harnesses/claude-code`; OAuth credentials remain exclusively in macOS Keychain.
- Isolated login and verification use `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `CLAUDE_SECURESTORAGE_CONFIG_DIR`. Normal AO Claude sessions continue using native default history and session IDs.
- Hot switching stages and verifies the target, snapshots rollback state, checkpoints the source, replaces the canonical credential under Claude-compatible locks, updates only `oauthAccount`, verifies the global identity, and advances the active pointer with CAS.
- Account-owned credential fields remain isolated per account. Only the allowlisted live machine-shared MCP and plugin fields survive activation.
- The API returns immediately after commit with a 30-second propagation-uncertainty window; it does not impose an artificial wait.

## Security and recovery

- No credentials, refresh tokens, Keychain service names, credential paths, or transcripts are stored in SQLite, descriptors, API responses, logs, or telemetry.
- Keychain access pins `/usr/bin/security`, keeps secret values out of argv, rejects oversized writes, and distinguishes missing credentials from unavailable or denied access.
- Account switching is disabled when daemon-level Anthropic or Claude credential overrides are present.
- Bootstrap reconciles external native logins when safe and exposes an unmanaged state instead of guessing when identity and credential state disagree.
- Durable recovery verifies whether canonical state matches the source or target and restores the complete rollback snapshot when necessary. Unverifiable rollback enters `recovery_required` and keeps launch exclusion active.

## Verification

- Focused Claude adapter, storage, service, session manager, review, HTTP, and usage-ingestion tests pass.
- `npm run sqlc` and `npm run api` pass with no generated drift.
- Claude Settings component/state tests and `npm run frontend:typecheck` pass.
- `npm run lint` passes with zero Go lint issues.
- The Electron production package and isolated desktop/daemon/API smoke test pass.
- Usage replay tests verify no historical cost duplication and exactly one event for one appended post-switch usage record.
- Crash tests cover durable phases, credential rollback, lock exclusion, shared-field preservation, account-field isolation, and unchanged native session identity.

## Manual release gate

The two-real-subscription-account A -> B -> A propagation check is intentionally left for manual verification because it mutates the device-global Claude credential. If an already-running Claude process remains on the old account after the cache window or produces token-family errors, hot switching must not ship; follow up with the separately planned exit-and-resume path instead of adding waits.

## Explicit v1 omissions

- No Claude conversation forking, profile-bound runtime sessions, forced restart, artificial wait, session exit/resume, API-key accounts, remote OAuth revocation, capacity/reset UI, Linux/Windows switching, or account-specific cost attribution during propagation.

title: fix: keep sidebar visible on first browser open
body:
## What

Keep the left sidebar visible when the docked Browser opens for the first time in an app session by animating it to AO's existing 200px minimum width.

## Why

The Browser should gain workspace without removing session navigation. The automatic adjustment must happen only once per app session, while explicit sidebar close and resize actions remain authoritative.

Closes #4545

## How

- Raise one transient sidebar-resize request when any session switches to Browser for the first time in the renderer session.
- Let `Sidebar` consume that request and animate the current width to 200px with the shared `SHELL_PANEL_SPRING`; reduced-motion users receive the final width immediately.
- Do not persist the automatic width or modify the durable sidebar-open preference.
- Keep manual close and drag-resize authoritative, including cancelling an in-flight automatic animation when a manual resize starts.
- Preserve the simplified manual sidebar/layout contract from #4823; this change does not restore the removed automatic compact/release system.

## Testing

- Focused Vitest: 4 files, 270/270 tests passed.
- `npm run typecheck`: passed.
- `npx vite build --config vite.renderer.config.ts`: passed; 3443 modules transformed.

GitHub created new Frontend and gitleaks runs for the rebased fork head, but both are awaiting maintainer approval and have not executed jobs. Their current `action_required` conclusions are approval-gate state, not test results.
