title: fix(agentauth): open Kimi's native /login platform picker
body:
Code changes: +103 -12  
Tests: +89 -4  
Others: +0 -0

Refs #5356 (Kimi portion; grok/cursor/droid/cline/kimchi remain open)

## Summary

The Kimi harness auth plan ran `kimi login`, which is a device-code-only flow (optional `--region` flag, no other choices). Kimi's platform picker — **Kimi Code (kimi.com/code)**, **Kimi Code (kimi.ai/code)**, **Kimi Platform (API key · platform.kimi.com)**, **Kimi Platform (API key · platform.kimi.ai)** — only exists in the interactive TUI behind the `/login` slash command (verified against kimi-code 0.39.1: `src/tui/commands/auth.ts` → `promptPlatformSelection`), so AO's Harness settings login never offered it.

## Fix

- `backend/internal/service/agentauth/plans.go` — Kimi's plan becomes a `terminalInputPlan` (same pattern as pi/droid/omp/prime-agent): launch the TUI, then inject the reviewed `/login` automatically once Kimi renders its stable unauthenticated-ready message (no button click or fixed delay needed). No API/frontend changes; plans are data.
- Kimi's first-run "Trust this folder?" dialog would swallow that input in AO's private auth workspace, so the plan gains a reviewed `prepareWorkspace` hook: `kimi.EnsureWorkspaceTrusted` pre-records Kimi's workspace-trust record (the exact shape Kimi writes itself) in the Kimi home the auth terminal runs against (`$KIMI_CODE_HOME`, else `~/.kimi-code`).
- `backend/internal/service/agentauth/service.go` — plans with a prepare hook use a stable per-harness auth workspace (`<dataDir>/auth-workspace/kimi`) instead of a throwaway per-handle dir, so the seeded trust persists across login attempts. Daemon wiring passes `cfg.DataDir`.

The auth terminal deliberately still runs against the user's real Kimi home, so credentials land where the existing session-prep seeding (`seedKimiCredentials`) harvests them into AO's isolated session home — that flow is unchanged.

## Validation

- New tests: `EnsureWorkspaceTrusted` seeds the real home and honors `KIMI_CODE_HOME` (`trust_test.go`); `Start(kimi)` uses the stable workspace and writes a trust record with the right root (`service_test.go`); plan matrix row updated.
- Verified end-to-end against the installed kimi-code 0.39.1 in a PTY with a fresh HOME: with the seeded trust record the TUI opens straight to the composer (no trust dialog) and injected `/login` renders the full 4-option platform picker; `kimi login` by contrast goes straight to device-code.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet`, and `go test -race` pass for all touched packages (`agentauth`, `kimi`, `daemon`), plus `internal/httpd/...`.
- Local full-suite note: `go test ./...` on this machine shows intermittent load-sensitive failures (`TestResolveGooseBinaryUsesValidFallbackAfterPathCollision`, tmux/httpd timing tests) that reproduce identically on a clean `upstream/main` checkout and pass standalone — unrelated to this diff. Relying on CI for the authoritative full-suite + golangci-lint result.

title: feat(mobile): pull request reviews are not available on the phone
body:
### What happens

On mobile there is no way to see a pull request's reviews. `packages/mobile` has no caller of
any review route, and no screen that shows review content — so a PR that has feedback on it
gives you a single "Unresolved comments" chip (`lib/prView.ts:240`) and nothing behind it.

Reported in Discord `#dev-chat` by @illegalcall: *"On mobile 1. Links dont open in AO browser
2. Review is not available"*. The first half is #5646.

### What desktop does

The session inspector has a Reviews tab (`frontend/src/renderer/components/SessionInspector.tsx`)
with two halves:

- **Review controls** — reviewer agent picker, Auto review toggle, Run / Re-run / Stop, kill.
- **The reviews themselves** — each reviewer's verdict and summary, their inline comments at
  `file:line`, Resolve, Request another review.

### Why this is mostly a client gap, not a daemon one

The phone already fetches the data for the second half. `GET /sessions/{id}/pr` is called on the
PRs tab (`lib/api.ts` → `lib/usePRSummaries.ts`), and the daemon's response already carries
`review.reviews[]` (reviewer, verdict, body), `review.resolvedBy[]` and
`review.unresolvedBy[].links[]` with file, line and body — see `SessionPRReviewSummary` in
`backend/internal/httpd/controllers/dto.go`. The mobile client type models only `decision`,
`hasUnresolvedHumanComments` and `unresolvedBy[].count`, so all of it is discarded on arrival.
Desktop's entire "External reviews" half is built from that same response.

The controls need `GET /sessions/{id}/reviews` plus the trigger / cancel / auto-review /
comments-resolve / rerequest routes. None of those are blocked on the LAN listener
(`lanControlBlockedPrefixes` in `backend/internal/httpd/lan_listener.go` covers `/api/v1/mobile`
and other loopback-only prefixes, not `/api/v1/sessions/…`), so they are reachable from a paired
phone today.

### Expected

A pull request's reviews are readable on the phone, and AO's own reviewer can be run or stopped
from there — the same things the desktop Reviews tab offers, in a shape that suits a phone.

### Notes

- Mobile-only change: no daemon change and no wire-contract change.
- Reported by @illegalcall.

title: fix(mobile): show pull request reviews and let AO review from the phone
body:
## Summary

On mobile there was no way to read a pull request's reviews. `packages/mobile` had no review
screen and no caller of any review route, so a PR with feedback showed one "Unresolved comments"
chip and nothing behind it. Reported in Discord `#dev-chat` by @illegalcall.

This adds a Reviews screen, reached from a new row on the PR card.

Most of the data was already reaching the phone. `GET /sessions/{id}/pr` — which the PRs tab
already fetches — carries `review.reviews[]`, `review.resolvedBy[]` and
`review.unresolvedBy[].links[]` with file, line and body. The mobile client type stopped at
`count`, so all of it was discarded on arrival. Widening the type is most of the read half;
the controls come from `GET /sessions/{id}/reviews` and the trigger / cancel / auto-review /
resolve / rerequest routes, none of which are blocked on the LAN listener.

No daemon change and no wire-contract change.

## Changes

| File | |
|---|---|
| `lib/api.ts` | `PRReviewCommentLink`, `PRReviewEntry`, `PRUnresolvedReviewer.links`, `review.reviews`/`resolvedBy`; `autoReviewEnabled` off the board poll; `getSessionReviews`, `triggerReview`, `cancelReview`, `setAutoReview`, `resolveReviewComment`, `requestRereview` |
| `lib/reviewsView.ts` (new) | Pure grouping, wording and ordering |
| `lib/reviewsView.test.ts` (new) | 23 tests |
| `app/pr/[number].tsx` (new) | The screen |
| `lib/PRCard.tsx` | The row that opens it |
| `app/_layout.tsx` | `headerShown: false`, like `project/[id]` |
| `lib/RouteErrorBoundary.test.ts` | Registers the route on the screen-fallback list |

## Decisions worth a look

**One list, not desktop's Agent/External split.** That split needs `GET /sessions/{id}/reviews`
to know which GitHub review id AO's reviewer produced. AO's reviewer submits through GitHub like
anyone else, so its pass is already in `review.reviews[]` — one list keyed by reviewer loses the
label, not the content.

**The card row is gated on the same derivation the screen renders**, so it cannot offer reviews
and then open empty.

**Reviews by the PR author are dropped**, matching desktop's `externalReviewActorMatchesPRAuthor`
— GitHub records an author's replies on their own PR as reviews.

**A reviewer who left only inline comments still gets an entry**, or the "N unresolved comments"
the card promises has nothing behind it.

**Verdict and run-action wordings are desktop's** (`githubVerdict`, `reviewSessionRunAction`), so
a PR in the same state reads the same on both surfaces.

**The Auto review toggle is the native switch** via `@expo/ui`, matching `app/settings.tsx`.
Manual run is disabled while auto review is on, as on desktop — otherwise the tap fights the
daemon.

**Not included:** the reviewer-agent picker (needs the agent catalog and a 21-entry sheet; the
daemon falls back to the project default when the trigger names none) and Kill review session
(destructive, and desktop hides it unless a reviewer pane exists).

## Verification

| | |
|---|---|
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| `npx vitest run` | 1164 → **1188** |
| `npx expo export` | ios and android both succeed |
| Mutation checks | 10 mutations of `reviewsView.ts` (author filter, comment-only reviewers, sort direction, comment identity, verdict wording, zero-link reviewer, ineligible gating, run-action labels, state lookup, state tone) — each caught by a test |
| Route inventory | fails before the new route is registered, confirmed |

**On device (iPhone 17 Pro simulator, against a real daemon).** Auto review toggled from the
phone and observed on the daemon: `autoReviewEnabled` `false → true → false`. Screen verified in
light and dark: verdict badges and tones, markdown bodies, inline comments at `file:line`, open
and resolved groups, comment-only reviewer, the author's own review dropped, and the card row
counting `4 reviewers · 3 unresolved comments` from a five-reviewer payload.

**Not verified:** the review bodies and inline comments were a fixture in the daemon's documented
shape — no PR reachable from this machine had real reviews on it. `packages/mobile` has no hook
or component renderer, so the screen's own load / refresh / failure / unpaired branches were
driven by hand rather than by test. Not run on the Android emulator; the bundle builds and the
native switch is the one `app/settings.tsx` already ships on both platforms.

Closes #5656

body:
PR description:

  Code changes: +2970 -91
  Tests: +1730 -25
  Others: +1088 -3

  ## Summary

  Adds the Local file browsing and review experience to Cloud sessions across Docker, NodeOps, and Coder.

  - Browse and search all repository files.
  - View and edit workspace files.
  - Categorize committed, staged, unstaged, and untracked changes.
  - Browse changes by commit.
  - Support unified and split diffs.
  - Add line-level feedback from Cloud file views.
  - Refresh file state from Cloud workspace events.
  - Protect edits with workspace revisions and file fingerprints.
  - Select the correct Git comparison baseline, including repositories whose default branch is not `main`.

  - Prevent duplicate feedback modals.
  - Make the file viewer scrollable.
  - Prevent unrelated patches from rendering for unchanged files.
  - Fix the React maximum update-depth loop while editing.
  - Stop pre-existing committed files from appearing as new changes.
  - Route file feedback through the Cloud session API, fixing “Unknown session”.
  - Repair legacy root-commit baselines by resolving the remote default branch.

  ## Architecture

  The frontend remains a thin Cloud UI. Repository inspection, diff generation, revision reads, and writes are handled through the control-plane and worker protocol.

  The implementation is provider-neutral and uses the same worker flow for Docker, NodeOps, and Coder.

  Local workspace review behavior is unchanged.

  ## Validation

title: bug(codex): cached executable path survives install/reinstall until daemon restart
body:
## Problem

`codex.Plugin` resolves the Codex executable once and caches the path in `resolvedBinary` for the life of the daemon. Nothing clears it when the user installs or reinstalls Codex from Settings, so the daemon keeps launching, probing, and listing models from the old executable until it is restarted.

## Reproduction

1. Start the daemon with Codex installed at path A.
2. Open any Codex Chat or model picker so the path is resolved and cached.
3. Reinstall or upgrade Codex so the executable now lives at path B, or path A is removed.
4. Trigger readiness, model discovery, or a launch. The daemon still uses path A.

## Why

`qwenBinary`/`codexBinary`-style resolvers guard the cache with a mutex but expose no way to reset it. `InvalidateAgentInstallation` in the readiness service only marks the readiness observation stale; the adapter's cached path survives.

## Fix direction

Give adapters that cache the path an optional invalidation capability and have `InvalidateAgentInstallation` call it, so the next operation re-resolves the current installation. The Qwen adapter caches the same way and needs the same treatment.

## History

A version of this fix shipped inside #5019 (Qwen Chat) as commit `c2ce82804`, bundled with a Reinstall button in Harness settings. That was out of scope for a Qwen PR and is being reverted (see the linked revert issue) so the fix can land on its own, aligned with #5003 and #5194, which own the installer-aware Codex update flow.

title: Blocker/non-blocker review findings — merge gate counts only blocking threads; reviewer must not resolve threads on behalf of the worker
body:
AO treats every unresolved review thread as a merge blocker and provides no way to mark a finding as non-blocking. This forces reviewers to resolve their own threads on behalf of the worker.

**Case:** the reviewer left two inline findings on a PR, explicitly marked as non-blocking observations deferred to the live run. The merge gate showed "Not mergeable yet — Unresolved review comments must be resolved", so the reviewer had to resolve his own threads just to clear it — breaking the rule that resolution belongs to the worker who applies the fixes.

## Proposal

1. **`blocking: true|false` on inline findings** — a field in the `comments` array of `ao review submit --reviews -` (default `true`). GitHub has no native flag on review threads, so store it in AO (the review already arrives as full JSON with `githubReviewId`) and optionally duplicate it as a `[non-blocking]` marker in the comment body.
2. **Merge gate counts only unresolved blocking threads.** Non-blocking ones stay open as the live-run checklist without gating the merge.
3. **Reviewer-task rule: the reviewer never resolves threads.** The reviewer files findings and replies on the merits; resolution is always the worker's job. With (1)–(2) in place this rule no longer conflicts with the gate.

## Open questions on the role model

- **Reviewer-merges:** in some configurations the reviewer also performs the merge — review, thread resolution and merge in one pair of hands. What compensators does AO intend (e.g. blocking threads resolvable only by the worker; self-merge blocked when reviewer and branch author share one account)?
- **Follow-up issues from review:** may the reviewer file issues (deferred observations, side bugs) instead of leaving them as inline threads that collide with the merge gate?
- **Role matrix:** an explicit action x role table (review / reply / resolve / merge / create issue / push) across {worker, reviewer, orchestrator, user} — today the rules live in task prompts and behavior is defined by whatever the gate blocks at the moment.

## Acceptance

- `blocking: false` findings do not affect mergeability; unresolved blocking threads still do;
- the reviewer-task template explicitly forbids resolving threads on behalf of the worker;
- blocking status is visible in the AO UI (and via marker in the GitHub comment body).

title: fix(chat): reap detached chat hosts after shutdown
body:
Detached chat hosts are started with Setsid but remain children of the long-lived AO daemon. Calling Process.Release() discards the handle without waiting, so an explicitly shut down chat-host can remain as a zombie owned by the daemon.

This replaces Process.Release() with an asynchronous Wait(), preserving detached/session restart behavior while ensuring the parent reaps the host when it exits.

The regression test starts a detached host, shuts it down, and asserts that its PID fully disappears from the process table rather than remaining as a zombie.

Observed live on Linux with AO commit 7e876efa1a947b41ff1284cb3da87bd74a2ab2f6: provider exited, session became terminated, but chat-host remained Z/defunct under the daemon; repeated runs accumulated zombies.

title: fix(browser): preserve host only cookies during profile import

title: fix(workspace): lock orchestrator worktree to prevent deletion during worker cleanup (#5598)
body:
Fixes #5598

### Summary of Changes

During multi-agent orchestration, an orchestrator session can inadvertently delete its own active worktree and branch when executing cleanup instructions aimed at worker sessions. Because the orchestrator process remains running without a backing worktree, subsequent turns fail with provider/service failures.

This change:
- Uses \git worktree lock\ upon creation (\Create\ and \CreateWorkspaceProject\) for orchestrator sessions (\domain.KindOrchestrator\) with a distinct lock reason (\^Gctive AO orchestrator workspace\) so that accidental \git worktree remove\ (or worker cleanup commands) cannot delete the orchestrator's own worktree.
- Parses \LockReason\ from \git worktree list --porcelain\ and ensures \destroy()\ only unlocks worktrees locked by AO with \orchestratorLockReason\ during legitimate teardown, while preserving user/external locked worktrees and refusing removal.
- Unlocks the worktree during forced teardown paths (\ForceDestroy()\, \ orceDestroyPath()\).
- Updates the orchestrator system prompt rules in \session_manager/prompt.go\ to explicitly instruct orchestrator agents never to delete their own worktree or branch, and directs them to use \^Go session kill\ and \^Go session cleanup\ for worker sessions.
- Adds an integration test \TestWorkspaceIntegrationOrchestratorWorktreeLockedAndProtected\ verifying worktree locking, resistance to \git worktree remove\, and successful cleanup during authorized destruction.
- Updates unit tests in \gitworktree\ and \session_manager\.

title: fix(gitworktree): remove worktrees with owner read-only dirs on Linux
body:
Code: +81 −5
Tests: +124 −0
Files removed: 0

## What

On Linux, AO could not delete its own worktree when a folder inside it was read-only for the owner (mode `0500`) and held a symlink. `renv` sandboxes create exactly this. Cleanup stopped with `openfdat ...: permission denied` and the worktree stayed on disk.

Deleting a file needs write permission on its parent folder, not on the file. A `0500` folder blocks that, and `removeAllWithRetry` gave up on the first error. Fixes #3807

- `remove_repair_other.go` — walks the worktree and gives owner `rwx` back to real folders only. It never calls `os.Chmod` on a symlink, so targets outside the worktree keep their contents and mode.
- Windows keeps its existing retry loop; the repair is a no-op there.

title: fix(cloud): make deploy tooling safe for a multi-provider control plane
body:
Two fixes so `deploy-staging.sh` / `promote-production.sh` work correctly on the staging control plane, which serves **multiple** sandbox providers (`AO_CLOUD_SANDBOX_PROVIDERS=nodeops,coder`; eleven_x runs on coder).

## 1. Preserve secrets for every sandbox provider (the important one)

The renderer plumbed only the single active `AO_CLOUD_SANDBOX_PROVIDER`'s secrets and pruned the rest. On a `nodeops`-primary deploy that **dropped all 8 `AO_CLOUD_CODER_*` secrets** (28 -> 20) and would have broken coder sandboxing for eleven_x. (Found live: a `deploy-staging.sh` render produced a 20-secret task-def vs the 28 the running CP carries.)

Now the tooling plumbs and preserves secrets for **every** provider in `AO_CLOUD_SANDBOX_PROVIDERS`:
- `deployment.py`: `resolve_sandbox_providers` + `build_task_definition` prune only providers **not** in the available set, require the **union** of all available providers' secrets, and stamp `AO_CLOUD_SANDBOX_PROVIDERS`. `validate_task_artifacts` derives the set from that env and rejects only non-served providers' secrets.
- `render-task-definition.py`: new `--sandbox-providers` (comma list; defaults to the single `--sandbox-provider`, so single-provider deploys are unchanged).
- `deploy-staging.sh` / `promote-production.sh`: resolve every provider in `AO_CLOUD_SANDBOX_PROVIDERS`, validate and plumb each one's secret block (`providers_has` gating), pass `--sandbox-providers`, and rebake the coder workspace whenever coder is served.

Single-provider deploys render byte-identically to before. **23 deployment tests pass** (19 existing + 4 new for the multi-provider paths).

## 2. Allowlist four unpatched base-OS CVEs

Adds `CVE-2026-8927`, `CVE-2026-8924`, `CVE-2026-8286` (curl) and `CVE-2026-85091` (zlib) to `SCAN_CVE_ALLOWLIST` in both scripts (kept in sync). All four are CRITICAL/HIGH findings in base-OS packages with no Debian fix yet, in the same class as the existing entries, and the worker exercises none of their vulnerable code paths (no proxy/cookie/STARTTLS curl use; git uses zlib inflate/deflate, not the gz file API). Already present in the running worker image; each clears on its own once Debian ships the backport.

Sources: [8927](https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2026-8927.html) · [8924](https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2026-8924.html) · [8286](https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2026-8286.html) · [85091](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/CVE-2026-85091)

## Related infra fix (done out-of-band, not in this PR)

The staging migrate task-def's container was named `migrate` while the codebase and production use `migration` (so `deploy-staging.sh`'s migration step would `StopIteration`). Fixed by re-registering `ao-cloud-staging-migrate` (rev 84) with container `migration` to match prod. That is a staging infra change, not code.

title: ci: run the SQLite package first so it stops starting last
body:
Code changes: +0 -0
Tests: +0 -0
Others: +22 -1

Part of #5116. **Stacked on #5632** — base is that branch, so the only variable in this diff is the package ordering.

## Summary

`go test` launches packages in import-path order, four at a time on `ubuntu-latest`. `internal/storage/sqlite` sorts 161st of 170 and is the longest package in the suite by a wide margin, so it starts last and then finishes alone.

Measured in [35435481761](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/35435481761), the warm-cache run on #5632:

| | |
| --- | ---: |
| packages listed before it | 160 (1358 package-seconds) |
| its start, into the Test step | 229s |
| its own runtime | 556.4s |
| Test step | 785s |
| work bound, 2091 package-seconds on 4 cores | 523s |

The 262s gap is the tail: three cores idle while the longest package runs by itself. Compilation is not the cause — with the cache restored by #5632 the first package result lands 2s into the step.

Listing it first should let the other 180 packages fill the slots behind it. Expected step near 560-600s, roughly 3 minutes.

## Why not a separate job

Giving the package its own job reaches about the same place — `max(556s, 1535/4)` — but renames the required check, which is a branch-protection change, and adds a second runner paying its own checkout and toolchain setup. One line of ordering is worth trying first.

## The list is asserted, not trusted

The obvious failure mode is a silent subset: if `go list` returns nothing, the command runs the SQLite package alone and the required check goes green having skipped the suite. That is the same class of bug as the test-result caching #5632 had to close, so the step counts what it is about to run:

```
want=$(printf '%s\n' "$all" | wc -l)
got=$(( $(printf '%s\n' "$rest" | wc -l) + 1 ))
```

Verified locally against all three paths:

| | result |
| --- | --- |
| normal | 181 packages, sqlite first, exit 0 |
| `go list` unavailable | exit 127 |
| filter over-matches | `package list mismatch: go list found 181, about to test 9`, exit 1 |

The `$` anchor keeps the subpackages — `sqlite/gen`, `sqlite/sqlitetest`, `sqlite/store` — in the second group where they belong.

## Validation

This PR's own CI run is the measurement. If the Test step does not drop, the revert is one line, and the fallback is the separate job described above.

title: Reviewer agent loops on dozens of consecutive no-op Bash true calls
body:
### Problem

Read-only reviewers cannot use `Write`/`Edit`, but the current reporting instructions require embedding review Markdown inside shell-quoted JSON for both GitHub publication and AO bookkeeping.

Reviewers can attempt to write a temporary payload, fall back to emitting it as ordinary response text—which AO does not consume—and enter the tool-call loops analyzed below (measured evidence preserved in the thread of closed PR #5863).

Fix the reporting contract rather than adding a loop detector or enabling file writes.

### Root cause (verified)

Verified from transcript re-analysis and the reviewer launch code:

- The reviewer is launched **read-only** (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/claudecode/claudecode.go`): allowlist is Read/Grep/Glob plus narrow Bash (`printf`, `gh`, read-only `git`, `ao review submit`); `Write`/`Edit`/`NotebookEdit`/`git push`/`git commit` are hard-denied, headless — nothing outside the allowlist can be approved. The payload-file workaround is blocked by the Write ban (upstream #4810).
- The review prompt (`backend/internal/review/prompt.go`) allows exactly one hand-off: inline the entire review Markdown as a JSON string literal inside a shell-quoted `printf`, piped into `gh api` (publication) and into `ao review submit --reviews -` (bookkeeping).
- Long reviews full of quotes, backticks and newlines must be hand-escaped into shell-quoted JSON. When escaping fails, submission fails while the review text is already composed. The model then probes the only remaining channel (trivial Bash commands) and/or emits the JSON payload as plain assistant text, which a headless run never consumes — until a human intervenes.
- Two loop forms confirmed across hung reviewer transcripts: **probe storms** (fresh trivial command each time, commonly non-empty output; worst measured: 176 calls / 44 min / ~26M input tokens) and **identical repeats** (dozens of same-file `Read` calls with identical offset/limit). In every series the finished review was already present in the preceding assistant text. Loops also occur with thinking enabled.
- Any repetition guard must tolerate legitimate retry streaks (observed: 5 consecutive `git rebase --continue` retries is normal operation).

### Decision: one submission to AO, breaking change

The reviewer submits only to AO through the existing `ao review submit` command:

```bash
printf '%s' 'Review summary in Markdown' | ao review submit \
  --session worker-1 \
  --run run-1 \
  --verdict changes_requested \
  --body - \
  --comment-path src/auth.go \
  --comment-line 42 \
  --comment-body 'Missing authorization check.'
```

(`--session` is the canonical form for reviewer invocations; the positional form remains for interactive use.)

- Read the review body as plain Markdown from stdin.
- Accept inline findings through repeatable `--comment-path`, `--comment-line`, and `--comment-body` flags. Pair values by occurrence; reject incomplete groups. Omit these flags when there are no inline findings.
- **Finding bodies are single-line by contract.** Multi-line prose belongs in the review body, not in flag values; the CLI rejects multi-line `--comment-body` values with a clear error instead of inviting fragile shell quoting again.
- Do not parse findings out of Markdown or require model-authored JSON, temporary files, or JSON escaping in shell commands.
- The CLI performs internal serialization.

**This replaces the old workflow, rather than adding another optional mode.**

- No `--publish` flag: submission always includes publication.
- Remove legacy JSON/file submission through `--reviews` and file-valued `--body`.
- Remove caller-supplied `--review-id`; GitHub review IDs are outputs, not inputs.
- Reject obsolete inputs clearly. Update prompts, help, documentation, and reviewer adapters to the new contract.

### Daemon responsibilities

Use the existing submission endpoint and GitHub integration.

The daemon validates the run, persists the submitted content, publishes one GitHub `COMMENT` review containing the summary and inline findings, and records the returned review ID. Resolve the PR and target commit from the run.

Return the publication result through the same CLI invocation. Preserve findings in AO bookkeeping and worker feedback.

Repeated identical submissions must not create duplicate GitHub reviews. Persist publication-attempt state before the external request; report uncertain outcomes explicitly rather than blindly reposting.

Remove direct GitHub publication permissions from reviewers while retaining required read operations and AO submission. Keep `Write`/`Edit` prohibited.

No new MCP server, publication command, HTTP endpoint, generic JSON editor, or transcript-output parser.

### Open question for whoever designed the review flow

This contract is a stopgap: the issue author patched the broken hand-off from the outside, as best they could, without access to the original design intent. Properly, this should be addressed to whoever designed the review submission flow itself: **how do you want this to work for all users and harnesses?** The day-to-day review loop in agent-orchestrator is genuinely good — the goal is to make it better, not to redefine it unilaterally. Input from the original designer or maintainers on the shape of this contract is explicitly requested before any upstream PR.

### Acceptance and rollout

- Reviews with zero, one, and multiple inline findings reach GitHub and AO.
- Quotes, multiline Markdown, and code blocks survive unchanged.
- Multi-line `--comment-body` values are rejected with a clear error.
- Obsolete inputs fail clearly.
- Retries, concurrent submissions, daemon restarts, and GitHub failures do not lose results or silently duplicate publication.
- Verify the previously failing workflow with `Write` disabled, including another supported harness.
- Validate on the fork and collect before/after evidence before opening an upstream PR. Do not claim this eliminates every possible model loop.

title: ci: scope the Go build cache to build-test, and trim the snapshot helper
body:
Code changes: +0 -0
Tests: +7 -16
Others: +11 -18

Follow-up to #5632, which merged while these cuts were still local. No behaviour change.

## Cache only where compilation is on the critical path

#5632 enabled the Go build cache on three jobs. Only one of them needed it:

| job | duration | cache worth it |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `build-test` | 13m40s | yes — this is the regression in #5116 |
| `windows-workspace` | 4m46s | no, and a second large cache competes for the repository's 10 GB quota against the one that matters |
| `cloud-build-test` | 25s | no |

Both revert to `cache: false`. The seven `-count=1` flags that existed only to stop those restored caches replaying test results go with them — `build-test` keeps its own, which is load-bearing and stays.

## Trim the snapshot helper

- `sync.Mutex` on the cache: the package has no `t.Parallel` and no `go func` anywhere, so it guards concurrency that does not exist. It also runs under `-race`, so whoever adds `t.Parallel` gets a loud map race rather than silence.
- Lazy nil-map init: the `var` can initialise its own map.
- `noForeignKeysDSN`: one use, inlined.
- `migratedDatabaseSnapshot` and `buildMigrationSnapshots` duplicated a copy between them; the cache-hit check folds into the accessor and the builder stops returning a value.

## Validation

- `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/storage/sqlite`: 78/78 pass, 423.3s — faster than the 463.6s measured on #5632, since the cuts remove a mutex and a redundant copy
- `go vet`, `gofmt -l`, and `golangci-lint v2.12.2`: clean, 0 issues

title: [Bug]: Cursor reviewer pane stalls on Cursor's MCP approval prompt — nobody is there to approve it
body:
## What went wrong?

A Cursor reviewer pane stops on Cursor's `MCP Server Approval Required` screen and the review never starts. Nobody is sitting at a reviewer pane, so there is no one to answer the prompt — the review just stays queued until a human notices the pane and clicks through by hand.

**Environment**

- AO desktop `0.13.1-nightly.202609191635` (nightly channel), macOS arm64
- `cursor-agent 2026.09.18-9a7762b`
- Reviewer harness `cursor`, configured via project config `reviewers: [{ harness: cursor, agentConfig: { model: <model> } }]`, with `autoReview` enabled

**Reproduction**

1. Use a repository that declares an MCP server in a checked-in `.cursor/mcp.json` (in my case one stdio server launched through the project's own CLI).
2. Let AO trigger an auto-review on a PR with the Cursor reviewer harness.
3. The reviewer pane opens and Cursor renders `MCP Server Approval Required` for the project server.
4. The review stays at `needs_review`, `cursor-agent` is alive, and no verdict is ever recorded. Approving by hand in the pane lets that one review proceed normally.

I saw this on two concurrent reviews: the one whose profile had no recorded approval stalled, the one that already had an approval from an earlier manual click ran to completion. That difference is what pointed at the profile rather than the harness.

**Why it recurs for every new session**

`reviewerProfileDir()` in `backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/cursor/config.go` keys the AO-owned Cursor profile on `sha256(inv.ReviewerID)[:8]`, and Cursor records approvals per profile at `<CURSOR_DATA_DIR>/projects/<workspace-slug>/mcp-approvals.json`. So a manual approval is scoped to that one reviewer's profile; the next session gets a fresh profile and prompts again.

## Exact current launch behaviour

`(*Reviewer).ReviewCommand` (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/cursor/cursor.go`) takes the argv from `agent.GetLaunchCommand` and splices the reviewer flags in ahead of the `--` separator:

```
cursor-agent --model <model> --trust --add-dir <ao-prompt-root> -- <task prompt>
```

with `CURSOR_DATA_DIR` pointed at the isolated AO reviewer profile. `--trust` trusts the workspace, but Cursor still gates repo-declared MCP servers behind the interactive approval screen. `ReviewRestoreCommand` delegates to `ReviewCommand`, so a restored pane hits the same screen.

## This is not the worker-path problem

#4333 / #4404 / #4495 covered the *worker* TUI path, where the fix was to stop losing sends while the approval screen is up (gate sends until the first agent hook arrives). That is a transport/ordering fix, and it is the right one for a worker, because a human is present and a follow-up is coming.

A reviewer pane has neither: there is no follow-up to gate and no one to approve. This issue is about **reviewer trust policy**, not send ordering, and I don't think the worker fix generalises to it.

## What I tested locally

I have a local one-line change that adds `--approve-mcps` to the reviewer flags:

```go
flags := []string{"--trust", "--approve-mcps"}
```

`insertBeforePrompt` already handles placement, so it lands before `--` and leaves `--model`, `--trust`, `--add-dir`, prompt delivery and the profile env untouched. Because `ReviewRestoreCommand` delegates to `ReviewCommand`, fresh and restore launches are both covered by that single site.

I added five argv regression tests in `cursor_test.go` — full fresh argv; ordering relative to `--trust` / `--add-dir` / `--`; the `insertBeforePrompt` no-separator fallback; restore argv identical to fresh; flag retained when `--add-dir` is omitted — each verified to fail with the change reverted and pass with it. `gofmt` and `go vet` clean, `go build ./...` passes, and `go test -race` passes across all reviewer adapters plus `internal/adapters/agent/cursor` and `pkg/agentruntime`. The worker path (`pkg/agentruntime.buildCursorLaunch`, which owns the `--force` / `--yolo` mapping) is untouched.

**I am not assuming that is the fix you want.** See the tradeoff below — I'd rather you pick the direction than have me land a permissive default.

## The tradeoff, stated plainly

`--approve-mcps` auto-approves the MCP servers **the reviewed checkout declares**. A `.cursor/mcp.json` specifies an arbitrary `command`, so on a branch from an untrusted contributor this means AO spawns a repo-controlled process during review without asking. Today the prompt is what stops that: it is a deadlock for AO, but it is also a real gate.

That sits awkwardly next to #2844 (least-privilege workers, "naked" unless opted in) and #3745 (enforce read-only tool access for reviewer harnesses). Options I can see, roughly least to most permissive:

1. **Disabled by default.** `installReviewerConfig` already owns the reviewer profile; it could write `mcp-disabled.json` alongside the config it writes today, so reviewers run with no MCP at all. No new CLI flag, no new trust, removes the stall, and it matches the direction in #2844. Cursor supports this — `cursor-agent mcp disable <id>` is what writes that file.
2. **Restricted / allowlisted.** Approve only servers the AO user has explicitly allowed for reviewers, rather than whatever the checkout happens to declare.
3. **Opt-in.** A per-project or per-reviewer setting that enables auto-approval, defaulting to off, so the permissive behaviour is a deliberate choice.
4. **Always approve** — the `--approve-mcps` change above. Simplest, and defensible if reviewing a branch is already treated as trusting it, but the most permissive.

My own preference is (1) or (3); I implemented (4) only because it was the smallest thing that unblocked me locally, and I'm happy to rework it into whichever direction you prefer, or to leave it with you entirely.

Either way the stall itself seems worth fixing: right now an auto-review on any repository with a checked-in `.cursor/mcp.json` silently never completes.

---

Investigated with agent assistance; the reproduction, environment and test results above are from my own machine.

title: feat(cloud): provision the coder flow on Azure (CP + DB stay on AWS)
body:
## What

Stand up the **coder flow on Azure** so cloud sessions with `provider=coder` run on Azure VMs/containers, while the control plane and its database stay on AWS. Goal: dogfood internally and demo to eleven_x on Azure credits without moving the CP or data.

## Why it needs no AO code change

The coder provider (`cloud/internal/sandbox/coder/`) already targets a Coder API endpoint (`AO_CLOUD_CODER_URL`), and `cloud/coder/main.tf` is a **Docker** template (workspace = a container via a Docker socket). So it already runs on any Docker host. "Coder on Azure" is therefore infra plus a one-line config repoint. The same `main.tf` and `Sandbox.Dockerfile` are reused verbatim.

## Contents

- `cloud/scripts/provision-coder-azure.sh` - one Azure VM running Docker + Coder + Postgres, plus a long-lived admin API token. Parameterized (region, VM size, names) and idempotent; retries the transient VM-create NIC race.
- `cloud/scripts/provision-coder-azure-template.sh` - builds the workspace image on the VM (bakes the release-matched `ao-worker` from the control-plane image; amd64, so no cross-arch worker gymnastics) and publishes the `ao-linux-docker` template.
- `cloud/coder/AZURE.md` - architecture, provisioning, CP wiring, the shared-CP guardrail, region guidance (Sweden Central next to `eu-north-1`), and teardown.

## Guardrail

Do not repoint the **shared staging CP** at the Azure Coder (it would move eleven_x's workspaces). Dogfooding uses a separate/dev CP; the coder config is a single endpoint per CP.

## Validation

Provisioned live in `swedencentral`: Coder healthy, template published, and a test workspace spun up a container on the Azure VM with the agent **connected**. Then torn down.

## Notes / follow-ups (in AZURE.md)

TLS + DNS in front of Coder, move Coder's Postgres to Azure Database for PostgreSQL, lock the NSG, and bake/push the workspace image for multi-VM scale.

title: style(review): quiet and flatten the review tab
body:
## What

A UI-only pass over the session inspector's **Reviews** tab, in two commits: the controls at the top, then the expanded review card below them. No behaviour is added or removed — every control, disclosure and action still does what it did.

## Why

The tab read as a settings form bolted onto a panel. The controls used ALL CAPS section labels, rows ruled off from one another, and labels written as instructions rather than names. The expanded review below them was a stack of same-weight parts: three filled surfaces nested inside each other, two disclosures styled identically despite doing different things, and four levels of nesting rendered flat.

One label was also simply wrong: the row keyed `inspector.review.session` rendered as "Trigger review" while holding the reviewer-session controls and restating the "Review latest commit" button beside it.

## How

**Controls**

- Row card loses its horizontal padding, so control rows share a left edge with their section heading and the review cards below. The tab keeps its own gutter.
- Section headings in sentence case, per [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) ("Never use ALL CAPS labels"), and matched to each other — "Review summary" had been a size larger than "Review controls".
- Row labels name the thing, following onboarding's `Coding agent` / `Credential type` pattern: "Select reviewer agent" → **Reviewer agent**, "Trigger review" → **Reviewer session**.
- The ⓘ beside "Auto review" is gone; the toggle and label already say what it does. That orphaned `inspector.autoReviewDescription`, dropped from all 8 locales.
- Dividers replaced by spacing; the agent dropdown sizes to its label instead of clipping at `11rem`.
- The reviewer session row is hidden while auto review is **idle**, where its controls are all disabled anyway. It deliberately returns while a review is **in flight** — stopping one is reachable from nowhere else, and `shows reviewing status and cancel action while auto-review is running` covers that path.

**Expanded review card**

- One surface instead of three; a hairline replaces the nested fill.
- Card header is a single centre line: avatar, reviewer and timing left, verdict and actions right. Name and timing wrap as a pair so a narrow rail drops the timing rather than clipping the reviewer's name to `cod…`.
- "Show more" no longer mimics the "Resolved comments" disclosure — no chevron, no underline, 10px, and positioned where the clamped text actually stops.
- The clamp's fade is gone; it half-erased a live line and read as a bug.
- Resolved comments are nested under their heading by a rule, with quieter bodies.

**Worth a reviewer's attention:** `useClampedTextEnd` is the one piece of real machinery here. `line-clamp` hides overflow without reporting where it cut, so anything pinned to an edge drifts away from text ending mid-line. The hook walks the rendered text with a `Range` to find the last character still inside the clamp box and positions the control there, re-measuring on resize. It falls back to the bottom-right corner when it cannot measure — which is what happens in jsdom, where rects are zero-sized. **That fallback is why the suite stays green, so the positioning path itself is not covered by tests**; it was verified by measuring in the running app.

Two smaller findings while doing this: `--color-bg-settings-row` resolves to `transparent`, so an overlay using it let text run straight through (the painted surface is `bg-background`); and `tailwind-merge` cannot distinguish `text-micro` (a size) from `text-passive` (a colour) and silently drops one, so the size now sits on a wrapper.

## Testing

- `npm run frontend:typecheck` — clean.
- `packages/product-ui` — 129/129 pass.
- `SessionInspector.test.tsx` — 119/119 pass, including the updated auto-review assertions.

title: Mobile UI touch-up: type, icons, keyboard and board fixes
body: A pass over the mobile app after driving it on a real iPhone for a few days. Three things drove everything here: it did not look like the desktop app, it fought the keyboard, and a few screens broke outright. SCREENSHOTS: @Prasad-D-Ware mostly just quality of life changes, improving parity with desktop app, and some ux improvements ## Type now comes from the renderer The app was drawing SF Pro because no family was bundled at all, and its own ramp used weight 700 and 800 for every title. The renderer stops at `--font-weight-semibold`, so the same screen looked heavier on the phone than on the desktop. Geist and Geist Mono are bundled and loaded before the first paint. Weights are 400, 500 and 600 only; 92 bold usages were normalised to semibold. Tracking follows the renderer's scale instead of SF Pro's optical values, which run positive at large sizes and were pulling the other way. A weight is a font file here, not a number: iOS draws whichever face the family name points at and ignores `fontWeight`, so every style that sets a weight names its face. `fontForWeight` in `lib/tokens.ts` is that mapping, and 310 inline styles were updated to use it. ## Icons come from the desktop's set The desktop draws from Lucide. The app drew from Feather, which is Lucide's ancestor, so most glyphs looked close enough and a few did not. `lib/icons.tsx` now imports `lucide-react-native` at the same version as the renderer (1.47.0) and maps the names the call sites already use, which keeps the diff to one file plus the import lines. MaterialCommunityIcons is gone from the pin rail and the sidebar destinations; pinning uses the desktop's Pin and PinOff. The native SwiftUI chrome keeps SF Symbols. Those are real SwiftUI views inside an `@expo/ui` Host and Lucide glyphs cannot be drawn there. ## The keyboard The composer snapped because we positioned it from `keyboardVisible`, a flag that turns over when the keyboard has finished moving. The dock did the same thing, which left its buttons hanging where the keyboard had been and then snapping back. Both now hold their resting position and ride the keyboard's own progress, so they travel with the keys. Two related bugs: the composer dismissed the keyboard after the send resolved rather than on the tap, which tied its exit to the network, and the dock's lift was computed from the library's animated `height`, which is the keyboard frame origin and negative while the keyboard is up, so the lift was always zero and the search field sat under the keys. The composer is one borderless capsule now, with Liquid Glass drawn behind the row. Its size comes from constants, not from layout: three attempts at a growing pill each ended with the material drawn at a different size than the pill it sat behind, because every one of them read that size at runtime while the keyboard was still moving. ## Board and session fixes Switching project filters showed two lists at once, recycled cells of the old grouping under the new data with the empty state on top. The list is now mounted per filter. The worker dock's menus open upward, and SwiftUI reverses an upward menu's items under its default order, which put "All projects" last. Both menus pin their order, and the projects row shows the selection alone rather than a prefix that wrapped. On iOS 26 the session header's actions button was drawing the system's shared bar-button background under our own glass, so it came out with two outlines and a squarer shape than the back button beside it. Glass controls in native headers are declared as header items with the shared background hidden. Page transitions showed a white seam between the outgoing and incoming screens, from the navigator's own container colour, which comes from the navigation theme and defaults to white. The theme now carries the palette. The seam is gone in the 93 frames I captured across pushes and pops. Also in here: the conversation start label and the message bubble border are gone, the session screen renders its content while it is still sliding in rather than after, and its header title is set on the first commit instead of a frame later. One crash fix that is not cosmetic. `expo-web-browser` arrived with an earlier branch and its native module was never added to this worktree's Pods project, so any tap that opens a GitHub link threw while the module was being imported and took the screen down. The dependency is now installed properly, and the import is guarded so a build without the pod falls back to the system browser the way this function used to. ## Since this was written Review turned up three things, each now fixed: the font load had no error path and kept no splash, so a face that failed to load left the app on a blank root forever; the header buttons lost the `isButton` trait when the glass surface moved from a `Button` to a `Group`; and the icon and font barrels were shipping their whole sets — a production iOS export carried 4,330 modules against 2,480 on main, and registered all 36 Geist faces for the four the app draws. Per-glyph and per-weight imports bring that export to 2,563 modules, four faces, and 5.38 MB against 8.46 MB. More days of driving it after that turned up the rest of what is in this branch: - **Merged has its own hue.** It was drawing the same muted grey as a session that had merely switched off, under the green that had just said "mergeable". The palette had a deliberate "no purple" rule enforced by a test — purple is in now, meaning exactly that one state, and the legend and the test were updated to say so rather than being left contradicting the code. - **"Needs you" and "Pinned" never fold.** Both could be hidden behind a chevron, so the board could show a clean, quiet screen with work waiting inside it. The rest still fold and stay folded. - **A row without a pull request names its branch.** Dropping the branch outright had left the second line blank on exactly the rows where the branch was the only thing naming the worktree. - **Back no longer dead-ends.** `router.back()` on an empty stack is an unhandled `GO_BACK`, and a screen with no other exit had no way out — a deep link or a notification tap that cold-starts the app is how a screen gets there. One `backOr` now covers all fourteen exits, with a source test that fails on an unguarded one. - **A working row's circle breathes.** It was drawn as a bare glyph, so the one status that means "still going" was the only one that never moved, while the same word breathed on the project cards. - **The spawn sheet stopped naming a model the provider will not run.** It showed the catalog's `isDefault` entry, and codex's is wrong — `gpt-6-astra` advertised while a new thread comes up on `gpt-5.6-sol` — and picking that value sent no model at all, so the session recorded nothing and the chat displayed whatever the thread happened to be running. - **The composer footer's label no longer draws over its neighbours** — the context meter, or the "sent after this" note when a message is queued. - **The Android swipe rail's buttons sit in the row's centre.** The rail spans the row's full height while its buttons are a fixed 76pt block, so they were top-pinned and would drift high on any row taller than the minimum. ## Checking it `tsc` is clean and the suite passes at 130 files and 1228 tests. Most of the visual work was checked by capturing the simulator while driving it, including frame-by-frame captures for the transition seam and the keyboard geometry. Two things I could not verify and would like a second pair of eyes on: the simulator's software keyboard refuses to appear on this machine, so the keyboard travel is verified by construction and by its endpoints rather than by watching it, and menus need a tap I cannot perform, so the menu order rests on the documented SwiftUI behaviour. ## Known gaps The Android drawer still uses FontAwesome for its two items, and the native SwiftUI chrome uses SF Symbols. Both would need shipped image assets to match Lucide exactly.

title: refactor(ui): converge the app on one design language
body:
Retargeted onto `main`. This branch used to sit on top of #5566; the only thing it needed from there was the onboarding button's radius and weight, which is `--radius-topbar-control: var(--radius-md)` here.

## What

Several parts of the app had competing implementations of the same thing. This pulls them onto one vocabulary. No layout changes.

**Focus** — one treatment (`outline-2` + `--ring`), replacing eight: 2px rings, 1px rings, brand-coloured rings, inset rings, and a width-less one, across 26 files.

**Colour naming** — `text-settings-muted`, `text-settings-label`, `settings-accent` and `color-text-import-title` were all aliases of existing roles *in the same context*; collapsed onto the roles themselves. `error` and `danger` resolve to the same hue as `destructive` in every theme, so 126 classes moved to the documented name — `DESIGN.md` uses "destructive" throughout, and the emitted values are byte-identical.

**Inputs** — `Input` (`default` | `field` | `bare`), a new `Textarea`, and `SearchField` (`field` | `menu`). Three CSS utilities that each re-spelled the same bordered field are deleted.

**Buttons** — gained the variants the app was already hand-rolling: `quiet`, `danger`, `rail`, `link`, `link-quiet`, `icon-xs`, `icon-lg`. Neutral hovers now share one wash, press uses the `scale-press` token, and the primitive honours `prefers-reduced-motion` — the hand-rolled copies did, the primitive didn't.

**Hover** — the sidebar's growing fill is now the default for every transparent button: `ghost`/`quiet` Buttons, the transparent topbar variants, and the inspector tabs. Chip triggers opt in through a new `highlight` prop; the composer's selectors also drop their carets.

**Chat composer** — 16px radius, and a border that no longer changes in any state.

## Verification

- Every touched module compiles through the Vite dev server.
- Run against a real database alongside several live instances. That caught a genuine regression — a converted `<Button>` with no import in `Sidebar.tsx` — which neither tag balance nor the transform detects, only running it.
- Token moves were checked value-exact rather than assumed: `text-error` and `text-destructive` both emit `color: var(--bridge-danger)`.
- After the move to `main`, the sweep was re-run across the whole tree: no remaining reference to a collapsed token, and the two dangling vars the re-base re-exposed are fixed (`--color-text-muted-foreground` → `--muted-foreground`, `--color-text-import-title` → `text-foreground`). The `packages/product-ui` views that the first pass missed now speak the same vocabulary as the renderer.
- **Not run:** the frontend test suite. Class-name assertions were updated where they were coupled (`TopbarButton.test.tsx`, `Sidebar.test.tsx`, `SessionInspectorView.test.tsx`).

## Deliberately left, and why

- `text-passive` measures **2.41:1** against a 4.5:1 requirement, and it's a chart-ramp step used as a text colour. Repainting it is a design call.
- Dialog widths have six vocabularies; converging them moves geometry by 8–72px, which is layout, not polish.
- ~178 raw `<button>` remain — many are rows, tabs and menu items that legitimately aren't Buttons — plus the sidebar's own focus wash, the last place not speaking the unified focus language.

title: feat(landing): add weekly changelog publishing flow
body:
## Summary

- Publish a concise weekly product changelog with individual permalinks and RSS.
- Cover every completed week from the repository's first commit: 32 continuous weekly windows.
- Use one editorial structure throughout: customer-focused major features, grouped improvements, grouped fixes, and learn-more links.
- Keep detailed version release notes accessible without mixing their different structure into the weekly feed.
- Rewrite historical feature headings in plain customer language instead of copying raw PR titles.
- Link every displayed PR number, including references preserved in detailed release write-ups.
- Reserve screenshots for substantial user-facing workflows, with at most one image per weekly entry and none under routine improvements or fixes.
- Exclude raw commit dumps, internal-only work, repeated items, and routine contributor roll calls.
- Keep contributor credit exceptional and explicit through the `changelog:credit` label.
- Automatically draft future weekly updates as reviewable pull requests; publishing still requires human review and merge.

## Human workflow

1. Read every merged PR collected for the week.
2. Remove internal, reverted, duplicated, superseded, or unavailable work.
3. Combine related PRs under one customer-facing feature.
4. Rewrite the headline, summary, and major features around what users can do.
5. Group smaller improvements and fixes by product area.
6. Add one real screenshot or demo only when a major workflow materially benefits from it.
7. Credit a contributor only for a genuinely exceptional contribution explicitly marked for credit.
8. Preview desktop and mobile layouts, verify links, wait for CI, and merge when ready.

## Validation

- `npm run changelog:test` — 8 passing
- `npm run changelog:validate` — passed
- `npm run changelog:ui-test` — passed against all 32 weekly feed entries
- `npm run build` — passed; 138 static pages generated
- Browser verification — 32 weekly articles rendered with no error overlay
- Detailed 0.11.0, 0.12.0, and 0.13.0 release pages remain directly accessible
- Continuous coverage verified from 2026-02-13 through 2026-09-20
- Validation prevents more than one image per week or media below the major-feature section
- No repeated PR badges within an entry
- No raw commit links in weekly entries
- No unlinked PR references in detailed release write-ups
- All required checks pass on the current head

## Review reminders

- Generated weekly changelog pull requests open as GitHub Draft PRs.
- `@somewherelostt`, `@illegalcall`, and `@AgentWrapper` are added as assignees and reviewers.
- One initial comment tags all three people with the editorial checklist.
- An hourly monitor posts a tagged reminder only after six elapsed hours, then every six hours while the PR remains open.
- Reminders stop automatically when the PR is merged or closed, and hidden markers prevent duplicate initial notifications or early reminders.

Validation: both workflows pass YAML parsing, actionlint, shell syntax checks, and current-head CI.

title: feat(cloud): gate sandbox providers on WorkOS org capabilities
body:
## Summary

Gate a sandbox provider (starting with `coder`) to specific organizations, using a per-org capability seeded from WorkOS organization metadata. Reuses AO's existing WorkOS org identity rather than a bespoke table, and is default-off so shipping it changes nothing until an operator opts in.

## How it works

- The WorkOS org resolver now also reads `metadata.capabilities` (a comma-separated list) and returns it; `auth.Verify` carries it on `Principal.OrgCapabilities`. This rides the existing cached (5-minute) org fetch, so there is no token/RBAC change and no extra per-request WorkOS call.
- A provider is gated only if it is listed in `AO_CLOUD_CAPABILITY_GATED_PROVIDERS` (comma-separated, default EMPTY). A gated provider then requires the active org to hold a capability of the same name. Empty set = every provider ungated = current behavior.
- `GET /me` filters the advertised providers by the org's entitlement, so the provider toggle is driven entirely by the server: a non-entitled org gets `coder` filtered out of `available`, and the frontend (which renders options from `available` and collapses the selector when only one remains) shows no coder toggle. No frontend change.
- `createSession` enforces the same check server-side (403 `provider_forbidden`) so the gate holds even against the raw API.

## Rollout (no lockout)

1. Merge + deploy: gate off, zero behavior change.
2. Flag entitled orgs in WorkOS: set org metadata `capabilities = coder` and add the members.
3. Set `AO_CLOUD_CAPABILITY_GATED_PROVIDERS=coder` on the control plane. `coder` is then offered and allowed only to entitled orgs; everyone else silently gets the default provider.

Extensible: `capabilities` is a list, so future providers or features gate the same way by adding a capability string.

## Tests

- `parseOrganizationCapabilities` (metadata parsing: trim / lowercase / dedupe / empty).
- `orgAllowsProvider` and `providersForOrg` (the gate and the org-filtered provider list).
- The ungated-default rollout-safe case (no gated providers means everything is allowed).
- Full cloud module test green (`go test ./...`), including the existing provider-inheritance / autolink tests.

title: bug(usage): long-running session undercounted ~100x — inspector showed 3.6M tokens processed, transcript shows ~342M
body:
## Bug

SessionInspector → USAGE & COST massively undercounts a long-running session — by ~100x.

Observed on a real ~10-hour Claude-harness session (model `glm-5.3-flash` via the claude harness, ~2,190 assistant turns, transcript activity 17:00–02:59 UTC). The inspector showed:

| Metric | Inspector | Ground truth (transcript) |
|---|---|---|
| Tokens processed | 3.6M | **≈ 342M** |
| Fresh input | 207.2K | 0.76M |
| Cache reads | 3.4M | **341.4M** |
| Output | 32.2K | 0.19M |
| Estimated cost | $0.15 | (off by the same factor) |

Ground truth = summing `message.usage` over all assistant records in the session's Claude Code transcript (`~/.claude/projects/<worktree-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl`): fresh input 757,393 + cache reads 340,699,328 + output 193,726 ≈ **341.65M** (plus 9.8M in the pre-resume transcript file). Hourly buckets of cache reads: 17:xx UTC alone is 3.16M — i.e. the inspector's 3.4M matches only the **first hour** of the session; ingestion stopped after that.

**Source:** live observation | **Reported by:** @axisrow | **Analyzed against:** `1c888193c` (origin/main, 2026-09-22; daemon self-built from that tree — the fork delta does not touch `internal/observe/usage`)
**Confidence:** Medium — mechanism localized to ingestion, exact break point not yet pinned.

## What the code says

- `backend/internal/observe/usage/parser.go`, `normalizeAnthropicUsage()` (~L765–780): `InputTokens = cache_read + (input + cache_creation)` — cache reads are included.
- `backend/internal/service/usage/summary.go`, `usageTotals()` (~L115–118): `ProcessedTokens = InputTokens + OutputTokens`.

So with full ingestion the UI would have shown ~342M. It shows 3.6M ⇒ this is not a formula error: the vast majority of usage events never reached the DB.

## Reproduction

1. Run a long-lived claude-harness session (hours, thousands of turns).
2. Let the daemon / usage collector restart at least once during the session (collector `restart-all` also triggers this).
3. Open SessionInspector → USAGE & COST: totals match only a small early slice of the session. Compare with a `jq` sum of `message.usage` over the transcript jsonl — off by orders of magnitude.

## Suspected root cause

The ingestor stops following the transcript early in the session's life. Candidates:

- watcher loses the file on transcript rotation (resume creates a new session-id file) and never re-scans;
- after a daemon restart the collector attaches by tailing new lines only, without replaying what it missed;
- related to the recent collector `restart-all` path (mutex contention fix era).

## Impact

- "Tokens processed" and estimated cost are wrong by orders of magnitude on long sessions — the sessions where spend matters most.
- The cost figure cannot be trusted for budgeting.

## Related

- [#5232](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5232) — same ingestion pipeline, different symptom (missing provider attribution → cost unavailable)
- [#4126](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4126) — earlier clarification of cache-token counting semantics

## Request

Add two derived metrics to the SessionInspector **USAGE & COST** panel:

1. **Turns** — number of assistant turns in the session. The usage pipeline already ingests one usage event per assistant message, so this is a `count(*)` over ingested events — no new collection needed.
2. **Throughput (tok/s)** — processed tokens per second of active session time, e.g. `ProcessedTokens / (last_usage_event_ts − first_usage_event_ts)`, shown alongside "Tokens processed".

Both are derivable from data the pipeline already stores; the panel already shows the components (fresh input, cache reads, output, hit rate, cost).

## Why

- Turns is the most intuitive "how much work happened here" counter; today it is not visible anywhere in the inspector.
- Throughput makes session comparisons meaningful (a 10h session and a 10min session with the same token count are not the same thing) and surfaces wedged sessions (throughput → 0).
- Concretely motivating case: a ~10h session processed ~342M tokens across ~2,190 turns — a turns/throughput row would have made the usage undercount from [#5745](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5745) (inspector showed 3.6M) obvious at a glance.

title: fix(usage): ingest resume continuation transcripts missing a hook
body:
## Summary

Fixes #5745 — the usage pipeline never followed resume continuations, so every resumed claude session silently lost all post-resume usage.

**Root cause (from the production incident):** `claude --resume` continues a conversation in a new native session file in the same project directory, with no back-reference to the old id. Discovery keyed only on the stored native id ([`discoverPath`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/main/backend/internal/service/usage/collector.go) globs `<ClaudeProjects>/*/<nativeID>.jsonl`), and the only intake for a new native id was a hook — which resume flows may never send (guard drops / daemon unreachable). fsnotify watches exact files, never directories, and the pipeline had no periodic backstop. In the incident session the pre-resume transcript was ingested fully and correctly (UI = DB = 3.6M), while the post-resume transcript (~342M across 2,249 assistant turns) had no binding and no source; schema-wide, no `claude_main` binding had ever followed more than one native id.

**Fix:**
- `ReconcileSources` now scans the current source's project directory for unregistered `*.jsonl` files, reads `sessionId`+`cwd` from a bounded window of leading records, and when `cwd` matches the session workspace (AO worktrees are per-session by design) registers the continuation binding + source through the same validated path hooks use. The write-once `(binding_id, source_event_key)` dedup keeps replay idempotent.
- A 3-minute safety-net tick fans into the coordinator refresh, healing both hookless resumes and silently lost fsnotify watches.
- The two silent hook guard drops (launch-id mismatch, session not live) now log a warning; behavior unchanged.

**Known limit:** bindings already in `complete` state are not reconciled, so a resume after finalization is still only recovered by a hook — noted for a future eligibility widening.

## Test

- New: `TestCollectorDiscoversClaudeContinuationInWorkspaceDir` (incident repro), `...IsIdempotent`, `...IgnoresCwdMismatch`, `...IgnoresPathBoundToAnotherSession`, `TestReadClaudeTranscriptMetaSkipsRecordsWithoutCwd`, and pipeline-level `TestPipelineIngestsDiscoveredClaudeContinuation` (aggregate = old + continuation, replay does not double count).
- `gofmt -l .` clean; `go test ./...` green for touched packages; `go test -race` and `golangci-lint run` clean on touched packages. Note: `internal/adapters/agent/crush` has a pre-existing local-env failure on clean `main`; `claudecode`/`goose` were flaky only under full-suite parallel load and pass in isolation.

## Live verification plan

On the incident machine, rebuilding the daemon from this branch and restarting it should: log `usage continuation source registered` for the orphaned transcript, register the missing binding/source (offset 0 → file size), and converge the session total to ~352M (from the previously shown 3.6M). Will be confirmed on the reporter's deployment; unit and pipeline-level repro are in the test suite.

title: fix(ci): rename reserved GraphQL variable in review leaderboard
body:
Code changes: +4 -4  
Tests: +5 -0  
Others: +0 -0

## Summary

Every run of the "Post trailing 7-day review stats" job has failed since #5750 merged, with:

```
Error: [@octokit/graphql] "query" cannot be used as variable name
```

`@octokit/graphql` reserves `query`, `method`, and `url` as option names, so passing `{ query, cursor }` as GraphQL variables throws before the request is sent. This renames the search variable to `searchQuery` in both the query document and the call site.

The test's fake `graphql` client now rejects those reserved names, so the workflow's "Test leaderboard calculation" step catches this class of mistake. Against main's script the new assertion fails with the same message; with the rename it passes.

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target` and checks out the default branch, so this fix only takes effect once merged. It cannot be verified by this PR's own leaderboard run. First observed on #5753.

## Tests

- `node --test .github/scripts/pr-review-leaderboard.test.mjs` — 4 pass
- Same command with main's script and the new assertion — 1 fail, confirming the guard reproduces the CI error

## Risks

- None beyond the rename. The fake client guard mirrors octokit's documented reserved names and does not affect production behaviour.

title: bug(inspector): merged PR failure keeps CI Failed timeline badge
body:
## Human report

In the **Review Prompt Audit** session, the Activity timeline showed **CI Failed** beside Working even though the session's current open PR had passing CI. The expected behavior is for the sidebar/inspector to reflect actionable CI on current open PRs, not a historical failure from a PR that has already merged.

Observed on macOS in the packaged AO desktop app on 2026-09-22.

## Agent-collected evidence

Collected read-only from the affected daemon, GitHub, and `~/.ao/data/ao.db` on 2026-09-22. Code was inspected at `28c68a08a39266760e58168c6f060114ea4bbf0a`.

- Open PR #5753 has eleven completed checks, all successful. AO's daemon reports its CI state as `passing`.
- PR #5754 is already merged. Its historical `Post trailing 7-day review stats` check failed before merge, and AO retains `ci_state=failing` for that merged PR.
- The daemon's SCM derivation correctly filters to open PRs through `openPRs()`.
- The inspector timeline's `scmTimelineStates()` independently iterates every `session.prs` entry and adds `ci_failed` whenever `pr.ci === "failing"`, without excluding `merged` or `closed` PRs.
- Therefore the visible red badge is sourced from merged PR #5754, not from current open PR #5753.

The screenshot supplied with the report is retained locally at `.ao/attachments/attachment-95f136075164d0dcec5afe827730589e.png`; it was not uploaded because the CLI issue API does not provide a safe local attachment upload path.

No exact duplicate was found in open or closed issue/PR searches.

title: feat(sidebar): give ad hoc agents their own Scratchpad section
body:
## What

Projectless ("ad hoc") agents were appended to the sidebar's project list as a
fake **Scratchpad** project, so adding one grew the project tree with a row that
is not a project — it can't be renamed, removed or reordered like one, and its
agents sat nested a level deeper than they belong.

They now render in their own **Scratchpad** section under Projects, with the same
header chrome as Projects and a `+` that opens a new ad hoc agent.

## Changes

- **Scratchpad is its own section.** The standalone workspace is filtered out of
  the project list and rendered by a new `ScratchpadSection` below it. Its agents
  are ordinary session rows, aligned with the project rows above them.
- **Both section headers collapse.** `Projects` and `Scratchpad` each toggle their
  own body; `Projects` was previously a static, non-collapsible label.
- **Each section's list is its own capped scroller**, not fit-content — a long
  list scrolls inside its section instead of pushing the section below it
  off-screen.
- **Each section starts at 10 rows** (was 12 for projects) with a `Show more` row
  beneath the scroller, *outside* it, so the cap can never hide its own release.
  `Show more` raises the cap and reveals the rest by scrolling.
- The session list's drag context moves into a shared `SessionReorderList`, so
  the Scratchpad list keeps drag-to-reorder without duplicating the DnD wiring.

## Notes

- Projects header stays in the fixed chrome above the scroll area, as
  `Sidebar.test.tsx` asserts ("only the project tree scrolls").
- `shell.showMoreAgents` added to all eight locale catalogs.
- The **Pinned** section is untouched — it keeps its fit-content body. Say the

## Testing

title: fix(updater): pick up nightly/hotfix builds within 15 min and surface API-discovered builds when the CDN check stalls
body:
## Problem

Two separate gaps kept published nightly/hotfix builds from reaching users:

1. The automatic re-check interval had been raised to 24h, so a session left open picked up a newly published nightly or hotfix build up to a day late. This is the regression reported in https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/5510.
2. On the nightly/feature channel the automatic check runs in two hops. First it hits api.github.com to list releases, verify the channel manifest asset exists, and point the feed at the matching release. That host answers reliably. Then electron-updater fetches the manifest yml, which 302-redirects to release-assets.githubusercontent.com, a separate CDN host. For users whose network reaches the GitHub API but not that CDN (HTTPS-inspecting AV or VPN, ISP/DNS blocking of githubusercontent, a dead anycast route, or MTU packet drops), that second hop stalls. The socket-inactivity timeout is 60s, and retryOnServerError only retries 5xx and EPIPE, never a hang, so the check takes one shot and gives up. These users never see an "update available" notification even though the API discovery already told us a newer build exists.

## Fix

Two independent changes:

**Re-check interval back to 15 minutes.** The periodic re-check was lowered from 24h to 15 min. A fresh check still runs on every launch, so this only governs sessions left open for a long stretch: a newly published nightly or hotfix is now picked up within minutes instead of after a day.

**Surface the API-discovered build when the CDN hop stalls.** During direct-prerelease feed setup we already fetch the release list from the API and know the newest completed prerelease tag and its notes. This records that discovery when the tag is strictly newer than the running version, and, in the automatic check's finally block, surfaces it as "available" if the electron-updater manifest fetch did not already settle to a more advanced state (available, downloading, preparing, downloaded). The user still gets a truthful "update available" notification when the CDN hop hangs.

No second checker, no new polling, and no new push channel. The CDN change reuses the result the existing check already produced. Both stay on the automatic path only, so the manual "check now" and remembered-update paths are untouched.

## Tests

Adds a test that stubs the API to return one nightly release with the platform manifest asset, forces autoUpdater.checkForUpdates to reject as if the manifest fetch timed out, and asserts the last status broadcast is "available" with the discovered version. Disabling the new call makes the test fail. The interval change updates the tests that pinned the 24h cadence to 15 min. Full auto-updater suite passes (189).
